verses.english: In the beginning of God’s creating the skies and the earth
verses.commentary:
According to TDRWFEROTMSOHK [Abbreviation for The Dynamic Read-Writable Free Encyclopedic Repository of the Modern State of Human Knowledge, hereafter abbreviated as “the Lord,” to save space.]

The word אלהים (Elhim) is a “defective spelling” of the word אלוהים (Elohim).

And if you look up that word, it says

The word אלוהים (Elohim) is from the plural of אלוה (Eloh) which means “god.”

And if you look around for some clarification, you'll find sentences like

This word is sometimes grammatically plural and sometimes singular.

And you may also stumble upon a sentence mentioning that particularly devout believers

Thus may prefer the term אלוקים (Elokim), so as not to abuse the name of God.

And so we're off to a pretty weird start

The abruptness of the reading at this point has led many commentators to posit a lacuna in the text;[1] still others have suggested it may be a haplography, or any of a number of other scholarly ways of saying something's missing.

Arguing against this, scholars have observed that the existing form preserves the poem's alternating A-T (aleph–tav) structure — the systematic use of the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet — without disruption, a consideration that weighs against the hypothesis of omission.

This has prompted a response from the first group of scholars that the original source text is not in fact composed in Hebrew, but in a notoriously difficult mixed orthography combining elements from a remarkably broad range of ancient and modern writing systems, perhaps in order to facilitate multilingual paranomasia.

According to this view, the work represents an ambitious, if incompletely understood, attempt to construct a system possessing all the syntactic, semantic, and orthographic flexibility conventionally attributed to Biblical Hebrew.

Though the field of Nameless Historical Studies (NHS) has recently undergone a revolution of sorts, both in the understanding of Nameless History (NH) and Nameless Script (NS), a systematic understanding of The Orthography (TO) in which the Original Text (OT) is written is not yet available.

At present, several distinguished contributors to NH/S have produced lengthy treatments of the problem.

These expositions are generally regarded as being no less difficult than the source material.

A smaller number have suffered nervous breakdowns.

Though the field has attracted much interest in recent years, only the most ambitious scholars can approach the OT on its own terms, in the original orthography.

A majority of such scholars simply have no alternative but to approach the text in translation.

HBL[Hevel, הבל]

Traditionally rendered “Abel” in English, the term literally means breath, vapor, mist, or something fleeting and insubstantial. It is the same word made famous by the book of Ecclesiastes. הבלים הבל” — “vanity of vanities,” or more literally, “vapor of vapors.” The traditional Ecclesiastical translation of “vanity” means not the modern sense of narcissism, but rather the sense of the term meaning “in vain.”

The name suggests something beautiful but short-lived: a puff of breath on a cold morning, a wisp of smoke, or a mist that disappears almost as soon as it appears. The irony is unmistakable. Hevel's life is as brief and fleeting as his name.

Genesis 4:7[]

One of the greatest misconceptions about Biblical Hebrew is the assumption that we understand it as well as Classical Greek or Latin. We do not. Hundreds of Hebrew words—and countless idioms, expressions, and passages—remain uncertain even to the world's leading scholars. Every translation must therefore make choices on the reader's behalf, sometimes explaining the uncertainty in a footnote, but more often leaving only the familiar refrain, “Meaning of Heb. uncertain.” Even when the meanings of Hebrew terms are well-known, it is often far from clear what an author was up to.

verses.original: וַיִּוָּלֵד לַחֲנוֹךְ אֶת עִירָד וְעִירָד יָלַד אֶת מְחוּיָאֵל וּמְחִויאֵל יָלַד אֶת מְתוּשָׁאֵל וּמְתוּשָׁאֵל יָלַד אֶת לָמֶךְ
verses.english: And Irad was born to Enoch, and Irad fathered Mehuya-el, and Mehuya-el fathered Metusha-el, and Metusha-el fathered Lamech.
verses.commentary:
Then Enoch has a kid and names it “city.”

Irad[עִירָד; ʿÎrāḏ] Cain's grandson and the son of Enoch (Gen. 4:18). The name is probably related to עִיר (ʿîr, “city”), though its etymology is uncertain.

City[עִיר; ʿîr] City, town, settlement. The standard Hebrew word for an inhabited, often fortified, urban center.

Then there are some people with the word “El” in their names.

Mehuja-el[מְחוּיָאֵל; Məḥûyāʾēl] Son of Irad. An early theophoric name containing אֵל (El). Its precise meaning is uncertain, with proposed translations including “struck by El” and “given life by El.”

Methusha-el[מְתוּשָׁאֵל; Məṯûšāʾēl] Son of Mehujael. Another early theophoric name containing אֵל. Its exact meaning is uncertain, though it is commonly understood as something like “man of El” or “one who belongs to El.”

Lots going on here.

El[אֵל; ʾēl] The name of the chief deity of the Canaanite pantheon, and also the generic Northwest Semitic word for “god.” Names containing אֵל were common throughout Canaan long before the worship of YHWH became dominant in Israel, and remained common in Israelite names such as Samuel, Ezekiel, Daniel, and especially Israel (“El strives” or “May El strive”).

Then there's this guy named LMK (Lamech).

Lamech[לֶמֶךְ; Lemeḵ] The meaning of his name is unknown; no convincing Hebrew or Northwest Semitic etymology has been identified.

Byblos[Greek: Βύβλος; also known as Jbail, Jebeil, Jbeil, Jubayl; Arabic جُبَيْل Jbeil, Jubayl] An ancient city in the Keserwan–Jbeil Governorate of Lebanon. The area is believed to have been first settled between 8800 and 7000 BC and continuously inhabited since 5000 BC. During its history, Byblos was part of numerous cultures including Canaanite, Egyptian, Phoenician, Assyrian, Persian, Hellenistic, Roman, Genoese, Mamluk, and Ottoman. Urbanisation is thought to have begun during the third millennium BC when it developed into a city, making it one of the oldest cities in the world, if not the oldest.

[5000] The Yahwist[J] The name traditionally given to the author or source whose stories characteristically use the divine name Yhwh from the beginning. J is associated with vivid, earthy narratives, anthropomorphic portrayals of God, and stories of family, sex, deception, and other timeless, universal human themes. Unlike the priestly sources, J places little emphasis on law, ritual, or moralizing, preferring to explore human nature through narrative. The J source also develops female characters more deeply than the other sources and appears not to have been a priest, but rather to have had some connection or affinity to the royal court of the Davidic monarchy.

J is commonly dated to around 922 B.C., making J the first and earliest author of the bible, apart from a handful of brief poems and songs. J is credited with writing most of the bible's best-known stories, including the Garden of Eden, Cain and Abel, Noah's Flood (with P), the Tower of Babel, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (with E and P), Joseph and his brothers (with E), baby Moses in the basket, the burning bush (with E), narrative sections of Numbers, and the death of Moses (with E, P, and D). Recent source analysis has shown J to have been additionally the probable author of much of Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, all of 2 Samuel, and the first two chapters of Kings.

Some scholars have argued that J was a woman. Some have argued J was not, in fact, a religious author, and that J's writing reflects one of the most subtle and well developed senses of humor in world literature, one rooted in irony, wordplay, and understatement that readers have been misunderstanding for nearly three thousand years.

No author in history has had a greater influence on world culture, religion, and literature, nor is any other author a close second.

J's back.

Ten is a bible number.You can figure out this one.

Forty is a bible number. No one knows why. Heb. “forty” (אַרְבָּעִים) is strikingly similar to “many” (רַבִּים): They are normally derived from distinct roots, רבע “four” and רבב “be many/great,” but the resemblance readily invites wordplay or folk association—especially where “forty” itself functions as a conventional large or round number.

verses.original: בִּשְׁנַת שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה לְחַיֵּי נֹחַ בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה נִבְקְעוּ כּל מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה וַאֲרֻבֹּת הַשָּׁמַיִם נִפְתָּחוּ׃
verses.english: In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, in the seventeenth day of the month, on this day all the fountains of the great deep were split open, and the apertures of the skies were opened.
verses.commentary: On February 17th it starts to rain. [Not really February. They had different months back then.]

tex.original: \hP{בִּשְׁנַת שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה לְחַיֵּי נֹחַ בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה נִבְקְעוּ כּל מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה וַאֲרֻבֹּת הַשָּׁמַיִם נִפְתָּחוּ׃}
tex.commentary:
On February 17th it starts to rain.\footnote{Not really February. They had different months back then.}

%	\footnote{
%		the fountains of the great deep … and the apertures of the skies were
%		opened. One must have a picture of the structure of the universe that is
%		described in Genesis 1 in order to comprehend the significance of the
%		destruction that is narrated in the flood story. The creation account
%		pictures a clear firmament or space holding back the waters that are
%		above the firmament and those that are below. Now the narrative reports
%		that “all the fountains of the great deep were split open, and the
%		apertures of the skies were opened.” The cosmic waters are able to spill
%		in from above and below, filling the habitable bubble, thus:
%	}

verses.original: וַיְהִי הַגֶּשֶׁם עַל הָאָרֶץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה׃
verses.english: And there was rain on the earth, forty days and forty nights.
verses.commentary: It rains for a bible number of days.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְהִי הַגֶּשֶׁם עַל הָאָרֶץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה׃}
tex.commentary: It rains for a bible number of days.

verses.original: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה בָּא נֹחַ וְשֵׁם וְחָם וָיֶפֶת בְּנֵי נֹחַ וְאֵשֶׁת נֹחַ וּשְׁלֹשֶׁת נְשֵׁי בָנָיו אִתָּם אֶל הַתֵּבָה׃
verses.english: In this very day Noah came, and Shem and Ham and Yaphet, Noah’s sons, and Noah’s wife and his sons’ three wives with them to the box,
verses.commentary: Family gets on boat.

tex.original: \hP{בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה בָּא נֹחַ וְשֵׁם וְחָם וָיֶפֶת בְּנֵי נֹחַ וְאֵשֶׁת נֹחַ וּשְׁלֹשֶׁת נְשֵׁי בָנָיו אִתָּם אֶל הַתֵּבָה׃}
tex.commentary:
Family gets on boat.
%	\footnote{
%		the ark. At the same time that the threat at the cosmic level is more
%		powerful than is usually pictured, the condition of the humans in the
%		story is more vulnerable. As commonly pictured in art, the “ark” that
%		bears the humans and animals through the floodwaters is a boat. This
%		would be a correct view of the vehicle in the Mesopotamian flood
%		account, now contained in one form in Tablet XI of the epic of
%		Gilgamesh. There the hero, Utnapishtim, takes his family, his
%		possessions, and the animals into a boat to escape a flood brought on by
%		the gods. The parallels to the biblical account are tantalizing:
%		Utnapishtim’s boat comes to rest on a mountaintop; he sends out three
%		birds, including a dove and a raven; and he builds an altar and offers a
%		sacrifice. A notable difference, however, is precisely that the biblical
%		flood hero, Noah, does not build a boat, but rather an ark. An ark is a
%		box. The measurements given for it in the text are rectangular, and
%		there is neither a keel nor a rudder nor a sail. The same applies to the
%		box in which the baby Moses is placed in Exod 2:3. Still, I must admit
%		that it is notable that the two objects called bh in the Hebrew Bible
%		both float on water. I have used the word “ark” here reluctantly because
%		it is now so familiar that readers would find any other word jarring.
%		Regardless of the word, though, the important fact is that, in such a
%		vessel, the humans and animals are utterly helpless, cast about in the
%		waters without any control over their fate. To appreciate the image that
%		this narrative sets before us, we must picture this helpless box of life
%		tossed about in a violent universe that is breaking at its seams.
%	}

come to Noah, and also to the boat.

Ok so God remembers Noah now. [He remembers everything in the boat too but I'm not typing all that.]

He apparently forgot between when he closed the door and now.

tex.commentary:
Ok so God remembers Noah now.%
	\footnote{
		He remembers everything in the boat too
		but I'm not typing all that.
	}

	He apparently forgot between when he closed the door and now.

	Then the water starts to go down.
%	\footnote{
%		God remembered. There is an old tradition that when the deity is called
%		God (’lîm) this refers to the deity’s aspect of being just, and that
%		when the deity is called YHWH it refers to the divine aspect of being
%		merciful. But in this verse the deity is being merciful but is still
%		called God. Rashi justifies this by saying that the standard of justice
%		is changed into the standard of compassion by means of the prayers of
%		virtuous people. That is a lovely interpretation, but it has no basis in
%		the text. Noah does not pray. (Noah never speaks in this text until
%		after the flood.) And, earlier, when the deity decides to destroy all
%		flesh, the name YHWH, which is supposed to stand for divine mercy, is
%		used (6:7). The fact is that this traditional distinction in the divine
%		names does not hold up through the biblical text. Rather, the
%		relationship between the justice and mercy of God is far more complex
%		than this.
%	}

Now YHWH's like “What smells good?”

He then sees what Noah's doing.

So YHWH says:

Note to self:

Stop trying to fix people with floods.

Humans just suck from birth.

verses.original: וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם וְחִתְּכֶם יִהְיֶה עַל כּל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ וְעַל כּל עוֹף הַשָּׁמָיִם בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּרְמֹשׂ הָאֲדָמָה וּבְכל דְּגֵי הַיָּם בְּיֶדְכֶם נִתָּנוּ׃
verses.english: And fear of you and dread of you will be on every living thing of the earth and on every bird of the skies, in every one that will creep on the earth and in all the fish of the sea. They are given into your hand.
verses.commentary: I made the animals scared of you. You can have them.

tex.original: \hP{וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם וְחִתְּכֶם יִהְיֶה עַל כּל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ וְעַל כּל עוֹף הַשָּׁמָיִם בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּרְמֹשׂ הָאֲדָמָה וּבְכל דְּגֵי הַיָּם בְּיֶדְכֶם נִתָּנוּ׃}

verses.english: Every creeping animal that is alive will be yours for food; I’ve given every one to you like a plant of vegetation,
verses.commentary:
You can eat all the animals.

They're like vegetables.

tex.commentary:
You can eat all the animals.
	
	They're like vegetables.

%	\footnote{
%		Every creeping animal. Elsewhere this term refers only to certain
%		animals that crawl on the ground, but here it is understood to refer to
%		all animals: “I’ve given one to you like a plant”—meaning that humans
%		are permitted to eat animals in addition to plants. Do humans eat
%		animals before this? Noah makes burnt offerings (lt) after the flood,
%		but that is a type of sacrifice that is not eaten. Abel brings a
%		different kind of offering (minh) to God, which is a type of sacrifice
%		that is understood later in the Torah to be eaten by humans. But, prior
%		to Genesis 9, all statements from the deity to humans concerning eating
%		refer only to plants (1:29; 2:16; 3:18). It is therefore commonly
%		understood that humans are not permitted to eat animals until after the
%		flood. Some say that God now permits it as a concession to human
%		appetites. I see no grounds in the text for this view. A more likely
%		explanation for the change in divine requirements is that humans have
%		saved all animal species by taking them in the ark. All animals now owe
%		their lives to humankind, and this may be why humans are now permitted
%		to take their lives for food.
%	}

If you kill people I'll kill you.

verses.english: “And I: here, I’m establishing my covenant with you and with your seed after you

tex.commentary:
I've decided to make a deal with your c\redacted{um}\eR{hildren}.

%	\footnote{
%		covenant. The flood event concludes with a contract between the deity
%		and humans: a covenant. The Noahic covenant is the first of four major
%		covenants that provide the structure in which nearly all of the Bible is
%		framed. (The exceptions, most notably the book of Job, are relatively
%		few.) The Noahic covenant promises the security of the cosmos. The
%		Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 15 and 17) promises the land to Abraham’s
%		descendants and makes YHWH their God. The Israelite (or Sinai, or
%		Mosaic) covenant (Exodus 20; 34; Deuteronomy 5; 7:12–15) promises
%		well-being in the promised land. And the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7;
%		Psalms 89; 132) promises kingship over Jerusalem and Judah to David and
%		his descendants.
%	}

verses.original: וְאֵת כּל נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר אִתְּכֶם בָּעוֹף בַּבְּהֵמָה וּבְכל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ אִתְּכֶם מִכֹּל יֹצְאֵי הַתֵּבָה לְכֹל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: and with every living being that is with you, of the birds, of the domestic animals, and of all the wild animals of the earth with you, from all those coming out of the box to every living thing of the earth.
verses.commentary: The deal is also with the animals.

tex.original: \hP{וְאֵת כּל נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר אִתְּכֶם בָּעוֹף בַּבְּהֵמָה וּבְכל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ אִתְּכֶם מִכֹּל יֹצְאֵי הַתֵּבָה לְכֹל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ׃}

verses.original: וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתְּכֶם וְלֹא יִכָּרֵת כּל בָּשָׂר עוֹד מִמֵּי הַמַּבּוּל וְלֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד מַבּוּל לְשַׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And I shall establish my covenant with you, and all flesh will not be cut off again by the floodwaters, and there will not be a flood again to destroy the earth.”
verses.commentary:
And also I've decided to make a deal with you.

And I won't do any more floods.

tex.original: \hP{וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתְּכֶם וְלֹא יִכָּרֵת כּל בָּשָׂר עוֹד מִמֵּי הַמַּבּוּל וְלֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד מַבּוּל לְשַׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
And also I've decided to make a deal with you.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים זֹאת אוֹת הַבְּרִית אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי נֹתֵן בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיכֶם וּבֵין כּל נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה אֲשֶׁר אִתְּכֶם לְדֹרֹת עוֹלָם׃
verses.english: And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant that I’m giving between me and you and every living being that is with you for eternal generations:
verses.commentary:
Every deal has a sign.

Sometimes the sign is a thing you have to do, like “circumcision” or “being good.”

This time the sign is a rainbow.

It's not entirely clear what constitutes a sign.

As long as rainbows are a thing, that's how you know the “No more floods” deal is still binding.

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים זֹאת אוֹת הַבְּרִית אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי נֹתֵן בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיכֶם וּבֵין כּל נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה אֲשֶׁר אִתְּכֶם לְדֹרֹת עוֹלָם׃}
tex.commentary:

verses.original: אֶת קַשְׁתִּי נָתַתִּי בֶּעָנָן וְהָיְתָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית בֵּינִי וּבֵין הָאָרֶץ׃

He lets Noah know where he put the rainbow.

Understandably, they were new.

Then he says it's the sign of the deal again.

verses.original: וְכוּשׁ יָלַד אֶת נִמְרֹד הוּא הֵחֵל לִהְיוֹת גִּבֹּר בָּאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And Cush fathered Nimrod. He began being a man of power in the earth.
verses.commentary:
Ok so Ethiopia gives birth to Nimrod.

In modern slang, the term Nimrod means idiot or moron.

This is understood to derive from a certain fictitious rabbit, common in the table of English speaking nations circa the 30th century A.D. [After David. Roughly the 20th century, C.E. (Common Era.)]

The transition from the term's original meaning of “mighty biblical hunter” to “incompetent idiot” arose from a chapter in the chronicles of the events of said rabbit in which he was engaged in a prolonged predator-prey style drama involving his pursuit by a rotund and, let us say, less than competent hunter.

Employing the timeless rhetorical device of sarcasm, the aforementioned rabbit refers to the less-than-mighty hunter as “Nimrod,” which the audience at the time, being native speakers of biblical English, would have understood to be the deployment of the above mentioned rhetorical device, namely sarcasm.

Subsequent generations, upon encountering the expression, had in the intervening years become less fluent in the bible and biblical minutiae, seeing as bible translations at the time were, to quote one contemporary scholar, “boring,” “pretentious” and “fit for burning.” [Lit. ראוי לשרפה in the original text, which, while referring to itself as “early biblical English,” in fact employs a rather infuriating mixed orthography that makes a translator rather long for a return to the simplicity of Babel.]

In summary, lacking knowledge of the bible, they thought Nimrod meant idiot. Not to prolong the already much too lengthy and borderline self-indulgent commentary on this verse, but in the interest of factual accuracy it bears pointing out that the responsible party for the redefinition of the aforementioned biblical term was in fact, not Bubs Gunny, nor Porpy Kig, but in fact, Daddy Fuck. (Editor's Note: The text appears to be corrupted here, and the surname of the individual in question has been lost.) Author's Note: Names of certain individuals have been changed in the interest of respecting the laws of biblical copyright in the early biblical English period.

verses.english: And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel and Erech and Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar.
verses.commentary:
At this point the table of nations gets extra interesting.

Remember the principle of “Sure these people are made up but they're actually also real non-fiction places”?

Ok so, at the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom were:

• Babel: That's Babylon.
• Erech: That's Uruk.
• Accad: That's Akkad.
• Calneh: Not a place. [Historical scholarship proposed candidate locations for the city of “Calneh”, but it is now considered most likely, in a suggestion going back to W.F. Albright (1944), that the word did not in origin refer to a city but has been corrupted from an expression meaning “all of them.”]
• Shinar: That's Sumer.

That's basically all the earliest cities.

In other words, these fake people are also a real actual history textbook.

The bible doesn't care about your genres.

verses.commentary:

• Hamathite: From Hamath, a major city on the Orontes River in central Syria. The name may mean “fortress” or “citadel.”

verses.commentary:
• Sidon: The northern end of Canaan, on the Mediterranean coast in modern Lebanon.
• Gerar: A Philistine city in the Negev, associated with Abraham and Isaac.
• Gaza: The southwestern corner of Canaan, on the Mediterranean coast.
• Sodom and Gomorrah: The infamous cities destroyed by God in Genesis 19.
• Admah and Zeboim: Two lesser-known cities destroyed alongside Sodom and Gomorrah.
• Lasha: Probably somewhere east or southeast of the Dead Sea, but its exact location has been lost.

verses.original: וַיְהִי בְּנסְעָם מִקֶּדֶם וַיִּמְצְאוּ בִקְעָה בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם׃
verses.english: And it was when they were traveling from the east: and they found a valley in the land of Shinar and lived there.
verses.commentary:
Ok so they come from out east back to Sumer and stay there.

Shinar is Sumer. Genesis itself locates unmistakably Sumerian cities in Shinar. Gen 10:10 says Nimrod’s kingdom began with Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), Akkad, and Calneh “in the land of Shinar.” Uruk is one of the defining Sumerian cities, Akkad is the capital/name-source of Akkad, and Babylon is in the same southern Mesopotamian plain. Whatever Shinar means etymologically, the author is pointing at Babylonia/Sumer-and-Akkad.

Y'know, where civilization started in real life.

So that's interesting.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמְרוּ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ הָבָה נִלְבְּנָה לְבֵנִים וְנִשְׂרְפָה לִשְׂרֵפָה וַתְּהִי לָהֶם הַלְּבֵנָה לְאָבֶן וְהַחֵמָר הָיָה לָהֶם לַחֹמֶר׃
verses.english: And they said to one another, “Come on, let’s make bricks and fire them.” And they had brick for stone, and they had bitumen for mortar.
verses.commentary:
Now the One People say to each other:

Hey. We can build, like, anything now.

[2]

Side note: Burnt bricks are hot technology at this point.

Cf. The prologue of Gilgamesh, where they brag about how good their bricks are, saying “Climb upon the wall of Uruk; walk along it, I say; regard the foundation terrace and examine the masonry: is it not burnt brick and good?” So fired bricks were something to brag about. I mean crappy mud-bricks had been around since forever,

r0.25

Jericho has some from like 9000-8000 BC, but they have this minor problem of turning back into mud when it rains, and leaving them out in the sun helps a bit, but nothing like just cooking the damn thing. So bricks cooked in ovens become a huge thing in southern Mesopotamian city building in the 3000-2000 BC era. They're almost as strong as rock, they don't become mud when it rains, and you don't have to have a friend with his own quarry. Changes everything. Everything is suddenly lego. I mean imagine you'd been making megalithic structures like Stonehenge all your life, dragging multi-ton chunks of mountain like 140 miles from Wales and then some lunatic starts manufacturing rocks at home by cooking dirt. So you can understand how the Babel people got excited. They could basically 3D print buildings now. Megalithic stuff gets all the credit, but dammit, bricks are cool. Ok, back to the story.

%	\footnote{
%		Go. Hebrew lek lk. Much has been made of the second word in this phrase,
%		lk, which means “for you.” No translation quite captures the sense of
%		the Hebrew (“Go you,” “Get you,” “Go for yourself”). The second element,
%		lk (or lkem), occasionally follows verbs in the Tanak. For example, in
%		Lev 26:1 we have l’ ta‘ lkem (you shall not make for yourselves; you
%		shall make you no …), and in Num 14:25 we have s‘ lkem (travel you;
%		travel for yourselves). I believe it is better to use no English term
%		than to use any of the possible equivalents, all of which are clumsy
%		English and do not convey the Hebrew. Footnote 12:1. your land, your
%		birthplace. But he is in Haran. He has already left Ur of the Chaldeans,
%		which was his land and birthplace. Rashi tries to solve the problem by
%		saying that this means “Go even farther from your land and birthplace.”
%		Ibn Ezra tries to solve it by saying that it means “God had said [i.e.,
%		earlier, back in Ur], ‘Go from your land …’” But these stretch the
%		meaning of the Hebrew beyond what is possible. And besides, Abraham
%		later sends his servant to get a wife for Isaac, saying, “Go to my land
%		and my birthplace” (24:4), and the servant goes to Haran (“to Aram
%		Naharaim, to the city of Nahor,” 24:10; which is identified as Haran,
%		27:43). On these grounds Ramban rejects Rashi’s and Ibn Ezra’s
%		solutions. Ramban’s own solution, though, falls short as well, requiring
%		that Abraham’s land and birthplace are Haran, not Ur. This is further
%		complicated by the fact that the Abrahamic covenant begins with God
%		saying to Abraham, “I brought you out of Ur …” (15:7). The truth is that
%		this is a case in which the contradiction is a result of the fact that
%		the Torah was composed from several sources. In this case, one of its
%		sources had Abraham coming from Ur, and another had him coming from
%		Haran. The aim of this commentary is to deal with the Torah in its
%		final, combined form and not to analyze its sources. (I have done that
%		elsewhere: in Who Wrote the Bible? and The Hidden Book in the Bible.)
%		Usually, the combination of sources has produced a richer, more complex
%		story in the Torah. But this passage is one of a few instances in which
%		the combination has produced an irreconcilable contradiction. In such
%		cases it is better to acknowledge the problem than to stretch to make
%		forced interpretations. Footnote 12:1. your land, your birthplace, and
%		your father’s house. But if he has left his land, then of course he has
%		left his birthplace and his father’s house. This is geographically
%		backwards. Therefore, the point of this order is not geographical. It is
%		emotional. The three steps are arranged in ascending order of difficulty
%		for Abraham. It is hard to leave one’s land, harder if it is where one
%		was born, and harder still to leave one’s family. And where is he to go?
%		To “the land that I’ll show you.” That is, he must leave his homeland
%		without knowing for what he is giving it up. The wording seems designed
%		to make it hard for Abraham. This pattern of testing will be repeated
%		when he is commanded to sacrifice Isaac, thus: “Take your son, your only
%		one, whom you love, Isaac.” And where is he to sacrifice him? “On one of
%		the mountains that I’ll say to you.” (See the comment on 22:2.)
%	}

%	\footnote{
%		all the families of the earth will be blessed through you. The Tanak is
%		so focused on the people of Israel that one can underestimate the
%		overwhelming significance of its opening section. The first eleven
%		chapters (Parashat Bereshit and Parashat Noah) are about the
%		relationship between God and the entire human community. That
%		relationship does not go well, and after ten generations the deity
%		decides to destroy the mass and start over with a single virtuous man’s
%		family. But it turns out that choosing a virtuous individual does not
%		guarantee that this individual’s descendants will be virtuous as well.
%		Another ten generations pass, and humans in general are not a
%		planet-full of Noahs. So once again the focus narrows to a single
%		virtuous person, Abraham. We must keep in mind what has happened up to
%		this point when we read this, or else we will lose the significance of
%		what is happening here. Wiping out everyone but a virtuous person did
%		not work. So God leaves the species alive but chooses an individual who
%		will produce a family that will ultimately bring blessing to all the
%		families of the earth. To make sure we get it, it is the final point of
%		God’s first revelation to Abraham: Go to the land I’ll show you. I’ll
%		make you a big nation. I’ll bless you. “And all the families of the
%		earth will be blessed through you” (Gen 12:3). To make sure we do not
%		forget it, it is repeated four times—and always in crucial moments of
%		revelation: during the appearance of the three visitors to Abraham (Gen
%		18:17–18); in the blessing following the near-sacrifice of Isaac
%		(22:16–18); in God’s first appearance to Isaac (26:2–4); and in Jacob’s
%		first encounter with God in the dream of the ladder at Beth-El
%		(28:10–14). It is important. In some way, at some time, the result of
%		the divine choice of Abraham is supposed to be some good for all
%		humankind. We are never told what this good is supposed to be. Is it
%		that Abraham’s descendants are supposed to bring blessing by being “a
%		light to the nations”—setting an example, showing how a community can
%		live: caring for one another, not cheating one another, not enslaving
%		one another, not lending to each other for profit, and so on and on? Or
%		is it that they are to bring blessing by doing things that benefit the
%		species: inventions, cures, literature, music, learning? It does not
%		say. But at minimum it must mean that the people of Israel do not live
%		alone or apart. Their destiny—our destiny—whatever it is, must be bound
%		up in the destiny of all humankind. This adds a dimension, an additional
%		layer of significance, to every story that will follow in the Torah.
%		When Abraham travels to Canaan, we might imagine it from a God’s-eye
%		view above the earth: the tiny movement of a man and his family along
%		the globe is a first step in a process that is to bring benefit for all
%		the earth. When Abraham travels to Egypt, this is the first in a series
%		of encounters that he and his descendants will have with the peoples of
%		the world. When he and Lot are forced to part, this is a step in
%		distinguishing his destiny from that of the families of his brothers
%		Haran and Nahor, though he and his descendants will continue to interact
%		with them. When he joins in a battle among kings in order to rescue Lot
%		(Genesis 14), he is being drawn into world events, and it is another
%		first step, an anticipation of all the times that his descendants, the
%		people of Israel, will be drawn into contact and interaction with
%		nations. When Abraham covenants with God (Genesis 15 and 17) the
%		ceremony includes specific references to Ur of the Chaldees, the land
%		from which Abraham has come; to Egypt, the land where his descendants
%		will be enslaved; and to ten peoples of the land that Abraham is
%		promised. It also includes the announcement of his coming son Isaac, the
%		key to the fulfillment of the destiny to be a blessing to all the
%		families of the earth—as will be confirmed explicitly following the
%		Aqedah. And in between the two chapters concerning the Abrahamic
%		covenant comes the story of the birth of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whose
%		descendants, the Ishmaelites, will be among Israel’s related neighbors.
%		All of these episodes are conveying the formative stages of a
%		development that begins with that narrowing of attention to Abraham. The
%		interpretive point is that we must understand every section of the Torah
%		with awareness of what has preceded it and what will come after it. The
%		social and moral point is that Abraham’s descendants are not to live by
%		themselves or only for themselves. Whether dealing with non-Jews who
%		live in Israel or dealing with non-Jews who are their neighbors in the
%		countries in which they reside, the Jews are a community that connects
%		its birth with a prediction (?), a promise (?), an obligation (?), a
%		destiny (?) to be a blessing to them all. Footnote 12:3. will be blessed
%		through you. Rashi takes the plain meaning of this phrase to mean that
%		non-Israelites will bless their children with words such as “May you be
%		like Abraham.” His proof for this reading is the wording of Jacob’s
%		blessing of his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh: “Israel will bless with
%		you, saying: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh’” (Gen 48:20).
%		But that passage uses an active form of the verb (the Piel), whereas all
%		the occurrences of this phrase in terms of the nations being blessed use
%		forms that are passive or reflexive (Niphal and Hitpael), which is a
%		different matter. If we take the meaning as passive, then it is as I
%		have translated it here: “the earth’s families will be blessed through
%		you.” If we take it as reflexive, then it can mean “they will bless
%		themselves through you,” which is Rashi’s understanding; but a reflexive
%		can also mean “they will get blessing through you.” Interpreters are
%		split on this. I believe that context settles the question. The issue in
%		the story until now has been the course of relations between God and all
%		the families of the earth. Now God makes a special bond with Abraham’s
%		family and lets him know that this is for the eventual benefit of all
%		families. (See the preceding comment.)
%	}

verses.original: וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ וַיֵּרֶד אַבְרָם מִצְרַיְמָה לָגוּר שָׁם כִּי כָבֵד הָרָעָב בָּאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to reside there because the famine was heavy in the land.
verses.commentary: There's no food, so he goes to Egypt, because there's no food.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ וַיֵּרֶד אַבְרָם מִצְרַיְמָה לָגוּר שָׁם כִּי כָבֵד הָרָעָב בָּאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary: There's no food, so he goes to Egypt, because there's no food.

verses.original: וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר הִקְרִיב לָבוֹא מִצְרָיְמָה וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ הִנֵּה נָא יָדַעְתִּי כִּי אִשָּׁה יְפַת מַרְאֶה אָתְּ׃
verses.english: And it was when he was close to coming to Egypt: and he said to Sarai, his wife, “Here, I know that you’re a beautiful woman.
verses.commentary:
Ok so when he was close to coming

To Egypt, he says to his wife,

“Look, you're hot.”

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר הִקְרִיב לָבוֹא מִצְרָיְמָה וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ הִנֵּה נָא יָדַעְתִּי כִּי אִשָּׁה יְפַת מַרְאֶה אָתְּ׃}
tex.english:
\eJ{
		And it was when he was close to coming to Egypt: and he
		said to Sarai, his wife, “Here, I know that you’re a
		beautiful woman.
	}
%	\footnote{12:11–13. Here, I know. Abraham’s words
%		to Sarah contain the first two occurrences of the Hebrew
%		word na’. It is sometimes rendered “now” in English and
%		sometimes rendered “please.” But neither is quite right.
%		It is an untranslatable particle that is a sign of polite
%		speech. Its most striking occurrence is in God’s words to
%		Abraham in the story of the binding of Isaac: “Take na’
%		your son … and offer him” (Gen 22:2). I do not translate
%		it with any English word, because it is closer to the
%		Hebrew to use no word than to use such words as “please”
%		or “now.”
%	}
tex.commentary:
Ok so when he was close to coming
	
	To Egypt, he says to his wife,
	
	``Look, you're hot.''

verses.original: וְהָיָה כִּי יִרְאוּ אֹתָךְ הַמִּצְרִים וְאָמְרוּ אִשְׁתּוֹ זֹאת וְהָרְגוּ אֹתִי וְאֹתָךְ יְחַיּוּ׃
verses.english: And it will be when the Egyptians see you that they’ll say, ‘This is his wife,’ and they’ll kill me and keep you alive.
verses.commentary: “The Egyptians are gonna take one look at you and kill me and keep you alive for, well, reasons.”

tex.original: \hJ{וְהָיָה כִּי יִרְאוּ אֹתָךְ הַמִּצְרִים וְאָמְרוּ אִשְׁתּוֹ זֹאת וְהָרְגוּ אֹתִי וְאֹתָךְ יְחַיּוּ׃}
tex.commentary: ``The Egyptians are gonna take one look at you and kill me and keep you alive for, well, reasons.''

verses.original: אִמְרִי נָא אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ לְמַעַן יִיטַב לִי בַעֲבוּרֵךְ וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ׃
verses.english: Say you’re my sister so it will be good for me on your account and I’ll stay alive because of you.”
verses.commentary:
Say you're my sister.

It'll be good for me.

And sure it won't exactly be good for—

Scratch that.

I'll stay alive because of you.

tex.original: \hJ{אִמְרִי נָא אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ לְמַעַן יִיטַב לִי בַעֲבוּרֵךְ וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ׃}
tex.commentary:
Say you're my sister.
	
	It'll be good for me.
	
	And sure it won't exactly be good for---
	
	Scratch that.
	
	I'll stay alive because of you.
%	\footnote{
%		Say you’re my sister … and I’ll stay alive. All commentators have
%		agonized over this. Abraham constructs a lie and puts Sarah in a
%		compromising position. This may mean that he thinks that he simply has
%		no real choice: it is either lie or die. Or it may convey that
%		Abraham—like other biblical heroes—is not perfect. We cannot know. In
%		either of these cases, he cannot be faulted for choosing to put Sarah in
%		a compromising position, because, in his understanding, Sarah would be
%		taken either way. The concern is that, without the lie, they would also
%		kill him. (In fact he turns out to be wrong. There is no evidence in the
%		Bible that the Egyptians or anyone else ever did what Abraham fears they
%		would do. Here and in two other cases in which Abraham and his son Isaac
%		claim that their wives are their sisters, the Egyptian and Philistine
%		kings send the couple away when they find out that she is his wife.)
%		Footnote 12:13. my sister. For a while it was common to cite tablets
%		from Nuzi as evidence that there was a Near Eastern practice of adopting
%		one’s wife as a sister. But the Nuzi case involved a single family, and
%		scholars recently have questioned whether it is justified to make so
%		much of it. Abraham’s actions here (and in Genesis 20; and Isaac’s
%		actions in Genesis 26) are treated as an unusual case. They require no
%		Near Eastern legal precedent.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְהִי כְּבוֹא אַבְרָם מִצְרָיְמָה וַיִּרְאוּ הַמִּצְרִים אֶת הָאִשָּׁה כִּי יָפָה הִוא מְאֹד׃
verses.english: And it was as Abram came to Egypt, and the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful.
verses.commentary: So that happens.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְהִי כְּבוֹא אַבְרָם מִצְרָיְמָה וַיִּרְאוּ הַמִּצְרִים אֶת הָאִשָּׁה כִּי יָפָה הִוא מְאֹד׃}

verses.original: וַיִּרְאוּ אֹתָהּ שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה וַיְהַלְלוּ אֹתָהּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה וַתֻּקַּח הָאִשָּׁה בֵּית פַּרְעֹה׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh’s officers saw her and praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken to Pharaoh’s house.
verses.commentary:
Abe's plan works.

The king sees his hot wife and takes her into his place.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיִּרְאוּ אֹתָהּ שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה וַיְהַלְלוּ אֹתָהּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה וַתֻּקַּח הָאִשָּׁה בֵּית פַּרְעֹה׃}
tex.commentary:
Abe's plan works.
	
	The king sees his hot wife and takes her into his place.

verses.original: וּלְאַבְרָם הֵיטִיב בַּעֲבוּרָהּ וַיְהִי לוֹ צֹאן וּבָקָר וַחֲמֹרִים וַעֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחֹת וַאֲתֹנֹת וּגְמַלִּים׃
verses.english: And he was good to Abram on her account, and he had a flock and oxen and he-asses and servants and maids and she-asses and camels.
verses.commentary:
He's really nice to Abe because of her.

He gives him lots of stuff.

Servants and maids.

He-asses and She-asses.

Also animals.

tex.original: \hJ{וּלְאַבְרָם הֵיטִיב בַּעֲבוּרָהּ וַיְהִי לוֹ צֹאן וּבָקָר וַחֲמֹרִים וַעֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחֹת וַאֲתֹנֹת וּגְמַלִּים׃}
tex.commentary:
He's really nice to Abe because of her.
	
	He gives him lots of stuff.

	Servants and maids.

	He-asses and She-asses.

	Also animals.

verses.original: וַיְנַגַּע יְהֹוָה אֶת פַּרְעֹה נְגָעִים גְּדֹלִים וְאֶת בֵּיתוֹ עַל דְּבַר שָׂרַי אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם׃
verses.english: And YHWH plagued Pharaoh and his house, big plagues, over the matter of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
verses.commentary:
YHWH, seemingly unaware of the finer points of moral philosophy, gives Pharaoh some plagues for being with Abe's wife.

Unacceptable, Pharaoh.

She was his wife.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְנַגַּע יְהֹוָה אֶת פַּרְעֹה נְגָעִים גְּדֹלִים וְאֶת בֵּיתוֹ עַל דְּבַר שָׂרַי אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם׃}
tex.commentary:
YHWH, seemingly unaware of the finer points of moral philosophy, gives Pharaoh some plagues for being with Abe's wife.

	Unacceptable, Pharaoh.

	She was his wife.

verses.english: And Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this you’ve done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?

So Pharaoh's like:

verses.original: לָמָה אָמַרְתָּ אֲחֹתִי הִוא וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה וְעַתָּה הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ קַח וָלֵךְ׃
verses.english: Why did you say, ‘She’s my sister,’ so I took her for a wife for myself! And now, here’s your wife. Take her and go.”
verses.commentary: I never would have... take your wife and go.

tex.original: \hJ{לָמָה אָמַרְתָּ אֲחֹתִי הִוא וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה וְעַתָּה הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ קַח וָלֵךְ׃}
tex.commentary: I never would have... take your wife and go.

verses.original: וַיְצַו עָלָיו פַּרְעֹה אֲנָשִׁים וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ אֹתוֹ וְאֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאֶת כּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh commanded people over him, and they let him and his wife and all he had go.
verses.commentary: And they do.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְצַו עָלָיו פַּרְעֹה אֲנָשִׁים וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ אֹתוֹ וְאֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאֶת כּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם הוּא וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְכל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ וְלוֹט עִמּוֹ הַנֶּגְבָּה׃
verses.english: And Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all he had and Lot with him, to the Negeb.
verses.commentary: So they leave Egypt and go back to Dry Place.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיַּעַל אַבְרָם מִמִּצְרַיִם הוּא וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְכל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ וְלוֹט עִמּוֹ הַנֶּגְבָּה׃}
tex.commentary:
So they leave Egypt and go back to Dry Place.
%	\footnote{
%		went up from Egypt … to the Negeb. Abraham’s movements prefigure the
%		future fate of the Israelites. As he returns from Egypt, going up into
%		the Negeb, so the Israelites will return from Egypt, and Moses will send
%		the first Israelites (the spies) to reenter the land with the words “Go
%		up there in the Negeb” (Num 13:17). (See the next comment.)
%	}

verses.original: וְאַבְרָם כָּבֵד מְאֹד בַּמִּקְנֶה בַּכֶּסֶף וּבַזָּהָב׃
verses.english: And Abram was very heavy with livestock and silver and gold.
verses.commentary: The weight of Abram's cargo is a silent comment that entrapment pays handsomely.

tex.original: \hJ{וְאַבְרָם כָּבֵד מְאֹד בַּמִּקְנֶה בַּכֶּסֶף וּבַזָּהָב׃}
tex.commentary: The weight of Abram's cargo is a silent comment that entrapment pays handsomely.

verses.original: וַיֵּלֶךְ לְמַסָּעָיו מִנֶּגֶב וְעַד בֵּית אֵל עַד הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר הָיָה שָׁם אהֳלֹה בַּתְּחִלָּה בֵּין בֵּית אֵל וּבֵין הָעָי׃
verses.english: And he went on his travels from the Negeb as far as Beth-El, as far as the place where his tent was at the start, between Beth-El and Ai,
verses.commentary:
He goes back to the place between House of God and Heap of Ruins.

Apparently he left his tent.

It's still there.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֵּלֶךְ לְמַסָּעָיו מִנֶּגֶב וְעַד בֵּית אֵל עַד הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר הָיָה שָׁם אהֳלֹה בַּתְּחִלָּה בֵּין בֵּית אֵל וּבֵין הָעָי׃}
tex.commentary:
He goes back to the place between House of God and Heap of Ruins.
	
	Apparently he left his tent.
	
	It's still there.
%	\footnote{
%		he went on his travels. This expression continues the prefiguring of the
%		fate of Abraham’s descendants, who went “on their travels” when they
%		left Egypt (Exod 17:1; Num 10:12).
%	}

verses.original: אֶל מְקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה שָׁם בָּרִאשֹׁנָה וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם אַבְרָם בְּשֵׁם יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: to the place of the altar that he had made there at the beginning. And Abram invoked the name YHWH there.
verses.commentary: He goes back to the altar he built and says YHWH again.

tex.original: \hJ{אֶל מְקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה שָׁם בָּרִאשֹׁנָה וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם אַבְרָם בְּשֵׁם יְהֹוָה׃}
tex.commentary: He goes back to the altar he built and says YHWH again.

verses.original: וְגַם לְלוֹט הַהֹלֵךְ אֶת אַבְרָם הָיָה צֹאן וּבָקָר וְאֹהָלִים׃
verses.english: And Lot, who was going with Abram, also had a flock and oxen and tents.
verses.commentary: His nephew Lot got a lot of stuff too.

tex.original: \hJ{וְגַם לְלוֹט הַהֹלֵךְ אֶת אַבְרָם הָיָה צֹאן וּבָקָר וְאֹהָלִים׃}
tex.commentary: His nephew Lot got a lot of stuff too.

verses.original: וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו׃
verses.english: And the land did not suffice them to live together, because their property was great, and they were not able to live together.
verses.commentary:
They look around in the wilderness and say to each other,

“This town's not big enough for the both of us.”

They got a Lot of stuff in Egypt.

tex.original: \hP{וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו׃}
tex.commentary:
They look around in the wilderness and say to each other,
	
	``This town's not big enough for the both of us.''
	
	They got a \textsc{Lot} of stuff in Egypt.

verses.original: וַיְהִי רִיב בֵּין רֹעֵי מִקְנֵה אַבְרָם וּבֵין רֹעֵי מִקְנֵה לוֹט וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי אָז יֹשֵׁב בָּאָרֶץ׃

So were the Perizzites, whose name means either “villagers” or “dwellers in the open country,” terms which I understood to be opposites in life before now.

	terms which I understood to be opposites in life before now.

verses.original: וַיִּבְחַר לוֹ לוֹט אֵת כּל כִּכַּר הַיַּרְדֵּן וַיִּסַּע לוֹט מִקֶּדֶם וַיִּפָּרְדוּ אִישׁ מֵעַל אָחִיו׃
verses.english: And Lot chose all the plain of the Jordan for himself, and Lot traveled east. And they separated, each from his brother.
verses.commentary:
Lot goes East.

And the uncle and nephew each separate from his brother.

Which is each other.

Don't overthink it. Fictive kin terms are a common thing in the ancient near East, the narrator calls Lot Abram's “brother” again in 14:14-16, and we have no textual evidence of any incest ever having occurred in this family at any point, not even in chapters 19 and 20.

verses.english: And the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah and the king of Admah and the king of Zeboiim and the king of Bela (that is Zoar) went out and aligned with them for war in the Siddim Valley
verses.commentary: Qere Ketiv.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם וּמֶלֶךְ עֲמֹרָה וּמֶלֶךְ אַדְמָה וּמֶלֶךְ (צביים) [צְבוֹיִם] וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע הִוא צֹעַר וַיַּעַרְכוּ אִתָּם מִלְחָמָה בְּעֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים׃}

verses.original: אֵת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם וְאַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר וְאַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת הַחֲמִשָּׁה׃
verses.english: with Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goiim, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Ellasar—four kings with five.

tex.original: \hOther{אֵת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם וְאַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר וְאַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת הַחֲמִשָּׁה׃}

verses.original: וְעֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים בֶּאֱרֹת בֶּאֱרֹת חֵמָר וַיָּנֻסוּ מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וַיִּפְּלוּ שָׁמָּה וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים הֶרָה נָּסוּ׃
verses.english: And Siddim Valley was pits, pits of bitumen, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and they fell there; and those who were left fled to the mountain.

tex.original: \hOther{וְעֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים בֶּאֱרֹת בֶּאֱרֹת חֵמָר וַיָּנֻסוּ מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וַיִּפְּלוּ שָׁמָּה וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים הֶרָה נָּסוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת כּל רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וְאֶת כּל אכְלָם וַיֵּלֵכוּ׃
verses.english: And they took all the property of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and they went.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת כּל רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וְאֶת כּל אכְלָם וַיֵּלֵכוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת לוֹט וְאֶת רְכֻשׁוֹ בֶּן אֲחִי אַבְרָם וַיֵּלֵכוּ וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב בִּסְדֹם׃
verses.english: And they took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, and his property when they went. And he had been living in Sodom.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת לוֹט וְאֶת רְכֻשׁוֹ בֶּן אֲחִי אַבְרָם וַיֵּלֵכוּ וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב בִּסְדֹם׃}

verses.original: וַיָּבֹא הַפָּלִיט וַיַּגֵּד לְאַבְרָם הָעִבְרִי וְהוּא שֹׁכֵן בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא הָאֱמֹרִי אֲחִי אֶשְׁכֹּל וַאֲחִי עָנֵר וְהֵם בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית אַבְרָם׃
verses.english: And an escapee came and told Abram the Hebrew, and he was tenting among the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; and they were covenant partners of Abram.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיָּבֹא הַפָּלִיט וַיַּגֵּד לְאַבְרָם הָעִבְרִי וְהוּא שֹׁכֵן בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא הָאֱמֹרִי אֲחִי אֶשְׁכֹּל וַאֲחִי עָנֵר וְהֵם בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית אַבְרָם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		the Hebrew. This is an unusual use of the word “Hebrew.” Elsewhere in
%		biblical stories it is used to identify Israelites only when one is
%		speaking among foreigners. It is not the standard term for the people,
%		which is rather “Israelite” at first and “Jew” later. Perhaps it is used
%		here because there are not yet any other Israelites around, and Abraham
%		himself is the foreigner. (Regarding the term “Hebrew slave,” see the
%		comment on Exod 21:2.)
%	}

verses.original: וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם כִּי נִשְׁבָּה אָחִיו וַיָּרֶק אֶת חֲנִיכָיו יְלִידֵי בֵיתוֹ שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַיִּרְדֹּף עַד דָּן׃
verses.english: And Abram heard that his brother had been taken prisoner, and he had his trained men, born in his house, unsheathe: three hundred eighteen. And he pursued as far as Dan.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם כִּי נִשְׁבָּה אָחִיו וַיָּרֶק אֶת חֲנִיכָיו יְלִידֵי בֵיתוֹ שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַיִּרְדֹּף עַד דָּן׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּחָלֵק עֲלֵיהֶם לַיְלָה הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו וַיַּכֵּם וַיִּרְדְּפֵם עַד חוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר מִשְּׂמֹאל לְדַמָּשֶׂק׃
verses.english: And he divided against them by night, he and his servants, and he struck them and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is at the left of Damascus.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֵּחָלֵק עֲלֵיהֶם לַיְלָה הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו וַיַּכֵּם וַיִּרְדְּפֵם עַד חוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר מִשְּׂמֹאל לְדַמָּשֶׂק׃}

verses.original: וַיָּשֶׁב אֵת כּל הָרְכֻשׁ וְגַם אֶת לוֹט אָחִיו וּרְכֻשׁוֹ הֵשִׁיב וְגַם אֶת הַנָּשִׁים וְאֶת הָעָם׃
verses.english: And he brought back all the property, and he also brought back Lot, his brother, and his property, and also the women and the people.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיָּשֶׁב אֵת כּל הָרְכֻשׁ וְגַם אֶת לוֹט אָחִיו וּרְכֻשׁוֹ הֵשִׁיב וְגַם אֶת הַנָּשִׁים וְאֶת הָעָם׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם לִקְרָאתוֹ אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ מֵהַכּוֹת אֶת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר וְאֶת הַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ אֶל עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה הוּא עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ׃
verses.english: And the king of Sodom came out to him after he came back from striking Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him at the Shaveh Valley. (That is the valley of the king.)

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם לִקְרָאתוֹ אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ מֵהַכּוֹת אֶת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר וְאֶת הַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ אֶל עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה הוּא עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ׃}

verses.original: וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן׃
verses.english: And Melchizedek, king of Salem, had brought out bread and wine. And he was a priest of El the Highest.

tex.original: \hOther{וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		the Highest. Hebrew ‘elyn. This is how God is known at the end of the
%		Torah also (Deut 32:8). There (and in Ps 82:6) this is the epithet that
%		is used for God in connection with the formation of the nations of the
%		earth. That makes it notable that here the priest who is associated with
%		El the Highest is not from Abraham’s family but from another group.
%		Abraham is not pictured as the only worshiper of this God on earth.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְבָרְכֵהוּ וַיֹּאמַר בָּרוּךְ אַבְרָם לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And he blessed him and said, “Blessed is Abram to El the Highest, creator of skies and earth.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיְבָרְכֵהוּ וַיֹּאמַר בָּרוּךְ אַבְרָם לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃}

verses.original: וּבָרוּךְ אֵל עֶלְיוֹן אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן צָרֶיךָ בְּיָדֶךָ וַיִּתֶּן לוֹ מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל׃
verses.english: And blessed is El the Highest, who delivered your foes into your hand.” And he gave him a tithe from everything.

tex.original: \hOther{וּבָרוּךְ אֵל עֶלְיוֹן אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן צָרֶיךָ בְּיָדֶךָ וַיִּתֶּן לוֹ מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם אֶל אַבְרָם תֶּן לִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְהָרְכֻשׁ קַח לָךְ׃
verses.english: And the king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give the persons to me, and take the property for you.”

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֹּאמֶר מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם אֶל אַבְרָם תֶּן לִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְהָרְכֻשׁ קַח לָךְ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם הֲרִמֹתִי יָדִי אֶל יְהֹוָה אֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I’ve lifted my hand to YHWH, El the Highest, creator of skies and earth,

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם הֲרִמֹתִי יָדִי אֶל יְהֹוָה אֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃}

verses.original: אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל וְאִם אֶקַּח מִכּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ וְלֹא תֹאמַר אֲנִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי אֶת אַבְרָם׃
verses.english: that, from a thread to a shoelace, I won’t take anything that is yours, so you won’t say, ‘I made Abram rich.’

tex.original: \hOther{אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל וְאִם אֶקַּח מִכּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ וְלֹא תֹאמַר אֲנִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי אֶת אַבְרָם׃}

verses.original: בִּלְעָדַי רַק אֲשֶׁר אָכְלוּ הַנְּעָרִים וְחֵלֶק הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר הָלְכוּ אִתִּי עָנֵר אֶשְׁכֹּל וּמַמְרֵא הֵם יִקְחוּ חֶלְקָם׃
verses.english: Except only what the boys have eaten and the share of the people who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. They shall take their share.”

tex.original: \hOther{בִּלְעָדַי רַק אֲשֶׁר אָכְלוּ הַנְּעָרִים וְחֵלֶק הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר הָלְכוּ אִתִּי עָנֵר אֶשְׁכֹּל וּמַמְרֵא הֵם יִקְחוּ חֶלְקָם׃}

verses.original: וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם׃
verses.english: And it was in the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goiim.
verses.commentary:
Regnal Year: unspecified.

Theater: Jordan Valley.

Eastern Coalition: Amraphel of Shinar; Arioch of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer of Elam; Tidal of Goiim.

tex.original:
\hOther{וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר
        כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם׃}

verses.original: עָשׂוּ מִלְחָמָה אֶת בֶּרַע מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם וְאֶת בִּרְשַׁע מֶלֶךְ עֲמֹרָה שִׁנְאָב מֶלֶךְ אַדְמָה וְשֶׁמְאֵבֶר מֶלֶךְ (צביים) [צְבוֹיִם] וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע הִיא צֹעַר׃
verses.english: They made war with Bera, king of Sodom, and Birsha, king of Gomorrah, Shinab, king of Admah, and Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela. (That is Zoar.)
verses.commentary: Opposing Coalition: Bera of Sodom; Birsha of Gomorrah; Shinab of Admah; Shemeber of Zeboiim; king of Bela (modern designation: Zoar). Hostilities commenced between the two coalitions.

tex.original:
\hOther{עָשׂוּ מִלְחָמָה אֶת בֶּרַע מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם
        וְאֶת בִּרְשַׁע מֶלֶךְ עֲמֹרָה שִׁנְאָב מֶלֶךְ אַדְמָה
        וְשֶׁמְאֵבֶר מֶלֶךְ (צביים) [צְבוֹיִם]
        וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע הִיא צֹעַר׃}

verses.original: כּל אֵלֶּה חָבְרוּ אֶל עֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח׃
verses.english: All these were allied at the Siddim Valley. (That is the Dead Sea.)
verses.commentary: Assembly Point: Valley of Siddim (modern designation: Dead Sea). The five western kings concentrated their forces there.

tex.original: \hOther{כּל אֵלֶּה חָבְרוּ אֶל עֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח׃}
tex.english: \eOther{All these were allied at the Siddim Valley. (That is the Dead Sea.)}
tex.commentary:
\aC{\textsc{Assembly Point}: Valley of Siddim (modern designation: Dead Sea). The
        five western kings concentrated their forces there.}

verses.original: שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה עָבְדוּ אֶת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מָרָדוּ׃
verses.english: Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and the thirteenth year they revolted,
verses.commentary: Political Status: Twelve years under Chedorlaomer. Year 13: western vassals revolted.

tex.original:
\hOther{שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה עָבְדוּ אֶת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר
        וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מָרָדוּ׃}
tex.english: \eOther{Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and the thirteenth year they revolted,}
tex.commentary: \aC{\textsc{Political Status}: Twelve years under Chedorlaomer. \textsc{Year 13}: western vassals revolted.}

verses.original: וּבְאַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה בָּא כְדרְלָעֹמֶר וְהַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ וַיַּכּוּ אֶת רְפָאִים בְּעַשְׁתְּרֹת קַרְנַיִם וְאֶת הַזּוּזִים בְּהָם וְאֵת הָאֵימִים בְּשָׁוֵה קִרְיָתָיִם׃
verses.english: and in the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came, and they struck the RephaimRephaim (Hebrew: רְפָאִים) in biblical and ancient Near Eastern contexts refers to a mythical race of ancient giants, and to the shadowy spirits of the dead in the underworld.Rephaim are like these really tall ghosts. in Ashteroth Karnaim and the Zuzum in Ham and the Emim in Shaveh Kiriataim
verses.commentary: Year 14: Chedorlaomer and allied kings commenced punitive operations. Rephaim struck at Ashteroth Karnaim; Zuzim at Ham; Emim at Shaveh Kiriathaim;

verses.original: וְאֶת הַחֹרִי בְּהַרְרָם שֵׂעִיר עַד אֵיל פָּארָן אֲשֶׁר עַל הַמִּדְבָּר׃
verses.english: and the Horites in their mountain Seir to El Paran, which is by the wilderness.
verses.commentary: Horites struck throughout the hill country of Seir as far as El Paran, on the wilderness frontier.

tex.original:

verses.original: וַיָּשֻׁבוּ וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל עֵין מִשְׁפָּט הִוא קָדֵשׁ וַיַּכּוּ אֶת כּל שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי וְגַם אֶת הָאֱמֹרִי הַיֹּשֵׁב בְּחַצְצֹן תָּמָר׃
verses.english: And they came back and came to En Mishpat (that is Kadesh) and struck the area of the Amalekites and also the Amorites who live in Hazazon Tamar.
verses.commentary: Return Advance: Coalition forces turned toward En Mishpat (modern designation: Kadesh), struck Amalekite territory, then the Amorites stationed at Hazazon Tamar.

verses.original: וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם וּמֶלֶךְ עֲמֹרָה וּמֶלֶךְ אַדְמָה וּמֶלֶךְ (צביים) [צְבוֹיִם] וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע הִוא צֹעַר וַיַּעַרְכוּ אִתָּם מִלְחָמָה בְּעֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים׃
verses.english: And the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah and the king of Admah and the king of Zeboiim and the king of Bela (that is Zoar) went out and aligned with them for war in the Siddim Valley
verses.commentary: Western Response: Kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela (Zoar) deployed for battle in the Valley of Siddim.

verses.original: אֵת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם וְאַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר וְאַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת הַחֲמִשָּׁה׃
verses.english: with Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goiim, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Ellasar—four kings with five.
verses.commentary: Order of Battle: Chedorlaomer of Elam; Tidal of Goiim; Amraphel of Shinar; Arioch of Ellasar. Strength: four kings against five.

tex.commentary:

verses.english: And Siddim Valley was pits, pits of bitumen, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and they fell there; and those who were left fled to the mountain.
verses.commentary: Terrain: Valley of Siddim heavily broken by bitumen pits. Result: Sodomite and Gomorrite forces routed. Some fell among the pits; surviving elements withdrew into the hills.

verses.original: וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת כּל רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וְאֶת כּל אכְלָם וַיֵּלֵכוּ׃
verses.english: And they took all the property of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and they went.
verses.commentary: Sodom and Gomorrah: Coalition forces seized all movable property and provisions and withdrew.

verses.english: And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, and his property when they went. And he had been living in Sodom.
verses.commentary: Captives: Lot, nephew of Abram and resident of Sodom, taken with his property during withdrawal.

verses.english: And an escapee came and told Abram the Hebrew, and he was tenting among the oaksYou know the ones. of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; and they were covenant partners of Abram.

This is one of several indications that the chapter lies outside the primary sources of the Torah and may preserve or imitate material belonging to the tradition of Mesopotamian royal inscriptions.] then encamped by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite. Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner were covenant allies of Abram.

verses.original: וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם כִּי נִשְׁבָּה אָחִיו וַיָּרֶק אֶת חֲנִיכָיו יְלִידֵי בֵיתוֹ שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַיִּרְדֹּף עַד דָּן׃
verses.english: And Abram heard that his brother had been taken prisoner, and he had his trained men, born in his house, unsheathe: three hundred eighteen. And he pursued as far as Dan.
verses.commentary: Mobilization: Upon confirmation that his kinsman had been captured, Abram mustered 318 trained household-born retainers. Pursuit: north to Dan.

verses.original: וַיֵּחָלֵק עֲלֵיהֶם לַיְלָה הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו וַיַּכֵּם וַיִּרְדְּפֵם עַד חוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר מִשְּׂמֹאל לְדַמָּשֶׂק׃
verses.english: And he divided against them by night, he and his servants, and he struck them and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is at the leftYes, they really just said something is “to the left” of a city. of Damascus.
verses.commentary: Night Action: Abram divided his force, attacked with his retainers, routed the enemy, and pursued as far as Hobah, north of Damascus.

tex.commentary:

verses.original: וַיָּשֶׁב אֵת כּל הָרְכֻשׁ וְגַם אֶת לוֹט אָחִיו וּרְכֻשׁוֹ הֵשִׁיב וְגַם אֶת הַנָּשִׁים וְאֶת הָעָם׃
verses.english: And he brought back all the property, and he also brought back Lot, his brother, and his property, and also the women and the people.The women are different from the people.
verses.commentary: Recovery: All seized property recovered. Lot and his property recovered. Women and other captives recovered.

verses.original: וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם לִקְרָאתוֹ אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ מֵהַכּוֹת אֶת כְּדרְלָעֹמֶר וְאֶת הַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ אֶל עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה הוּא עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ׃
verses.english: And the king of Sodom came out to him after he came back from striking Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him at the Shaveh Valley. (That is the valley of the king.)
verses.commentary: Return: Following the defeat of Chedorlaomer and allied kings, Abram was met by the King of Sodom at the Valley of Shaveh (modern designation: King's Valley).

verses.original: וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן׃
verses.english: And Melchizedek, king of Salem, had brought out bread and wine. And he was a priest of El the Highest.
verses.commentary: Salem: Melchizedek, King of Salem and priest of El Most High, brought out bread and wine.

verses.original: וַיְבָרְכֵהוּ וַיֹּאמַר בָּרוּךְ אַבְרָם לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And he blessed him and said, "Blessed is Abram to El the Highest, creator of skies and earth.

verses.english: And blessed is El the Highest, who delivered your foes into your hand." And he gave him a tithe from everything.
verses.commentary: and blessed be El Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand.” Tribute: Abram transferred one tenth of all recovered goods to Melchizedek.

tex.original:
\hOther{וּבָרוּךְ אֵל עֶלְיוֹן אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן צָרֶיךָ בְּיָדֶךָ

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם אֶל אַבְרָם תֶּן לִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְהָרְכֻשׁ קַח לָךְ׃
verses.english: And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give the persons to me, and take the property for you."
verses.commentary: Sodomite Claim: King of Sodom requested return of the persons; Abram was authorized to retain the property.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם הֲרִמֹתִי יָדִי אֶל יהוה אֵל עֶלְיוֹן קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I've lifted my hand to YHWH El the Highest, creator of skies and earth,
verses.commentary: Abram's Oath: “I have raised my hand to YHWH [This verse is one of only 5 occurrences of the name YHWH outside the J source prior to the name being revealed in Exodus 3 and Exodus 6. Overall, the word YHWH occurs about 3,190 times in the Primary History (Genesis through II Kings.) 1,829 times in the Torah (Genesis through Deuteronomy), and 211 times from the beginning of Genesis to the end of Exodus 6. After Exodus 3, the E source begins using the name YHWH, while also continuing to use the term God (Elohim). After Exodus 6, the P source does the same. This first exception to the rule is not particularly interesting, given that the entirety of Genesis 14 appears not to have been written by any of the primary authors of the Torah. Regardless, the idea that two of the three primary authors of the Torah have this idea that the name YHWH was not known until the time of Moses in Egypt is a fact worth noting. This was among the earliest forms of evidence that eventually allowed us to determine how the Torah was written, and by whom.] El Most High, creator of heaven and earth,

verses.original: אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל וְאִם אֶקַּח מִכּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ וְלֹא תֹאמַר אֲנִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי אֶת אַבְרָם׃
verses.english: that, from a thread to a shoelace, I won't take anything that is yours, so you won't say, 'I made Abram rich.'
verses.commentary: I will take neither thread nor sandal strap nor anything belonging to you, so that no claim may be made that the King of Sodom enriched Abram.

verses.original: בִּלְעָדַי רַק אֲשֶׁר אָכְלוּ הַנְּעָרִים וְחֵלֶק הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר הָלְכוּ אִתִּי עָנֵר אֶשְׁכֹּל וּמַמְרֵא הֵם יִקְחוּ חֶלְקָם׃

verses.english: And she called the name of YHWH who spoke to her “You are El-roi,” for she said, “Have I also seen after the one who sees me here?”
verses.commentary:
Now the text says she called the name of “YHWH who spoke to her.”

So I guess we figured out who the messenger was.

She says “You are El-roi” which is like “The God who sees.”

Now she says a phrase that translators can't seem to agree on the meaning of.

Here's some of their choices:

• I have now seen the One who sees me.
• Have I also here seen Him who sees me?
• Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.
• Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?
• Have I even remained alive here after seeing Him?
• Here also I looked after him seeing me.

verses.english: And Abram was ninety years and nine years old, and YHWH appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am El Shadday. Walk before me and be unblemished,
verses.commentary:
Cut to thirteen years later.

Abe is older now.

Ninety years old. And nine.

And all of a sudden, possibly for the first time in thirteen years...

A familiar voice is heard.

No mistaking that voice. It's YHWH, and he says:

“I am El Shadday.”

This is the first appearance of God in which he refers to himself as El Shaddai. El Shaddai. Probably “El, the One of the Mountain.” The traditional translation of “God Almighty” is impossible to justify linguistically. In Akkadian the root appears in šadu rabu, “great mountains” and the šdyn of the Deir 'Alla inscription. Another proposal derives Shadday from the Hebrew שד, “breast,” suggesting an association between fertility and this version of the deity. Another connects it with שדד, “destroy, devastate.” The etymology remains uncertain.

Ok so don't quote me on this, I'm new here, but let's give this one a shot.

Putting an `i' at the end of a Hebrew word X is like “my X.”

For example:

אבי | אב | אב + י | my father
אמי | אם | אם + י | my mother
אחי | אח | אח + י | my brother
בני | בן | בן + י | my son
בתי | בת | בת + י | my daughter
אישי | איש | איש + י | my man
אדני | אדון | אדון + י | my lord
מלכי | מלך | מלך + י | my king
אלי | אל | אל + י | my God

Now El is the generic term for a god, and Shaddai is שדי.

And שד means demonic, mischievous, deceitful, and malicious (as an adjective), and demon, devil, genie, ghost, or, apparently, breast (as a noun).

However, people don't usually parse the word that way.

Apparently ancient translators were equally confused by the word. So by the time people started translating the bible, we'd already reached a point where nobody knew what Shaddai meant anymore. The ancient Greek translators translate it a bunch of different ways instead of just translating it like a normal word. The common translation “god almighty” comes from this guy named Jerome (c. 347–420 CE). Jerome translated it into Latin as omnipotens, “almighty,” and Western Bible translators have been saying “almighty” ever since.

So these days it's usually translated as Almighty or just left untranslated, presumably because we don't actually know what the damn word means and so it's usually defensible for a translator to just skip it, possibly after making a token comment about Akkadian or mountains or tits.

... How was that?

So on that note:

Nobody knows what Shaddai means.

Appearances of the name El Shaddai are conspicuously associated with fertility, for example:

Verse | Name | Speaker | What Shaddai is doing / what is being discussed
Gen 17:1–21 | El Shaddai | God | Promises to multiply Abram's seed exceedingly.

Gen 28:3–4 | El Shaddai | Isaac | May El Shaddai bless you, make you fruitful, and multiply you.

Gen 35:11–12 | El Shaddai | God | “I am El Shaddai: Be fruitful and multiply.” A nation and an assembly of nations will come from Jacob, and kings will come from his loins. El Shaddai promises the land to his seed.

Gen 43:14 | El Shaddai | Jacob | As Benjamin is sent to Egypt, Jacob asks El Shaddai to give his sons mercy before Joseph so that Benjamin and Simeon will return. The immediate subject is therefore the preservation of Jacob's sons.

Gen 48:3–4 | El Shaddai | Jacob | Jacob tells Joseph that El Shaddai appeared to him at Luz, saying: “I will make you fruitful and multiply you; I will make you an assembly of peoples.”

Gen 49:25 | Shaddai | Jacob | Shaddai blesses Joseph with “blessings of sky above, blessings of the deep lying below, blessings of the breasts and womb” (שדים ורחם). The fertility context is explicit.

Exod 6:3 | El Shaddai | God | God tells Moses: “I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai, and I was not known to them by my name, YHWH.” While true in the P source (and in E until Exodus 3, modulo the occasional lapse in Genesis), it is manifestly false in the recieved text of the Torah. This anomaly was one of the original clues that led to the Documentary Hypothesis and to our modern understanding of the bible's origins, authors, and content.

Num 24:4 | Shaddai | Balaam | Balaam introduces his oracle as one who “sees the vision of Shaddai.” What he then sees is Israel flourishing: beautiful tents, seed beside abundant waters.

Num 24:16 | Shaddai | Balaam | Again Balaam “sees the vision of Shaddai.” The oracle concerns Israel's future power: a star comes from Jacob, a scepter rises from Israel.

verses.original: וַיִּפֹּל אַבְרָהָם עַל פָּנָיו וַיִּצְחָק וַיֹּאמֶר בְּלִבּוֹ הַלְּבֶן מֵאָה שָׁנָה יִוָּלֵד וְאִם שָׂרָה הֲבַת תִּשְׁעִים שָׁנָה תֵּלֵד׃
verses.english: And Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said in his heart, “Will he be born to someone who’s a hundred years old?! And will Sarah, who’s ninety years old, give birth?!”
verses.commentary:
Abe falls on his face laughing. Apparently, for some reason, Abraham thinks YHWH is funny.

Abe reminds YHWH that he was already 75 when they met, and that was a while ago. According to the text, Abram was 75 years old when YHWH first spoke to him. Then they hung out for 11 years. Then YHWH went away for 13 years. Then he showed up again, introducing himself under a different name. Then he renames Abe. And his wife, who's also old. Hence the laughter.

Basically his hundredth birthday is coming up.

Abe keeps listening, in a respectful sort of silence.

“Wow tough audience.

%	\footnote{
%		My Lord. Why does Abraham run to the three people and bow to them but
%		then speak to God? Is he meeting God, people, or angels? Several of the
%		biblical stories involving angels contain confusions such as this, i.e.,
%		confusions between when it is the deity and when it is the angel who is
%		speaking or doing something. But it is confusing only so long as we
%		imagine angels as beings who are independent or separate from God. These
%		texts indicate that angels are rather conceived of here as expressions
%		of God’s presence. The consistent biblical conception of God is that God
%		cannot possibly be seen by a human (“A human will not see me and live,”
%		Exod 33:20) and cannot possibly be contained in any known space (“The
%		heavens … will not contain you,” 1 Kings 8:27). God, in this conception,
%		can nonetheless make Himself known to humans by a sort of emanation from
%		the Godhead that is visible to human eyes. It is a hypostasis, a
%		concrete expression of the divine presence, which is otherwise
%		inexpressible to human beings. What the human sees when such a
%		hypostasis is in front of him or her looks like “people,” like a “man.”
%		And the word for such a thing is “angel.” Thus Jacob can encounter an
%		angel and still say “I’ve seen God face-to-face” (Gen 32:31). And
%		Abraham can face three angels and address “my Lord.” And an angel can
%		speak God’s words in first person or can speak about God in third
%		person. All this is so because in some ways an angel is an identifiable
%		thing itself, and in some ways it is merely a representation of divine
%		presence in human affairs. (See The Hidden Face of God, pp. 10–11.)
%	}

verses.english: Let me go down, and I’ll see if they’ve done, all told, like the cry that has come to me. And if not, let me know.”
verses.commentary:
I think what he's saying here is:

“I'll go down and see if it's really as bad as I've heard. If not, I'll find out.”

The “let me know” in the translation is more like “let it be the case that I know.”

The Hebrew אֵדָעָה is a first-person cohortative, a verbal form often expressing resolve, intention, or desire. Here it means something like “I'll know,” “I'll find out,” or “let me find out,” not the modern English sense of the idiom “let me know.”

Point being: I don't think he's asking himself to tell himself what happened.

%		I have two daughters.... do to them as is good in your eyes. Some say
%		that this is a matter of ancient Near Eastern hospitality: Lot as the
%		host must do anything to protect his guests. Some say that daughters
%		were held in low esteem in that world’s values. Ramban and others say
%		that this shows that Lot had an evil heart. It seems to me that it is
%		not the Near Eastern tradition of hospitality but of bargaining that
%		accounts for what is going on here. When Abraham goes to buy a tomb for
%		Sarah, the seller says to him, “I’ve given it to you!” (Gen 23:11). But
%		he does not give it. Then Abraham says, “I’ve given the money” (23:13).
%		Then the seller says, “Land worth four hundred shekels of silver: what’s
%		that between me and you?!” (23:15) as if this were a small sum. But it
%		is a very large sum. And Abraham pays it without another word.
%		Interpreters have frequently noted the traditions of negotiating there:
%		deliberate overstatement, saying things one does not mean: “gracious
%		insincerity.” I suggest that they apply here as well. Lot is supposed to
%		make an extraordinary gesture. He offers his own daughters. But no one
%		is supposed to take him up on it. And then, in this horrible town, the
%		gesture does not work anyway. The people only become angry. (In the
%		parallel story in Judges 19, in a similar circumstance a host offers his
%		own daughter and his guest’s concubine to the crowd. But the guest gives

II Samuel 24 | Araunah's floor and oxen | 50 | 20 threshing-floor purchases

Mesopotamian texts | Typical house | ∼10–100 | ∼10–100 houses

Mesopotamian texts | Large estate | Several hundred | A few large estates

Genesis 20 | Abimelek's gift | 1,000 | Princely public restitution

Entrapment pays handsomely.

And Sarah looks over at sisterwife's son.

The text says she sees him “fooling around,” which is a pun on Isaac. (No time to explain, just trust me, the Hebrew word's not the point here.)

The Greek text has “fooling around with her son Isaac,” which can connote either playing with Isaac or mocking him. The word in Hebrew is מצחק, which is a pun on the name Isaac. It will occur again in the story of Isaac, Rebekah, and Abimelek (Gen 26:8).

Anyways the point is that this new E character seems to like puns too.
