• J's entire universe is stitched together from a dense fabric of puns and sex and subtext.
• E's universe is one in which God exists and his name's YHWH [Though in E we don't learn this until Exodus 3.] but it's not illegal to have fun, and in which writing a bible doesn't rule out the occasional pun.
• P's universe is one in which language, all languages, and each language according to its words, are a tool of holiness. It is a holy thing. And in the holy medium of language, all languages, and each language according to its words, puns are an abomination and simply must not be done. When anyone brings a pun into the world by bringing it into one's mind and conceiving of it, he must bring his pun or puns to the Tabernacle and present it in front of Aaron and his sons. And he shall lay his hand on the head of the pun and slaughter it at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Aaron's sons the priests shall sprinkle the blood all around against the sides of the altar. Then he shall remove all the letters from the insides of the word of his pun (if it is a single word pun) or the words of his pun (if it is a multiword pun), and then Aaron's sons are to burn it to smoke on the altar; it is a literative offering, a literation pleasing to the Lord. After these things, any male in a priest’s family may hear the words of the pun; it is a holy thing. I am YHWH who makes you holy, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. I am YHWH.

Abe: Take Isaac, go to Moriah, figure out which mountain, go there, and then what

God: Then

burn him alive.

Any time you want to meet girls in the ancient near east, go to a well.

Apparently fetching water is a thing that only young girls do.

Long story short, any time you go to a well in the bible, you end up with a wife.

Only exception to this law is that two out of three times you end up with several wives.

Like eventually I mean.

One girl at a time, at first, when you meet, then multiple at once once they're moved in for the coming century.

Look I'm just saying polygamy requires patience.

It being the cultural default doesn't mean you don't still get yelled at. That's just gonna happen. A lot.

That's something you're gonna have to just accept. Suck it up and deal with it.

Abe got yelled at in 16:5 for doing what his wife told him to do in 16:1.

... anyways not saying it's a Better Life For Everyone Involved At All Times compared to our more modern equitable system of monogamy and nuclear families with between 0.75 and 0.40 children per person on average and no nearby extended kin network to help out on the one hand, or a venture backed algorithm driven mating system which when mixed with the timeless ancient and highly understandable female psychology of hypergamy and then stirred all together into a chemical cocktail by the shaking hands of lonely isolated desperation leads unsurprisingly via the basic laws of chemistry to an unstable isotope of mating and dating known as poly-without-even-the-basic-requirement-of-gamy which is (1) highly basic as can be gathered from the name and (2) a brownish sort of liquid that winds up mostly on the sheets.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמַר יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם הַקְרֵה נָא לְפָנַי הַיּוֹם וַעֲשֵׂה חֶסֶד עִם אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		make something happen. The Hebrew includes the particle n’, conveying
%		that this is a polite request. Even as a request, though, it is
%		remarkable: the servant himself asks for a miraculous sign from God, and
%		he himself names what that sign should be. No human thus far, including
%		Abraham himself, has gone this far. Abraham had told this servant that
%		his God “will send His angel ahead of you,” and this is presumably what
%		gives the servant the confidence to do this. Still, it is noteworthy as
%		one of a chain of steps that humans are taking toward increasing control
%		of miracle in the Tanak.
%	}

verses.commentary:
Qere Ketiv.

Ok so YHWH goes into poetic prophetic oracle genre for his answer.

In this case it seems to be a way of not answering the question.

The Hebrew grammar here basically says “The older the younger will serve.”

Which is grammatically weird enough that it could actually mean either thing.

So basically YHWH says “It's twins. One will be stronger than the other.”

Biblical Hebrew normally puts an imperfect (i.e., unfinished, ongoing action type) verb before its subject and object: “serve older younger” means “the older will serve the younger.” Here older comes first: “older serve younger.” Both adjectives are masculine singular, and neither is marked as the object, so the words can mean either “the older will serve the younger” or “the younger will serve the older.” The traditional reading chooses the first, but the original author of the text here (J) appears to have carefully crafted this sentence to be deliberately ambiguous.

Now, as you know by now, all the main people in Genesis are places. At least the guys.

Pretty soon we're gonna hear that Esau is Edom.

Edom is the country just south of ancient Israel.

And Seir is...

Well, I'll let the map explain.

Also Edom is 𐤀𐤃𐤌. [They eventually add a 𐤅 in the middle when matres lectiones catch on.]

• Edom
• Red
• Adam (the word for human)

verses.english: And the boys grew up, and Esau was a man who knew hunting, a man of the field, and Jacob was a simple man, living in tents.
verses.commentary:
Ok so the text notes that:

• Esau's a man's man, a hunter.
• Jacob is more simple and intense.

The translation here is a bit strange.

Most translate (תם) as “simple.”

The word is from the same root as in Genesis 6:9 when Noah is called “blameless” (תמים).

So it's possible that J's saying something more like “Jacob was an innocent homebody.”

Which would be particularly ironicAka, very J given what's about to happen.

Let's go see.

verses.english: And there was a famine in the land (other than the first famine, which was in Abraham’s days), and Isaac went to Abimelek, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.
verses.commentary:
Now apparently it's not just Esau in the previous chapter who can't find food.

Here we learn there's a famine in the land.

verses.original: וַיַּעְתֵּק מִשָּׁם וַיַּחְפֹּר בְּאֵר אַחֶרֶת וְלֹא רָבוּ עָלֶיהָ וַיִּקְרָא שְׁמָהּ רְחֹבוֹת וַיֹּאמֶר כִּי עַתָּה הִרְחִיב יְהֹוָה לָנוּ וּפָרִינוּ בָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And he moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it, and he called its name Rehovot and said, “Because now YHWH has widened for us, and we’ve been fruitful in the land.”
verses.commentary: There's other fish in the sea so they head over to the seaward parts and get another seaword hole there and they call this one Broad [Curiously, the name of this well (RḤB, Heb. רחב, meaning Wide, Broad, or Spread Out) is also the name of a prostitute (RḤB, Heb. רחב, meaning Wide, Broad, or Spread Out) in the book of Joshua chapter 2, which scholars have argued was written by the same author as this section, both coming from the source known as J. Further, RḤB is also the root from which the name of the king Rehoboam was derived. The evidence suggests that J was likely alive in the time of Rehoboam. In summary, though this section of the bible is not among the more popular or well known stories, from what we can gather, it involves a big wet hole that's so big that all the guys can share, and also is the same name as a whore, and also the king at the time.]The bible ladies and gentlemen. because now YHWH has widened for us and there's enough room for everyone to share the fruits of this hole's wetness.

verses.english: And Isaac said to Jacob, “Come over, and I’ll feel you, my son: is this you, my son Esau, or not?”
verses.commentary:
So Isaac's like “Let me feel you to see if you're really Esau.”

Technical flaws in this approach are discussed in the footnote below. Isaac's approach here relies on the well known fact that the first requirement for any Esau detection system is “if not hairy, then not Esau.” By modus tollens, this is equivalent to the contrapositive “If Esau, then hairy.” However, as every Esau detection system engineer well knows, the inverse (If hairy then Esau) and converse (If not Esau, then not hairy) of Isaac's sentence do not follow! The first known Esau detection system, namely Isaac in Gen 27:21, famously failed to recognize this, due to (a) the existence of goats, and (b) the degradation of visual capacity in Gen 27:1, commonly known The Blinding of Isaac, which combined to form a security vulnerability that allowed an attacker to authenticate as Esau and exfiltrate the blessing.

Isaac now has two conflicting cues.

Let's see if Isaac's Esau detection system has two factor authentication enabled.

At this point, one might expect Isaac to notice something is up, since goat and game animals do not, in fact, taste the same.

However, as one scholar has pointed out, this is the ancient near east.

And if you put enough cumin on anything it all eventually tastes the same.

So Jacob's food is believable (because cumin) and his costume is believable (because apparently Esau is that hairy.)

tex.original: \hJ{כִּשְׁמֹעַ עֵשָׂו אֶת דִּבְרֵי אָבִיו וַיִּצְעַק צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה וּמָרָה עַד מְאֹד וַיֹּאמֶר לְאָבִיו בָּרְכֵנִי גַם אָנִי אָבִי׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר בָּא אָחִיךָ בְּמִרְמָה וַיִּקַּח בִּרְכָתֶךָ׃
verses.english: And he said, “Your brother came with deception, and he took your blessing.”
verses.commentary: Blessing call failed with message: We cry. [Lit. brk call failed with message: ENOMEM in the original text. The former is presumably a Latin alphabet rendering of Heb. brk (ברכ) meaning “blessing,” given the benedictory context, and the latter presumably a similar rendering of Heb. אנו meaning We, and of Heb. “mem,” as above, given the nosistic and ibidem contexts respectively.]

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר הֲכִי קָרָא שְׁמוֹ יַעֲקֹב וַיַּעְקְבֵנִי זֶה פַעֲמַיִם אֶת בְּכֹרָתִי לָקָח וְהִנֵּה עַתָּה לָקַח בִּרְכָתִי וַיֹּאמַר הֲלֹא אָצַלְתָּ לִּי בְּרָכָה׃

Then they make puns about how they really shouldn't have named the other brother Usurper.

They're like “Isn't that why he's called Jacob? He's Jacob'd me twice now!”

verses.commentary: Laughter and the Human can't believe Usurper got the blessed of them.

verses.commentary: Dad's like “Life's gonna be rough, son.”

So the Red man hates Usurper.

verses.commentary:
She's like “Run time kid.”

And she says to go stay with her brother White.

He lives in Haran.

Remember that.

Jacob's going to Haran.

verses.original: וְיָשַׁבְתָּ עִמּוֹ יָמִים אֲחָדִים עַד אֲשֶׁר תָּשׁוּב חֲמַת אָחִיךָ׃
verses.english: and live with him for a number of days until your brother’s fury will turn back,
verses.commentary: Live with him until Esau calms down.

verses.original: וַתֹּאמֶר רִבְקָה אֶל יִצְחָק קַצְתִּי בְחַיַּי מִפְּנֵי בְּנוֹת חֵת אִם לֹקֵחַ יַעֲקֹב אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת חֵת כָּאֵלֶּה מִבְּנוֹת הָאָרֶץ לָמָּה לִּי חַיִּים׃
verses.english: And Rebekah said to Isaac, “I’m disgusted with my life because of the daughters of Heth! If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these daughters of the land, why do I have a life!”
verses.commentary:
Previously on: P.

Ok so last we left off in P, we were in Gen 26:34-35.

Esau had just married a girl named “Jewish Girl,” and another one named Basemath. [There was a \usepackage[latex]{basemath} joke here but it kept breaking the build.]

And mom and dad were NOT happy about that.

So now in this verse, Rebecca is suddenly mad about the daughters of Heth, which means the Hittites, which suggests we're picking back up where Gen 26:35 left off.

Then the chapter abruptly ends.

tex.original: \hP{וַתֹּאמֶר רִבְקָה אֶל יִצְחָק קַצְתִּי בְחַיַּי מִפְּנֵי בְּנוֹת חֵת אִם לֹקֵחַ יַעֲקֹב אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת חֵת כָּאֵלֶּה מִבְּנוֹת הָאָרֶץ לָמָּה לִּי חַיִּים׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא יִצְחָק אֶל יַעֲקֹב וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתוֹ וַיְצַוֵּהוּ וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹ לֹא תִקַּח אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת כְּנָעַן׃
verses.english: And Isaac called Jacob, and he blessed him and commanded him, and he said to him, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
verses.commentary:
Ok, a quick recap before we proceed.

One sentence before this, Rebecca is disgusted with her life because of the daughters of Heth, which is the Hittites.

Two sentences before this, they're a bitterness of spirit to Rebecca.

Three sentences before this, we find out that Esau married a girl named Judith (“Jewish Girl”) and another one named Basemath (“Smells Good”) who are supposedly Hitties.

Now in this sentence, Isaac gives Jacob his blessing, and says he hopes that Jacob doesn't turn out how Esau did, specifically, he doesn't want him marrying any Canaanites, which “includes” the Hittites. [In the bible, Hittites are a type of Canaanites. That's an understandable inference, but not exactly true, as far as we can tell archaeologically. That is, since the text depicts Rebecca as not liking the Hittites, it's as if she's mad that her son married two girls named Sakura and Nahyun, and then the dad says to Jacob “Don't go and marry a bunch of Chinese girls like your brother did.” An understandable mistake. They're not exactly connoisseurs of the people in question.]

So Jacob gets his father's blessing fair and square because Jacob and Rebecca are mad that Esau married two birds from up north.

verses.original: קוּם לֵךְ פַּדֶּנָה אֲרָם בֵּיתָה בְתוּאֵל אֲבִי אִמֶּךָ וְקַח לְךָ מִשָּׁם אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת לָבָן אֲחִי אִמֶּךָ׃
verses.english: Get up. Go to Paddan Aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take a wife from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.

So that's why they tell Jacob to go to Laban's place and marry his cousins.

Now remember, Laban means white.

So his daughters are white girls.

He won't make the parents sad like Esau's wives did.

Also Laban lives Paddan Aram.

Remember that.

Jacob's going to Paddan Aram.

verses.english: And may El Shadday bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so you’ll become a community of peoples,
verses.commentary: And may God of the Mountain (or God of Breasts, we're not sure, but it's possible that Shaddai means something about fertility) give you lots of fertility (what a coincidence.)

verses.commentary:
Jacob turns his rock pillow up vertical and pours oil on it.

It's not clear why. [Jacob is turning his pillow-rock into a sacred standing stone (maṣṣēbâ): he stands it upright and pours oil over it to consecrate it. This was a normal ancient West Semitic way of marking a divine presence or holy place; Jacob does it again at Bethel (Gen 35:14), and erects other standing stones in Gen 31:45 and 35:20. The point becomes explicit in 28:22: “this stone … shall be God’s house”—part of the story’s explanation of Bethel, bêt-ʾēl, “House of God/El.” Strikingly, Deut 16:22 later outright bans erecting a maṣṣēbâ.]

verses.commentary: “And keep me safe until I get back to daddy, then YHWH will become my God,” [The 5th out of 5 uses of the name YHWH outside of J prior to the big reveal of the name of god in Exodus 3 (and 6). The Evidence: Dreams are heavily E-associated: Gen 20:3, 6; 28:12; 31:10–11, 24; 37:5–10; 40:5–23; 41:1–32. Standing stones also recur in E-linked Jacob material: Gen 28:18, 22; 31:45, 51–52; 35:14. And the actual sentence says, “If Elohim is with me ... then YHWH will be my God.” Jacob does not start by casually calling Elohim “YHWH”; YHWH appears in the result of the condition. E may therefore be deliberately saying: if the Elohim who appeared to Jacob actually protects him, Jacob will accept YHWH as his God.]

Lots going on here. Mandrakes are a well-known aphrodisiac/fertility drug resembling a human baby, with a forked root that often bears striking resemblance to a male phallic organ of considerable size. verses.original: וַיָּסַר בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת הַתְּיָשִׁים הָעֲקֻדִּים וְהַטְּלֻאִים וְאֵת כּל הָעִזִּים הַנְּקֻדּוֹת וְהַטְּלֻאֹת כֹּל אֲשֶׁר לָבָן בּוֹ וְכל חוּם בַּכְּשָׂבִים וַיִּתֵּן בְּיַד בָּנָיו׃
verses.english: And in that day he removed the he-goats that were streaked and spotted and the she-goats that were speckled and spotted, every one that had white in it, and every brown one among the sheep, and set them in his sons’ hand
verses.commentary:
Note: Heel (עקב) in Paleo-Heberew is עקב. Streaked (עקד) in the same system is עקד. He (יעקב) is up to something נקד and עקד. Whatever's going on here, they're not white. The White sheep are Laban's because לבן. Just make a note of that and let's move on.

he-goats | תיש | Noun: he-goat, male goat, buck.
streaked | עקד | Verb: bind, tie, bind up. Adjective: bound, banded, striped, streaked. Noun: binding; later especially the Akedah, “Binding,” of Isaac.
speckled | נקד | Verb: mark, mark with points or dots, punctuate, point a text. Adjective: dotted, speckled, spotted. Noun: point, dot, mark; later, vowel-point or diacritic.
spotted | טלא | Verb: patch, cover with patches, spot, variegate. Adjective/participle: patched, spotted, mottled, variegated.
white | לבן | Adjective: white. Verb: be white, become white, make white, whiten. Noun: whiteness, white material. Proper noun: Laban.
brown | חום | Adjective: dark-colored, dark brown, blackish. The consonants are also associated etymologically with warmth/heat, though the Biblical Hebrew adjective here is specifically a color word.
sheep | כשב | Noun: sheep, individual sheep, lamb/sheep as livestock; variant spelling of כבש.

verses.original: וַיָּשֶׂם דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים בֵּינוֹ וּבֵין יַעֲקֹב וְיַעֲקֹב רֹעֶה אֶת צֹאן לָבָן הַנּוֹתָרֹת׃
verses.english: and put three days’ distance between him and Jacob. And Jacob was tending Laban’s remaining sheep.
verses.commentary:
Jacob's got the non-Laban sheep.

Then he goes three days away.

We're about to hit a pretty weird scene.

remaining | יתר | Verb: remain, be left, survive, be left over; leave over, preserve. Noun: remainder, rest, residue, excess, abundance; also cord/string under a separate noun. Adjective: remaining, additional, excessive, superior.

verses.original: וַיִּקַּח לוֹ יַעֲקֹב מַקַּל לִבְנֶה לַח וְלוּז וְעַרְמוֹן וַיְפַצֵּל בָּהֵן פְּצָלוֹת לְבָנוֹת מַחְשֹׂף הַלָּבָן אֲשֶׁר עַל הַמַּקְלוֹת׃
verses.english: And Jacob took a rod of fresh poplar and one of almond tree and one of plane tree, and he peeled white stripes in them, exposing the white that was on the rods.
verses.commentary:
He takes a wooden rod and peels back the outer layer.

Under the outer layer there's something לבן.

poplar | לבנה | Noun: poplar, traditionally white poplar. Noun: something white / whiteness by derivation from לבן. Proper noun: Libnah.
almond tree | לוז | Noun: almond, almond tree. Proper noun: Luz, a place-name associated with Bethel and also another town. In later Jewish tradition, לוז is also the name of a supposedly indestructibly hard bone.
plane tree | ערמון | Noun: plane tree; exact ancient botanical identification is uncertain. In later Hebrew the same word can refer to chestnut.
peeled | פצל | Verb: peel, strip, peel off bark; split, divide. Noun-related senses: strip, split, division, fissure.
stripes | פצלות | Noun: peeled strips, peeled streaks, stripes, exposed strips; derived from פצל “peel/split.”
exposing | חשף | Verb: uncover, expose, strip, bare; draw out, reveal. Adjective/participle: bare, exposed, uncovered.

verses.original: וַיַּצֵּג אֶת הַמַּקְלוֹת אֲשֶׁר פִּצֵּל בָּרְהָטִים בְּשִׁקְתוֹת הַמָּיִם אֲשֶׁר תָּבֹאןָ הַצֹּאן לִשְׁתּוֹת לְנֹכַח הַצֹּאן וַיֵּחַמְנָה בְּבֹאָן לִשְׁתּוֹת׃
verses.english: And he set up the rods that he had peeled in the channels in the watering troughs at which the flock came to drink, facing the flock. And they copulated when they came to drink.
verses.commentary:
He takes his stick and sticks it in the wet bit.

Now the sheep come when they're in heat.

verses.original: וַיִּקַּח אֶת אֶחָיו עִמּוֹ וַיִּרְדֹּף אַחֲרָיו דֶּרֶךְ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים וַיַּדְבֵּק אֹתוֹ בְּהַר הַגִּלְעָד׃
verses.english: And he took his brothers with him and pursued him seven days’ journey and caught up to him in the mountain of Gilead.
verses.commentary:
It takes 7 days for Laban to catch up.

Let s_𐤉 = Jacob's speed, s_𐤋 = Laban's speed.

Laban put three days' journey between himself and Jacob, so assuming that's three days at Laban speed, d_0 = 3s_𐤋.

Jacob gets t days to run before Laban comes after him. After Laban has been chasing him for τ days, the gap is Δ_t = τ. 3s_𐤋 + (t+τ)s_𐤉 - τ s_𐤋.

Laban catches him when Δ_t(τ)=0.

Jacob gets three days before Laban notices.

Then Laban catches him after seven days. So t=3, τ=7.

Plug it in: 3s_𐤋 + 10s_𐤉 - 7s_𐤋 =0.

Therefore 10s_𐤉 = 4s_𐤋,

so s_𐤋 = 2.5s_𐤉 .

So Laban appears to be moving at 2.5× Jacob-speed.

If “three days' journey” was measured at Jacob-speed instead, then d_0=3s_𐤉, which gives 3s_𐤉 + 10s_𐤉 = 7s_𐤋,

and therefore s_𐤋 = 13/7s_𐤉 ≈ 1.86s_𐤉 .

In summary, nothing's faster than the Speed of White.

The classical derivation above is lacking, in that it analyzes the Speed of White against a background of absolute space and time.

If instead there is a universal invariant White Speed, c=s_𐤋, then s_𐤉 = 0.4c.

The Lorentz factor is therefore γ = 1/ 1- s_𐤉^2/c^2 = 1/1-0.4^2 ≈ 1.091.

So seven days in the ground frame is only Δτ = Δ t/γ = 7/1.091 ≈ 6.42 days for Jacob.

Likewise, Jacob measures distances along the direction of travel as contracted by L = L_0/γ ≈ 0.9165L_0.

There is, however, no corresponding “Laban's perspective”: at the universal speed of White, γ, so White has no rest frame and no proper time.

In summary, no real object can travel faster than White Speed, and Jacob Isreal.

QED.

verses.original: הָיִיתִי בַיּוֹם אֲכָלַנִי חֹרֶב וְקֶרַח בַּלָּיְלָה וַתִּדַּד שְׁנָתִי מֵעֵינָי׃
verses.english: I was … In the daytime heat ate me up, and ice in the night. And my sleep fled from my eyes.
verses.commentary: I worked all day. All night too. All for ewe.

tex.original: \hE{הָיִיתִי בַיּוֹם אֲכָלַנִי חֹרֶב וְקֶרַח בַּלָּיְלָה וַתִּדַּד שְׁנָתִי מֵעֵינָי׃}
tex.commentary:
I worked all day. All night too. All for ewe.

%	\footnote{
%		I was … In the daytime heat. The first words of the verse, “I was,” have
%		no referent or continuation in the rest of the sentence. Commentators
%		and translators have taken it to mean “Thus I was: in the daytime heat
%		ate me up,” etc. But perhaps the confusion that results from this break
%		in the sentence is precisely the point. Jacob is speaking up after
%		twenty years. He is rattling off a list of his complaints as fast and as
%		strongly as he can. And, as people often do in such bursts of anger, he
%		starts a point and then interrupts himself and says something else that
%		occurs to him. Indeed, it is at this juncture that Jacob changes
%		directions. He has been listing his merits; now he suddenly switches and
%		points out the abuses that he has been suffering.
%	}

verses.original: זֶה לִּי עֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה בְּבֵיתֶךָ עֲבַדְתִּיךָ אַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה בִּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתֶיךָ וְשֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים בְּצֹאנֶךָ וַתַּחֲלֵף אֶת מַשְׂכֻּרְתִּי עֲשֶׂרֶת מֹנִים׃
verses.english: This twenty years I’ve had in your house: I worked for you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my pay ten times.
verses.commentary:
I worked fourteen years four these two wives.

Then we had 12 kids and 10 times you cut my pay.

tex.original: \hE{זֶה לִּי עֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה בְּבֵיתֶךָ עֲבַדְתִּיךָ אַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה בִּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתֶיךָ וְשֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים בְּצֹאנֶךָ וַתַּחֲלֵף אֶת מַשְׂכֻּרְתִּי עֲשֶׂרֶת מֹנִים׃}
tex.commentary:
I worked fourteen years four these two wives.

	Then we had 12 kids and 10 times you cut my pay.

verses.original: לוּלֵי אֱלֹהֵי אָבִי אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם וּפַחַד יִצְחָק הָיָה לִי כִּי עַתָּה רֵיקָם שִׁלַּחְתָּנִי אֶת ענְיִי וְאֶת יְגִיעַ כַּפַּי רָאָה אֱלֹהִים וַיּוֹכַח אָמֶשׁ׃
verses.english: If I hadn’t had my father’s God, the God of Abraham and Fear of Isaac, by now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my degradation and my hands’ exhaustion, and He pointed it out last night.”
verses.commentary:
If it hadn't been for my dad's God, the Abraham's God and Isaac's Nightmare, by now you would have sent me away with nothing.

God came and talked to me last night and he agrees, what you're doing's just not white.

tex.original: \hE{לוּלֵי אֱלֹהֵי אָבִי אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם וּפַחַד יִצְחָק הָיָה לִי כִּי עַתָּה רֵיקָם שִׁלַּחְתָּנִי אֶת ענְיִי וְאֶת יְגִיעַ כַּפַּי רָאָה אֱלֹהִים וַיּוֹכַח אָמֶשׁ׃}

	Isaac's Nightmare, by now you would have sent me away
	with nothing.

	God came and talked to me last night and he agrees,
	what you're doing's just not white.

verses.original: וַיַּעַן לָבָן וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל יַעֲקֹב הַבָּנוֹת בְּנֹתַי וְהַבָּנִים בָּנַי וְהַצֹּאן צֹאנִי וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה רֹאֶה לִי הוּא וְלִבְנֹתַי מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה לָאֵלֶּה הַיּוֹם אוֹ לִבְנֵיהֶן אֲשֶׁר יָלָדוּ׃
verses.english: And Laban answered, and he said to Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, and the sons are my sons, and the flock is my flock, and everything that you see: it’s mine. But what shall I do to my daughters, to these, today, or to their children to whom they’ve given birth?
verses.commentary:
The daughters are my daughters.

The kids are my kids.

The kids... the goat type, those are mine.

Everything is mine.

But what am I gonna do, cut off my kids and grandkids and goatkids?

You're blessing [Lit. brking in the original, presumably from the Heb. ברך.] my Lords, [Lit. Ba'als in the original, a Canaanite term meaning lord, master, owner, or husband.]

And irking [Lit. ירך in the original.] my irk. [Ibid.]

verses.original: וְעַתָּה לְכָה נִכְרְתָה בְרִית אֲנִי וָאָתָּה וְהָיָה לְעֵד בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ׃

verses.commentary:
So come now, let's make a covenant.

Just you and me.

verses.english: And Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar,
verses.commentary: Jacob takes a rock and sets it up straight.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּקַּח יַעֲקֹב אָבֶן וַיְרִימֶהָ מַצֵּבָה׃}

They also have dinner.

	They make a big rock pile.

	They also have dinner.

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא לוֹ לָבָן יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא וְיַעֲקֹב קָרָא לוֹ גַּלְעֵד׃
verses.english: And Laban called it ygar shdta’, and Jacob called it gal-‘d.
verses.commentary:
And Jacob calls it “Look at this Pile.” [Heb. 𐤂𐤋 𐤏𐤃, meaning “Witness Pile.”]

And Laban calls it “Look at this Pile” [Aram. 𐡉𐡂𐡓 𐡔𐡄𐡃𐡅𐡕𐡀, meaning “Witness Pile,” in this case Aram., for some reason.]

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּקְרָא לוֹ לָבָן יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא וְיַעֲקֹב קָרָא לוֹ גַּלְעֵד׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר לָבָן הַגַּל הַזֶּה עֵד בֵּינִי וּבֵינְךָ הַיּוֹם עַל כֵּן קָרָא שְׁמוֹ גַּלְעֵד׃
verses.english: And Laban said, “This pile is a witness between me and you today.” On account of this he called its name Gal-Ed.
verses.commentary:
Laban says “This pile is a witness between us.

That's why it's called Witness Pile.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר לָבָן הַגַּל הַזֶּה עֵד בֵּינִי וּבֵינְךָ הַיּוֹם עַל כֵּן קָרָא שְׁמוֹ גַּלְעֵד׃}

verses.original: וְהַמִּצְפָּה אֲשֶׁר אָמַר יִצֶף יהוה בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ כִּי נִסָּתֵר אִישׁ מֵרֵעֵהוּ׃
verses.english: (And Mizpah, because he said, “May YHWH observe between me and you when one is hidden from the other.”)
verses.commentary:
Also “Watchtower,” because Laban says:

“May YHWH watch us when we can't see each other.”

verses.original: אִם תְּעַנֶּה אֶת בְּנֹתַי וְאִם תִּקַּח נָשִׁים עַל בְּנֹתַי אֵין אִישׁ עִמָּנוּ רְאֵה אֱלֹהִים עֵד בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ׃
verses.english: “If you degrade my daughters and if you take wives in addition to my daughters, no man is with us. See: God is witness between me and you.”
verses.commentary:
“If you treat my daughters badly, or go get more wives, nobody's gonna be there to see it.

But God will.”

tex.original: \hE{אִם תְּעַנֶּה אֶת בְּנֹתַי וְאִם תִּקַּח נָשִׁים עַל בְּנֹתַי אֵין אִישׁ עִמָּנוּ רְאֵה אֱלֹהִים עֵד בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר לָבָן לְיַעֲקֹב הִנֵּה הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְהִנֵּה הַמַּצֵּבָה אֲשֶׁר יָרִיתִי בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ׃
verses.english: And Laban said to Jacob, “Here is this pile, and here is the pillar that I’ve cast between me and you.
verses.commentary:
Laban points at the pile and the pillar:

“These are the border between you and me.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר לָבָן לְיַעֲקֹב הִנֵּה הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְהִנֵּה הַמַּצֵּבָה אֲשֶׁר יָרִיתִי בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ׃}

verses.original: עֵד הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְעֵדָה הַמַּצֵּבָה אִם אָנִי לֹא אֶעֱבֹר אֵלֶיךָ אֶת הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְאִם אַתָּה לֹא תַעֲבֹר אֵלַי אֶת הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְאֶת הַמַּצֵּבָה הַזֹּאת לְרָעָה׃
verses.english: This pile is a witness, and the pillar is a witness that I won’t cross this pile to you and you won’t cross this pile and this pillar to me for bad.
verses.commentary:
You don't come to my side of the Ancient Near East, and I won't come to your side.

The rocks are here to keep us honest.

Should any future disputes arise, the rocks will be called as witnesses and the pillar with be called to the stand as a witness here against us.

tex.original: \hE{עֵד הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְעֵדָה הַמַּצֵּבָה אִם אָנִי לֹא אֶעֱבֹר אֵלֶיךָ אֶת הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְאִם אַתָּה לֹא תַעֲבֹר אֵלַי אֶת הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְאֶת הַמַּצֵּבָה הַזֹּאת לְרָעָה׃}

verses.original: אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם וֵאלֹהֵי נָחוֹר יִשְׁפְּטוּ בֵינֵינוּ אֱלֹהֵי אֲבִיהֶם וַיִּשָּׁבַע יַעֲקֹב בְּפַחַד אָבִיו יִצְחָק׃
verses.english: Let Abraham’s God and Nahor’s gods, their father’s gods, judge between us.” And Jacob swore by the Awe of his father, Isaac.
verses.commentary:
Laban says “Let Abraham's God and Nahor's gods judge between us.”

Jacob doesn't swear by any of those.

He swears by his dad Laughter's nightmare. פחד (paḥad): fear, dread, terror, panic, alarm—the kind of fear that suddenly seizes you. It can mean either the terror itself or the terrifying thing that causes it. Here it appears in place of the term “God,” to refer to YHWH's relationship to Isaac, a relationship that was, at times, at least moderately startling, to put it mildly.

Laban's either talking about “God” singular or “gods” plural here, we can't tell.

tex.original: \hE{אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם וֵאלֹהֵי נָחוֹר יִשְׁפְּטוּ בֵינֵינוּ אֱלֹהֵי אֲבִיהֶם וַיִּשָּׁבַע יַעֲקֹב בְּפַחַד אָבִיו יִצְחָק׃}

verses.original: וַיִּזְבַּח יַעֲקֹב זֶבַח בָּהָר וַיִּקְרָא לְאֶחָיו לֶאֱכל לָחֶם וַיֹּאכְלוּ לֶחֶם וַיָּלִינוּ בָּהָר׃
verses.english: And Jacob made a sacrifice in the mountain and called his brothers to eat bread, and they ate bread and spent the night in the mountain.
verses.commentary:
Jacob makes a sacrifice.

Then everybody eats together and spends the night on the mountain.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּזְבַּח יַעֲקֹב זֶבַח בָּהָר וַיִּקְרָא לְאֶחָיו לֶאֱכל לָחֶם וַיֹּאכְלוּ לֶחֶם וַיָּלִינוּ בָּהָר׃}

verses.original: וַיַּשְׁכֵּם לָבָן בַּבֹּקֶר וַיְנַשֵּׁק לְבָנָיו וְלִבְנוֹתָיו וַיְבָרֶךְ אֶתְהֶם וַיֵּלֶךְ וַיָּשָׁב לָבָן לִמְקֹמוֹ׃

Laban gets up early and says goodbye to his progeny like Abe.

Then he goes home.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יַעֲקֹב כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָם מַחֲנֵה אֱלֹהִים זֶה וַיִּקְרָא שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא מַחֲנָיִם׃

verses.commentary:
Strap in folks, this one's a doozy.

Now Jacob's all by himself.

He wrestles with a man [Lit. אדמ in the original.] until sunrise. “Wrestled” is ʾ-b-q (אבק), a verb found only twice in the Bible, both in this scene (Gen. 32:25–26). BDB derives it from ʾabaq, “dust”: literally something like “dust oneself up with someone,” hence grapple or wrestle; Strong's memorably glosses it “to bedust.” The word may also be playing on the nearby river Jabbok (Yabboq), whose name in turn sounds suspiciously like Jacob (Yaʿaqob): Jacob Yaʿaqob ʾ-b-qs at the Yabboq. So the famous “wrestling” is, at the lexical level, two men rolling around and raising dust, inside a dense little knot of nearly matching sounds. The ordinary noun means fine, easily airborne dust or powder, including the dust kicked up by horses (Ezek. 26:10). For context, Ezekiel 25 is about Ammon, Moab, and Edom; Ezekial 24 is about burning bones and lewdness; and Ezekiel 23 contains the famous line, “There she lusted after her lovers, whose genitals were like those of donkeys and whose emission was like that of horses.” `Bless” is b-r-k (ברך), the same consonantal root as berek, `knee.” The root can also mean to kneel or bow, and the plural “knees” can mean the lap—the space formed by the knees when sitting. Thus the semantic cloud around b-r-k includes blessing, kneeling/bowing, knee, and lap. The overlap is especially suggestive here: Jacob demands a b-r-k, a blessing, in a scene already obsessively concerned with his thigh, hip, and groin—and the same three consonants also point toward kneeling and the lap.

And he I can't even with this. touched the inside of his Red can't handle this. thigh The usual translation, “thigh,” understates the range of the term ירך. Across its 34 occurrences (32 verses) in the Masoretic Text, it means thigh/hip/haunch (Gen 32:26–33; Judg 3:16,21; Ps 45:4), groin/loins (Gen 24:2,9; 47:29; Exod 28:42), reproductive source—descendants literally “come out of” one's ירך (Gen 46:26; Exod 1:5; Judg 8:30)—and, spatially, the side/flank of the tabernacle or altar (Exod 40:22,24; Lev 1:11; Num 3:29,35) and base/shaft of the menorah (Exod 25:31; 37:17; Num 8:4). Num 5:21–27 likewise uses it for the woman's reproductive/groin region; Song 7:2 for the curves of the thighs/hips; Jer 31:19 and Ezek 21:17 for striking the thigh in distress; Ezek 24:4 for an animal haunch; and Judg 15:8 in the idiom שוק על ירך. Thus the range—thigh/hip/haunch groin/loins/reproductive source, and side/flank base—is directly attested in Biblical Hebrew, not merely reconstructed from cognates. Comparative caution: Phoenician KAI 4's yrk is the verb “prolong,” not this noun; Akkadian likewise has no simple yarku “thigh,” though warkatu/urkatu means rear/backside/buttocks (while words such as qablu can denote loins/hips). Consequently Gen 24:2,9 and 47:29's “place your hand under my ירך” can carry much stronger groin/loins/reproductive force than “under my thigh.” Gen 32:26–33's כף ירך, typically translated as thigh, is expressed with the same word elsewhere used for the reproductive loins. The lexical connection between the oath scenes and Jacob's injury is therefore considerably more suggestive than the English gloss “thigh” makes apparent.

And the inside of Jacob’s thigh is dislocated. In Gen. 32:26, “dislocated” is wattēqaʿ (ותקע), from t-q-ʿ (תקע), a remarkably broad verb meaning drive/thrust in, fix or fasten, strike, clap, or blow a horn; “dislocate” here is inferred from context. It is also the verb used throughout Josh. 6 for what the seven priests do with their horns as Israel circles Jericho for seven days, with the rear guard following the Ark. Most suggestively, the same verb occurs in Num. 25:4 for what is to be done to the Israelite leaders after the Baal-Peor apostasy—an episode associated with a fertility cult and explicitly with sexual relations between Israelite men and Moabite women—where its disputed sense may be “hang,” “impale,” or “expose.” The underlying physical range is thus something like forcefully drive, strike, fix, or leave out of position; Gen. 32:26's specific sense “wrench/dislocate” is possible, but hardly lexically inevitable.

Nobody knows what's going on in this line or why it's here. There are some remarkable Semitic comparanda for the sound sequence r-ʾ-l. Classical Arabic raʾl means a young ostrich, with associated imagery of rapid, frightened or wild movement, and Rʾl is independently attested as a personal name in ancient Safaitic. Most strikingly, Ibn Manzur preserves an old poem in which a woman propositions a man and touches his penis; in the immediately following line the speaker describes what happens to his raʾl, which the lexicographer explains through the behavior of the young ostrich. Thus raʾl does not lexically mean “penis,” but an explicitly penile metaphor using the word is independently attested. A neighboring but phonologically distinct Arabic root, r-ʿ-l, means to stab, pierce, or thrust violently, while Aramaic r-ʿ-l means “tremble.” Farther north, the obscure form ʾ-r-ʾ-l occurs in Hebrew and, remarkably, in the Moabite Mesha inscription in connection with Israel; its meaning is disputed, with proposals ranging from a cultic object to a human leader. No corresponding anatomical r-ʾ-l has been securely found in Ugaritic or Akkadian. None of this establishes an etymology for Israel—whose apparent final r-ʾ-l crosses the ordinary morpheme boundary before El—but it supplies an unusually rich set of ancient sound-associations for possible paronomasia, including, rather inconveniently, an independently attested sexual one.

verses.original: וַ יִּשְׁאַל יַעֲקֹב וַיֹּאמֶר הַגִּידָה נָּא שְׁמֶךָ וַיֹּאמֶר לָמָּה זֶּה תִּשְׁאַל לִשְׁמִי וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתוֹ שָׁם׃
verses.english: And Jacob asked. And he said, “Tell your name.” And he said, “Why is this that you ask my name?” And he blessed him there.
verses.commentary:
So Jacob asks. The verb here is שאל (š-ʾ-l), conventionally “ask,” but its semantic range is much wider. Biblical Hebrew uses the root for ask, question, request, petition, seek, desire, demand, beg. One can שאל for information, for an object or favor, for permission, for someone's welfare, or for an answer, favor, or decision from a deity or oracle. The intensity is therefore supplied largely by context.

The same semantic center is ancient and widespread in Semitic. Ugaritic šʾl means to ask or inquire; Akkadian šaʾālu/šâlu covers asking, questioning, inquiring, consulting, asking for, and related petitionary uses; Aramaic and Syriac šʾl include asking, questioning, consulting, requesting, entreating, and demanding; and cognates occur more widely in Semitic. The common idea is not specifically “asking a question,” but seeking something from another by asking—information, an answer, an object, permission, assistance, or compliance.

The grammar of this verse is consequently worth preserving exactly. It does not say “Jacob asked him.” It says “and Jacob שאל, and he said”; the object of שאל is unstated. The following “Tell your name” makes a demand concerning the saying of some name of someone, but “him” is supplied by translators rather than expressed by the Hebrew. Nor does the following “and he said” identify its subject by name: Hebrew simply continues with another masculine singular “he.”

This matters especially in a passage whose masculine pronouns are already remarkably slippery. The lexical range permits the first clause to be heard in a variety of ways, without specifying in the verb itself exactly what was sought or from whom. Only the ensuing speech provides the contextual clue. The response then repeats the same root: שאל, conjugated here as ישאל, which, curiously, is one letter away from ישראל (Israel). Lit. “Jacob begs” in the original text.

He says “What's your שמ?”

He blesses [Lit. ברכ in the original, a verb meaning “to kneel, bend the knee” in the standard Qal form. The form here is the Piel form, the intensified form of the same verb, commonly translated as “bless.”] him שמ.

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא יַעֲקֹב שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם פְּנִיאֵל כִּי רָאִיתִי אֱלֹהִים פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים וַתִּנָּצֵל נַפְשִׁי׃
verses.english: And Jacob called the place’s name Peni-El, “because I’ve seen God face-to-face, and my life has been delivered.”
verses.commentary: Deliverance! The root נ־צ־ל has the basic sense of taking away, stripping away, or pulling something out from somewhere. In the Niphal, as here, it means to be delivered, rescued, saved, or to survive—literally something like being pulled out of danger. The same root develops quite differently in the Piel: to make use of, exploit, or abuse someone or something, presumably from the idea of taking something out of it. Thus “my life has been delivered” can retain a concrete undertone: Jacob's life has been pulled out intact from his face-to-face encounter with God.

verses.original: עַל כֵּן לֹא יֹאכְלוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה אֲשֶׁר עַל כַּף הַיָּרֵךְ עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה כִּי נָגַע בְּכַף יֶרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב בְּגִיד הַנָּשֶׁה׃
verses.english: On account of this the children of Israel to this day will not eat the tendon of the vein that is on the inside of the thigh, because he touched the inside of Jacob’s thigh, the tendon of the vein.
verses.commentary: End of class folks, great job all, no further questions. The singular gid (“sinew/tendon”) here is effectively a hapax in this anatomical construction: outside Gen. 32:32 the noun is rare, appearing only in Isa. 48:4 (an “iron sinew”) and in the plural in Job 10:11; 40:17 and Ezek. 37:6,8. The surrounding vocabulary does little to make “ordinary thigh tendon” secure. Kaf denotes a palm, hollow, sole, or other concave region; Ezekiel's plural “sinews” occurs beside bones and flesh in deliberately graphic bodily imagery; and Job 40:17 is especially suggestive: immediately after the creature's zanab (“tail”), its gide are said to be tightly interwoven around its dual pahad. The latter notoriously uncertain word was understood by the KJV/Strong's tradition as “stones,” i.e. testicles, while many modern versions euphemize it as “thighs”; some translations accordingly render the whole phrase “sinews of his male organs.” Relatedly, pahad is also the ordinary word “fear/dread,” and Genesis itself gives it an extraordinary prominence only one chapter earlier: in Gen. 31:42,53 Jacob calls his father's deity the “Fear of Isaac” and then swears “by the Fear of his father Isaac.” The anatomical pahad of Job 40:17 and the divine title Pahad Isaac need not be the same lexical sense; nevertheless, the juxtaposition is striking in this particular narrative. Jacob swears by Isaac's pahad; Abraham's oath had required Jacob's future father-in-law's predecessor to put his hand “under my yarek”; and shortly afterward Jacob's own yarek is struck at its kaf and associated with a unique singular gid. Thus Isaiah's “iron sinew,” Ezekiel's anatomical usage, Job's tail + paired pahad + tightly woven sinews, Genesis's kaf + yarek (independently capable of denoting the reproductive loins), and Genesis's peculiar “Fear of Isaac” terminology are not individually decisive. Together they provide several independent reasons to suspect that “sinew of the thigh/hip”—and perhaps even the earlier “put your hand under my thigh”—is considerably more anatomically polite than the Hebrew. There are, in short, an awkward number of roads in this vocabulary leading toward the family jewels.

verses.english: And Shechem, son of Hamor, the Hivite, the chieftain of the land, saw her. And he took her and lay with her and degraded her.
verses.commentary:
And Shechem, son of Ass, the guy who runs the land of Shechem, sees her.

And Shechem, now in Dinah, comes to know her better.

Lots of translations call this section “the rape of Dinah.”

Now the text never says rape. It just says degraded. The wording does not necessarily imply rape. “Take” (לקח), “lie with” (שכב), and “degrade” (ענה) can all describe sexual relations without force (cf. Deut 22:13, 23–24). Biblical accounts that unambiguously describe rape add language of physically seizing the woman (Deut 22:25; 2 Sam 13:11–14), which is absent here.

Let's go learn more about this so-called rape.

%		used even to mean marriage (Deut 22:13); and to “lie with” (škab) and to
%		“degrade” (‘innh) are both used in a case that is specifically ruled not
%		to be a rape (Deut 22:23–24). The following case there adds the words
%		“he took hold of her” (22:25), and that case is ruled to be a rape. Also
%		the story of Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13) is comparable to the Dinah
%		story in a notable number of details and terms. In that story there is
%		unquestionably a rape, and it uses the terms “lay with her” and

%		That determining verb in Deuteronomy and in the Tamar story is not
%		present here in the Dinah story. It may be a rape, but we cannot be

verses.commentary:
And just as her soul was leaving her body—she dies by the way—she named the boy Ben-oni. [Lit. Ben-鬼 in some manuscripts. Some pseudepigrapha have Benono, or in one infamous manuscript, 屄nono. Inline Recursive Footnote: The character 屄 is composed of two Chinese radicals: 尸, meaning “body” or “corpse,” and 穴, meaning “hole” under the 尸. These two radicals combine to form 屄, a character whose meaning is rather deep, and of which a more penetrating analysis is not possible in the current footnote.]

We don't know what Ben-oni means. Ben-oni means “son of my sorrow,” fitting Rachel’s death in childbirth; but אוֹן can also mean “strength” or “virility” (cf. Gen. 49:3), giving the name a possible double meaning: “son of my sorrow” and “son of my strength.”

But for some reason Jacob's not happy with that name.

Because the love of his life was gone now.

And all he has left now is his right hand. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” And three other wives.

%	\footnote{
%		Isaac expired. Isaac’s life is markedly different from the lives of his
%		father Abraham and his son Jacob. They both spend time in the two great
%		centers of civilization at that time, Mesopotamia and Egypt, but Isaac
%		never leaves the land of the covenant. They both have multiple wives and
%		concubines, but Isaac has only Rebekah. They both have their names
%		changed, but Isaac does not (see the comment on Gen 17:19). They both
%		fight, but Isaac does not. There are fewer stories about Isaac, and he
%		is a fairly passive figure in them. Regarding the two most famous
%		stories of Isaac: in the story of his near-sacrifice he is acted upon by
%		his father, and in the story of Jacob’s appropriation of Esau’s blessing
%		he is acted upon by his son. Perhaps the explanation for his being
%		different is that he once lay on the altar as a sacrifice, and so his
%		life is consecrated in a singular way. Footnote 35:29. Esau and Jacob,
%		his sons. It is hard to miss the order here: Esau before Jacob. It is
%		not simply a matter of birth order, because Isaac is listed before
%		Ishmael in the corresponding passage (25:9). This seems rather to be a
%		sign of recognition, compassion, and compensation to Esau for his
%		displacement by Jacob.

verses.original: עֵשָׂו לָקַח אֶת נָשָׁיו מִבְּנוֹת כְּנָעַן אֶת עָדָה בַּת אֵילוֹן הַחִתִּי וְאֶת אהֳלִיבָמָה בַּת עֲנָה בַּת צִבְעוֹן הַחִוִּי׃
verses.english: Esau had taken his wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon, the Hittite, and Aholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon, the Hivite,
verses.commentary:
Proper name | Hebrew | Possible Meaning
Adah | עָדָה (ʿĀdāh) | Usually “ornament/adornment,” from עדה in an adornment-related sense. BDB also notes an Arabic comparison possibly suggesting “morning.”
Elon | אֵילוֹן (ʾÊlôn) | “Terebinth/oak” or “oak-grove,” related to אַיִל/אֵלָה tree vocabulary.
Hittite | חִתִּי (Ḥittî) | No persuasive Hebrew lexical etymology. The Hittites were an ancient Anatolian people in the Bronze Age whose empire was centered in what is now modern Turkey.
Aholibamah | אָהֳלִיבָמָה (ʾĀholîbāmāh) | “Tent of the high place”: אֹהֶל “tent” + בָּמָה “high place/elevation.”
Anah | עֲנָה (ʿĂnāh) | Could be compared with ענה, “answer/respond,” but the proper-name derivation is not certain.
Zibeon | צִבְעוֹן (Ṣibʿôn) | Often connected with צבע, “color/dye,” hence “colored/variegated”.
Hivite | חִוִּי (Ḥiwwî) | No secure Hebrew etymology; proposals involving חוה or animal vocabulary are speculative.

Ok so Esau's wives are:

• Beauty, daughter of Oak Tree the Turkey.
• My Tabernacle is Exalted, daughter of Defile daughter of Hyena the Tent Dweller of Wickedness.

verses.english: And these are the kings who ruled in the land of Edom before a king ruled the children of Israel.
verses.commentary:
Proper name | Hebrew | Possible Meaning
Edom | אֱדוֹם | “Red.”
Israel | יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yiśrāʾēl) | Genesis 32 explains it through שרה, “strive/contend,” + אל: roughly “you have striven with God”; morphologically the name may also be understood with El as subject, “El strives/rules.”

These are the kings who ruled Redland before Israel even had a king. Already in the eleventh century AD, the scholar known as Yitzḥaqi—often identified with Isaac ibn Yashush (982–1056), though the identification is uncertain—argued that this list could not have been written by Moses. He dated the passage to the reign of Jehoshaphat, apparently identifying its Edomite kings with figures known from the later monarchy. We know his argument only because Abraham ibn Ezra quotes it here in order to attack it; Ibn Ezra rejects the proposal vehemently, declaring Yitzḥaqi's book רָאוּי לְהִשָּׂרֵף (rāʾûy ləhissārēf) worthy of being burned. Despite his pretense of rejection, Ibn Ezra himself went considerably further. He cryptically pointed to five verses: (1) “the mystery of the twelve” (perhaps the final twelve verses describing Moses' death), (2) “And Moses wrote,” (3) “the Canaanite was then in the land,” (4) “on YHWH's mountain it will be seen,” and (5) “Behold his bedstead was a bedstead of iron,” referring to Og's iron bed still being displayed in Rabbah. Whoever understands these five things, he says, will “recognize the truth”; elsewhere, on the Canaanite problem, he adds: “there is a secret here, and the wise will keep silent” (יש לו סוד והמשכיל ידום).

Midian | מִדְיָן (Midyān) | Biblical Hebrew can associate it with strife/contention vocabulary, but historical ethnonym uncertain.

Jetheth | יְתֵת (Yəṯêṯ) | Derivation explicitly uncertain in the major lexica; older glosses such as “nail” are not secure.

verses.english: And Er, Judah’s firstborn, was bad in YHWH’s eyes, and YHWH killed him.
verses.commentary:
So YHWH kills Lit. ער. (who was bad Lit. רע. for some reason (no one knows why.))

No one. Knows. Why.

Here are some comments scholars have made over the years on this topic:

Er's wickedness was like Onan's wickedness: he deliberately prevented Tamar from becoming pregnant so that pregnancy would not spoil her beauty.
—Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 34b (ca. 500 CE); cf. Rashi (ca. 1040–1105)

Scripture does not tell us Er's sin. His death nevertheless shows that he died for his own wickedness, rather than as punishment upon Judah for the sale of Joseph.
—Nachmanides (1194–1270)

Since Er was evil specifically “in YHWH's eyes,” his crime was apparently hidden from other people but known to God.
—Sforno (1475–1550)

Perhaps Er committed the same sexual offense as Onan; others proposed still other “unnatural” sexual acts.
—Christian commentators, ancient–early modern (ca. 400–1700)

Er was notoriously wicked; whatever his unnamed crime was, it must have been sufficiently grave to provoke extraordinary divine judgment.
—common Protestant interpretation (ca. 1600–1900)

Er was “a Sodomite, say the Hebrews”—though this is “hard to say.” Still, he was “too wicked to live,” and “you may know him to be the son of a Canaanitess.”
—John Trapp (1650s)

Er was “notoriously wicked,” and YHWH slew him “in some extraordinary and remarkable manner.”
—Matthew Poole (1680s)

Er was guilty of some “very heinous sin.” Perhaps, as one tradition held, he had intercourse with Tamar in the “sodomitical” manner.You know the one. YHWH either struck him dead immediately or sent a disease which quickly carried him off.
—John Gill (1748–1763)

Finally, after several thousand years, there appeared the voice of one crying in the wilderness, a man named Adam, the first among men, and he came to all the people of the earth, and he spoke to them, saying:

The Hebrew word expressing Er's wickedness is his own name with the letters reversed: ער, Er; רע, bad.
—Adam Clarke (1762–1832; commentary 1810s)

But the people heeded not the voice of Adam, and they continued their search for the ancient lost secret of Er's wickedness. And their exegesis continued, as they spoke to us, saying.

Er lived “in defiance of God, and his law.” His untimely and childless death was accordingly a divine punishment.
—Joseph Benson (ca. 1811–1818)

In what particular forms he showed his wickedness we are not told; but being the son of a Canaanitish woman, he probably imbibed, in his earliest years, the spirit of Canaanitish idolatry and vice.
—Daniel D. Whedon (ca. 1870s)

Judah had married into a Canaanite family, “casting off the restraints of religion,” so it is “not surprising” that the family produced “bold and unblushing wickedness.” Er was, “in all likelihood,” addicted to the “abominable vices of Canaan.”
—Jamieson, Fausset & Brown (1871)

Two thousand years of commentators thus attempted to discover what terrible thing Er had done. The narrator supplies no crime. Even commentators who eventually noticed something curious about the spelling often went right on looking for the crime. The search continues to the present day.

And Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of the LORD. The nature of his moral failing remains unspecified, but given the insistent pattern of reversal of primogeniture in all these stories, it seems almost sufficient merely to be firstborn in order to incur God’s displeasure: though the firstborn is not necessarily evil, he usually turns out to be obtuse, rash, wild, or otherwise disqualified from carrying on the heritage.
—A comment on AR from someone named R.A. (1997).

		\begin{quote}
		\aC{
			\textsl{Er's wickedness was like Onan's wickedness: he deliberately
			prevented Tamar from becoming pregnant so that pregnancy would not
			spoil her beauty.}\\
			\hfill ---Babylonian Talmud, \emph{Yevamot} 34b (ca. 500 CE); cf. Rashi (ca. 1040--1105)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Scripture does not tell us Er's sin. His death nevertheless
			shows that he died for his own wickedness, rather than as punishment
			upon Judah for the sale of Joseph.}\\
			\hfill ---Nachmanides (1194--1270)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Since Er was evil specifically ``in YHWH's eyes,'' his crime
			was apparently hidden from other people but known to God.}\\
			\hfill ---Sforno (1475--1550)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Perhaps Er committed the same sexual offense as Onan;
			others proposed still other ``unnatural'' sexual acts.}\\
			\hfill ---Christian commentators, ancient--early modern (ca. 400--1700)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Er was notoriously wicked; whatever his unnamed crime was,
			it must have been sufficiently grave to provoke extraordinary
			divine judgment.}\\
			\hfill ---common Protestant interpretation (ca. 1600--1900)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Er was ``a Sodomite, say the Hebrews''---though this
			is ``hard to say.'' Still, he was ``too wicked to live,'' and
			``you may know him to be the son of a Canaanitess.''}\\
			\hfill ---John Trapp (1650s)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Er was ``notoriously wicked,'' and YHWH slew him
			``in some extraordinary and remarkable manner.''}\\
			\hfill ---Matthew Poole (1680s)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Er was guilty of some ``very heinous sin.''
			Perhaps, as one tradition held, he had intercourse
			with Tamar in the ``sodomitical'' manner.\fB{You know the one.}
			YHWH either struck him dead immediately or sent a disease which
			quickly carried him off.}\\
			\hfill ---John Gill (1748--1763)

			\medskip

			\aA{
			Finally, after several thousand years, there appeared
			the voice of one crying in the wilderness, a man named
			Adam, the first among men, and he came to all the people
			of the earth, and he spoke to them, saying:
			}

			\medskip

			\textsl{The Hebrew word expressing Er's wickedness is
			his own name with the letters reversed:
			\heb{ער}, Er; \heb{רע}, bad.}\\
			\hfill ---Adam Clarke (1762--1832; commentary 1810s)

			\medskip

			\aA{
			But the people heeded not the voice of Adam, and they
			continued their search for the ancient lost secret of
			Er's wickedness. And their exegesis continued, as they
			spoke to us, saying.
			}

			\medskip

			\textsl{Er lived ``in defiance of God, and his law.''
			His untimely and childless death was accordingly a
			divine punishment.}\\
			\hfill ---Joseph Benson (ca. 1811--1818)

			\medskip

			\textsl{In what particular forms he showed his wickedness we
			are not told; but being the son of a Canaanitish woman, he
			probably imbibed, in his earliest years, the spirit of
			Canaanitish idolatry and vice.}\\
			\hfill ---Daniel D. Whedon (ca. 1870s)

			\medskip

			\textsl{Judah had married into a Canaanite family, ``casting
			off the restraints of religion,'' so it is ``not surprising''
			that the family produced ``bold and unblushing wickedness.''
			Er was, ``in all likelihood,'' addicted to the ``abominable
			vices of Canaan.''}\\
			\hfill ---Jamieson, Fausset \& Brown (1871)

			\medskip

			\aA{
			Two thousand years of commentators thus attempted to discover
			what terrible thing Er had done. The narrator supplies no
			crime. Even commentators who eventually noticed something 
			curious about the spelling often went right on looking
			for the crime. The search continues to the present day.
			}

			\medskip

			\textsl{And Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of the LORD.
			The nature of his moral failing remains unspecified, 
			but given the insistent pattern of reversal of 
			primogeniture in all these stories, it seems almost 
			sufficient merely to be firstborn in order to incur God’s 
			displeasure: though the firstborn is not necessarily evil, 
			he usually turns out to be obtuse, rash, wild, or otherwise 
			disqualified from carrying on the heritage.}\\
			\hfill ---A comment on AR from someone named R.A. (1997).
		}
		\end{quote}

verses.commentary:
But Onan knew the laws of levirate marriage, which meant that to commemorate the dead broth Er, his kid would be called:

Something, son of Er.

And he didn't like the sound of that, we aren't told why.

So he comes to his brother's wife, but he commits a great sin, this Onan.

He comes in a strange way entirely outside the vanilla manner.

Not in the manner from which progeny arise but rather outside it entirely.

His name has for this reason survived to this day. Onanism primarily means masturbation or coitus interruptus, the withdrawal method during sexual intercourse. According to her biographers, the legendary American writer, poet, and satirist Dorothy Parker, had a pet canary named Onan. Whenever people asked Parker about the bird's unusual name, she would reply, “Because he spills his seed upon the ground.” David Foster Wallace's novel Infinite Jest takes place in the Organization of North American Nations (O.N.A.N.), a supernation formed by the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

So Pharaoh makes some calls and they pull Joseph out of the pit. The pit is the jail. Jails were different back then.

They give him a makeoverHe's been in the pit for a couple years. and bring him to the king.

And the other cows.

• A = B

	}

verses.commentary:

And he drives around the kingdom with guys shouting “Kneel” at people on the street. The word translated “Kneel” here is אברך. Nobody knows what it means, but it is often translated as “kneel,” due to 1. context 2. some Rabbinic interpretations, and 3. similarity to the word ברך, which means both “to kneel” and “to bless.” It's the word from that “I won't let you go until you ברך me” scene, spoken by Jacob (or maybe his unidentified night wrestling partner) right at the end before he (who?) ברךs him. Welcome to the bible. It's wild in here. Despite the common claim that abrek is Egyptian for `kneel,” the required Egyptian verb *brk `kneel” is unattested, and the initial a- is morphologically suspect. The resemblance is actually stronger within Semitic: Hebrew itself has BRK `kneel/make kneel,” while Syriac ʾabrek and Arabic ʾabraka mean `make kneel.” The term may simply be a Hebrew speaking author dressing up a Semitic root to sound foreign.

	\egypt{𓋴𓃀𓏏𓀁 𓋴𓃀𓏏𓀁 𓋴𓃀𓏏𓀁𓁿𓁿𓀿}!

	Then he comes back and wipes the tears off
	and takes Simeon and locks him up in front
	of the others.\fB{
		The oldest brother didn't want to sell him.
		So naturally, second oldest goes to jail.
	}

%	\footnote{
%		Simeon. Since Reuben, the oldest, had originally opposed selling Joseph
%		and had not been present at the time of the deed, it was Simeon, the
%		second oldest, who was responsible, so his imprisonment is a hidden
%		recompense.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְצַו יוֹסֵף וַיְמַלְאוּ אֶת כְּלֵיהֶם בָּר וּלְהָשִׁיב כַּסְפֵּיהֶם אִישׁ אֶל שַׂקּוֹ וְלָתֵת לָהֶם צֵדָה לַדָּרֶךְ וַיַּעַשׂ לָהֶם כֵּן׃
verses.english: And Joseph commanded that they fill their containers with grain and to put their silver back in each man’s sack and to give them provisions for the road. And he did that for them.
verses.commentary: Joseph has their food boxes filled with grain and secretly puts the money they paid back in each brother's bag, as a little prank to freak them out when they eventually realize.

verses.original: וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת שִׁבְרָם עַל חֲמֹרֵיהֶם וַיֵּלְכוּ מִשָּׁם׃
verses.english: And they loaded their grain on their asses and went from there.
verses.commentary: They pack up their asses and go.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת שִׁבְרָם עַל חֲמֹרֵיהֶם וַיֵּלְכוּ מִשָּׁם׃}

verses.original: וַיִּפְתַּח הָאֶחָד אֶת שַׂקּוֹ לָתֵת מִסְפּוֹא לַחֲמֹרוֹ בַּמָּלוֹן וַיַּרְא אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ וְהִנֵּה הוּא בְּפִי אַמְתַּחְתּוֹ׃
verses.english: And one opened his sack to give fodder to his ass at a lodging place, and he saw his silver, and here it was in the mouth of his bag.
verses.commentary: One opens up his bag at a hotel to refuel the donkey, and he realizes he forgot to pay for the food to the guy who has their other bro captive.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל אֶחָיו הוּשַׁב כַּסְפִּי וְגַם הִנֵּה בְאַמְתַּחְתִּי וַיֵּצֵא לִבָּם וַיֶּחֶרְדוּ אִישׁ אֶל אָחִיו לֵאמֹר מַה זֹּאת עָשָׂה אֱלֹהִים לָנוּ׃
verses.english: And he said to his brothers, “My silver’s been put back, and here it is in my bag, too.” And their heart went out, and the brothers trembled to one another, saying, “What is this that God has done to us?”
verses.commentary: They realize they maybe made an oopsie and got another brother killed.

verses.original: וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל יַעֲקֹב אֲבִיהֶם אַרְצָה כְּנָעַן וַיַּגִּידוּ לוֹ אֵת כּל הַקֹּרֹת אֹתָם לֵאמֹר׃
verses.english: And they came to Jacob, their father, to the land of Canaan, and told him all the things that happened to them, saying,
verses.commentary:
They get back to dad's house.

Jacob's like “How was Egypt boys?”

verses.original: דִּבֶּר הָאִישׁ אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ אִתָּנוּ קָשׁוֹת וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָנוּ כִּמְרַגְּלִים אֶת הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: “The man, the lord of the land, spoke with us hard and accused us of spying on the land.
verses.commentary:
They're like

• The king called us spies.
• He kept asking about our family.
• We said Benjamin's at home and Joseph's, well.
• He wanted us to prove Benjamin existed.
• By bringing him there.
• Then he kept us in jail for three days.
• Then he sold us some food.
• He kept Simeon in jail to make sure we're honest.
• Then we realized we forgot to pay him.
• How've you been?

tex.original: \hJ{דִּבֶּר הָאִישׁ אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ אִתָּנוּ קָשׁוֹת וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָנוּ כִּמְרַגְּלִים אֶת הָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
They're like

	\begin{enumerate}
	\item The king called us spies.
	\item He kept asking about our family.
	\item We said Benjamin's at home and Joseph's, well.
	\item He wanted us to prove Benjamin existed.
	\item By bringing him there.
	\item Then he kept us in jail for three days.
	\item Then he sold us some food.
	\item He kept Simeon in jail to make sure we're honest.
	\item Then we realized we forgot to pay him.
	\item How've you been?
	\end{enumerate}

verses.original: וַנֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו כֵּנִים אֲנָחְנוּ לֹא הָיִינוּ מְרַגְּלִים׃
verses.english: And we said to him, ‘We’re honest. We weren’t spying.
verses.commentary: Their version is a bit slower.

verses.original: שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר אֲנַחְנוּ אַחִים בְּנֵי אָבִינוּ הָאֶחָד אֵינֶנּוּ וְהַקָּטֹן הַיּוֹם אֶת אָבִינוּ בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן׃
verses.english: We’re twelve brothers, our father’s sons; one is no more, and the youngest is with our father in the land of Canaan today’.
verses.commentary: They explain about item two.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלֵינוּ הָאִישׁ אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ בְּזֹאת אֵדַע כִּי כֵנִים אַתֶּם אֲחִיכֶם הָאֶחָד הַנִּיחוּ אִתִּי וְאֶת רַעֲבוֹן בָּתֵּיכֶם קְחוּ וָלֵכוּ׃
verses.english: And the man, the lord of the land, said to us, ‘By this I’ll know that you’re honest: leave one brother from among you with me, and take for the famine in your houses and go,
verses.commentary: We've sort been over this.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלֵינוּ הָאִישׁ אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ בְּזֹאת אֵדַע כִּי כֵנִים אַתֶּם אֲחִיכֶם הָאֶחָד הַנִּיחוּ אִתִּי וְאֶת רַעֲבוֹן בָּתֵּיכֶם קְחוּ וָלֵכוּ׃}

verses.original: וְהָבִיאוּ אֶת אֲחִיכֶם הַקָּטֹן אֵלַי וְאֵדְעָה כִּי לֹא מְרַגְּלִים אַתֶּם כִּי כֵנִים אַתֶּם אֶת אֲחִיכֶם אֶתֵּן לָכֶם וְאֶת הָאָרֶץ תִּסְחָרוּ׃
verses.english: and bring your youngest brother to me, so I may know that you aren’t spies, that you’re honest. I’ll give you your brother, and you’ll go around in the land.’”
verses.commentary:
Spies don't have younger brothers.

They also can't hire someone to pretend.

verses.english: And it was: they were emptying their sacks, and here was each man’s bundle of silver in his sack, and they saw the bundles of their silver, they and their father, and they were afraid.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם יַעֲקֹב אֲבִיהֶם אֹתִי שִׁכַּלְתֶּם יוֹסֵף אֵינֶנּוּ וְשִׁמְעוֹן אֵינֶנּוּ וְאֶת בִּנְיָמִן תִּקָּחוּ עָלַי הָיוּ כֻלָּנָה׃
verses.english: And their father, Jacob, said to them, “You’ve bereaved me! Joseph is gone, and Simeon’s gone, and you’ll take Benjamin. All these have happened to me!”
verses.commentary: Now Jacob's mad, which makes sense in either source.

verses.english: And Reuben said to his father, saying, “Kill my two sons if I don’t bring him back to you. Put him in my hand, and I’ll bring him back to you.”
verses.commentary:
Reuben, the eldest brother, pipes up with a highly responsible idea, saying:

Dad it's fine! If Simeon doesn't make it back alive, you can kill two of your grandsons!

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר רְאוּבֵן אֶל אָבִיו לֵאמֹר אֶת שְׁנֵי בָנַי תָּמִית אִם לֹא אֲבִיאֶנּוּ אֵלֶיךָ תְּנָה אֹתוֹ עַל יָדִי וַאֲנִי אֲשִׁיבֶנּוּ אֵלֶיךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא יֵרֵד בְּנִי עִמָּכֶם כִּי אָחִיו מֵת וְהוּא לְבַדּוֹ נִשְׁאָר וּקְרָאָהוּ אָסוֹן בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכוּ בָהּ וְהוֹרַדְתֶּם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִי בְּיָגוֹן שְׁאוֹלָה׃
verses.english: And he said, “My son will not go down with you. Because his brother’s dead, and he’s left by himself, and if some harm would happen to him on the way in which you’re going then you’ll bring down my gray hair in anguish to Sheol.”
verses.commentary:
Jacob is not convinced.

Benjamin's staying.

verses.english: And the famine was heavy in the land.
verses.commentary: The famine's still a thing.

tex.english: \eJ{And the famine was heavy in the land.}

verses.original: וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר כִּלּוּ לֶאֱכֹל אֶת הַשֶּׁבֶר אֲשֶׁר הֵבִיאוּ מִמִּצְרָיִם וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵיהֶם אֲבִיהֶם שֻׁבוּ שִׁבְרוּ לָנוּ מְעַט אֹכֶל׃
verses.english: And it was when they had finished eating the grain that they had brought from Egypt: and their father said to them, “Go back. Buy us a little food.”
verses.commentary:
They run out of food again.

Dad thinks it might be time for another Egypt trip.

He gives each brother some clothes.

He gives Benjamin five time more clothes.

He also gives Benjamin infinity dollars.

Ok so, as we learned from the “brothers sell Joseph” episode, And also from the two “Joseph makes his brothers think they forgot to pay” episodes. the price of a family member is 20 of these silver money units.

Family members can be sold for 20 money, in this family, according to the brothers.

Joseph's presumably been thinking about that fact a lot over all those years while he was becoming the unofficial king of everything down here.

Now, if a family member costs 20 money, then:

(10 half-brothers + 1 Dinah + 1 Dad + 1 Leah + 1 Bilhah + 1 Zilpah)*20

is 15 peopleMom's dead, so she doesn't count. times 20 silver.

That is, 300 money units.

Now, Joseph has one full brother, Benjamin.

Joseph and Benjamin don't figure into the calculation, because they're about to do something funny. Ready?

Joseph gives exactly that amount of money to Benjamin.

And also 5x the clothes.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה אֶל אֶחָיו מַה מַּעֲשֵׂיכֶם וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה רֹעֵה צֹאן עֲבָדֶיךָ גַּם אֲנַחְנוּ גַּם אֲבוֹתֵינוּ׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your work?” And they said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, both we and our fathers,”
verses.commentary:
And the king's like,

So, what do you all do for a living?

So naturally they're like “Sheep.”

The brothers call themselves shepherds despite Joseph's advice to say cattlemen (46:33–34). This tension occurs within J, rather than between sources: they refuse to disguise their occupation. Pharaoh grants them good land, but then addresses Joseph instead and offers them work managing cattle anyway.

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה אֶל יוֹסֵף לֵאמֹר אָבִיךָ וְאַחֶיךָ בָּאוּ אֵלֶיךָ׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, saying, “Your father and your brothers have come to you.
verses.commentary:
So nowLit. tsoʾno (Heb. צאנו) in O.T. Pharaoh blacks out and forgets verses 1-4.

And Pharaoh says to Joseph, “Your family is here.”

REF: This section, 47:5–12, comes in the middle of a J text. But Jacob says here that he is 130 years old and that Abraham and Isaac lived longer, while in J YHWH has decreed that no human will live more than 120 years. It is in P that ages are given and that Abraham and Isaac live longer. Moreover, this section has other characteristics of P: The phrases “the days of the years” and “the years of your life” occur only in P. The terms “residences” and “possession” occur only in P. The phrase “as he commanded” occurs fifty-three other times in Genesis–Numbers, and fifty-two are in P. And it is in P that the people live in Rameses. Nonetheless, we should recognize that it is possible that the Redactor combined some material from J or E with P to form this section. The reference to Goshen (v. 6) may be in conflict with the reference to Rameses, and P never mentions Goshen elsewhere. The words “Let them live in Goshen” may have originally read “they lived in Goshen,” which would look the same in the consonantal text. And Goshen is what the brothers requested in the J text (v. 4). Further, this matter is complicated by the fact that the Septuagint text is different, which may be related to the recurrence of the words “let them live in the land of Goshen” in vv. 4 and 6.

tex.english:

		And Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my
		residences are a hundred thirty years. The days of the
		years of my life have been few and bad, and they haven’t
		attained the days of the years of my fathers’ lives, in
		the days of their residences.”
	}
tex.commentary:
\aC{
	He says he's 130.

	And it's been a short, bad life.%
	}
%	\footnote{
%		few and bad, and … haven’t attained. Jacob is critical of his life, in
%		itself and in comparison with Abraham’s and Isaac’s lives. This is
%		consistent with the telling of the story until now, which has not
%		excused or sanitized Jacob the way some Sunday schools, early
%		commentaries, and modern interpreters do. The biblical writers seem to
%		have been quite content to leave their heroes imperfect. Why? Why even
%		conceive of such a story? Perhaps the author thus pointed to deception
%		in the world and said, “It comes back.” Or perhaps the author conceived
%		it in literary protest against the ancient Near Eastern practice of
%		glorifying national heroes. As has frequently been observed, to read the
%		ancient reports one would think that no Near Eastern king ever lost a
%		battle. A clear majority of the biblical authors, however, show their
%		heroes with weaknesses and imperfections, making errors and committing
%		offenses. For whatever purpose the author of the Jacob cycle conceived
%		this story, the fact is that this author exhibited an historical,
%		realistic impulse, a sense of the psychological complexity of families:
%		sibling rivalry, fathers and sons in conflict, mothers finding channels
%		of influence in male family structures, women torn between fathers and
%		husbands. Further, it may be said that by not glorifying its human
%		heroes the text glorifies its other central figure, the deity. The
%		message here may well be that God can work through anyone: through an
%		all-obedient man, a passive, dim-eyed patriarch, or a deceiver.
%	}

verses.english: And I: when I was coming from Paddan Aram, Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan on the way when there was still a span of land to come to Ephrat, and I buried her there on the Ephrat road. That’s Bethlehem.”
verses.commentary: I buried Rachel at Bethlehem, on the road to Fertility. This is still El Shaddai talking by the way. REF: Verse 7 fits uncomfortably in its context, connecting neither to the preceding nor to the following verses. And it merges elements of two sources: It refers to Paddan Aram, which is characteristic of P, but it says “there was still a span of land to come to Ephrath,” and it refers to Rachel’s being buried on the Ephrath road, which comes from E (Gen 35:16–20). It therefore appears to be an addition that the Redactor made to the text. Perhaps its function was to separate the two conflicting passages about Ephraim and Manasseh that precede and follow it. See the next note. Alternatively, this verse might after all be P, because it fits with the next P passage (49:29–33). As a unit these two passages could be saying: “As for me: Rachel died and was buried on the road, but when I die I want to be buried back in my ancestral tomb with the other patriarchs and matriarchs.” It is therefore uncertain whether v. 7 is P or R.

verses.original:
מיד אביר יעקב

משמר ר־בני ישראל

מרע
verses.english: From the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, from the Keeper of the sons of Israel, from the Shepherd.
verses.commentary:
Are we still talking about Joseph?

As recognized by most scholars, MT does not make sense, and is also overly long. In the first two words of the colon, משם רעה, there is a conflated reading. One or two letters have dropped out by haplography, the original variants being miššōmēr and mērō'ê; written out in early orthography the text would have appeared something like this, משמר<מא>רע or משמר<רע>.

The word אבן is impossible in this context. What is required is a parallel to ya'ăqōb, and “Israel-stone,” whatever that might mean, will not do. The simplest emendation is to read bənê (בני) for 'eben; the intrusion of the aleph might be due to the influence of אביר in the first colon of vs. 24b.

verses.english: and Joseph saw children of Ephraim’s of the third generation. Also children of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph’s knees.
verses.commentary:
Ok so in Exod 34:6–7, we hear about how merciful YHWH is, because he only “visits the wrongdoing of fathers upon children and upon children’s children, upon the third and upon the fourth [generation].”

So if you're a dad or mom, you're the 0th generation.

Then children are the first generation, grandchildren the second, and great-grandchildren the third.

Thus “children of Ephraim's of the third generation” is someone's great-grandkids.

Could be Joseph's great-grandkids, or maybe Ephraim's.

The second half of the sentence describes some other great-grandkids in a different way, which may or may not mean there's a different number of generations in that half of the sentence.

Fortunately, some people who love begat lists more than anything else in the world wrote something called the book of Chronicles, which fails to clarify the issue, and makes the confusion worse.

Moving on.

verses.english: And they set commanders of work-companies over it in order to degrade it with their burdens. And they built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses.
verses.commentary:
So they set up this wild system that's sort of like slavery but instead of being owned by an individual person you just have to spent like N% of your effort and energy and time during the year working on stuff for the government.

Just like now.

The Hebrew missîm means compulsory labor imposed on a community, rather than private household slavery. Israel builds cities while living apart in Goshen (8:18; 9:26). Solomon later imposes similar labor, and Israelites eventually kill the official responsible (1 Kings 5:27–28; 12:18). Such state control over their bodies clashes with a national identity grounded in escape from slavery.

verses.commentary:
His sister stands still at a distance to see what happens. Heb. ותתצב, from יצב, means to station oneself or take one's stand. In the bible this verb is never used for walking, running, or otherwise moving around; it consistently describes taking or holding a stationary position. So “stood still” captures the sense well. This detail has been surprisingly little discussed.

Many popular depictions of this scene depict the sister running after the basket, while the others show her walking after it while it drifts away. To our knowledge, no depiction of this scene has yet had the biblical literalism or balls to show the scene as it is depicted in the text.

This little detail is important because it determines whether or not the baby in question already lived at the pharaoh's house to begin with.

God I love this book.

verses.commentary:
The baby gets older.

Eventually, the mom brings the baby to Pharaoh's daughter.

At this point they finally give the baby a name. He was just “baby” before this.

The king's daughter chooses the name, which turns out to be (1) an Egyptian throne name common around the 1200s B.C., and (2) not described as an Egyptian name by the text, even though the Egyptian girl names the boy, and (3) described by the text as (surprise) a Hebrew pun, and the king's daughter decides to name him (drumroll)

Drew.

Because I drew him from the water.

Heb. מְשִׁה (msh) because מְשִׁיתִֽהוּ (mshitho) from the water.
