%	\footnote{
%		Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. The story is
%		intriguingly
%		similar to the legend of the Mesopotamian king Sargon,
%		found in Assyrian
%		and Babylonian texts, in which a priestess places her
%		infant son in a
%		basket of rushes with pitch on its exterior and casts
%		him into the
%		river, and a water-drawer retrieves the baby and rears
%		him as his son.
%		This and other literary parallels to the birth account
%		of Moses suggest
%		how enigmatic the biblical story is. Freud observed that
%		such stories
%		generally involve three steps: (1) a child is born of
%		noble or royal
%		lineage, (2) the child comes to be brought up as a
%		commoner, and (3) the
%		child grows up and eventually arrives back at his
%		rightful place in a
%		royal house. Freud noted that such stories were
%		conceived etiologically,
%		composed as justifications of cases in which commoners
%		rose to thrones.
%		The historical truth in such cases lay in the second
%		step: the king
%		really came from commoner roots. The story was composed
%		to legitimize
%		his kingship, as an answer to those who would deny his
%		royal blood.
%		Freud considered the birth story of Moses against this
%		background and
%		suggested the possibility that here, too, the truth
%		behind the etiology
%		lay in the second step, that Moses was an Egyptian, and
%		that the birth
%		story was composed to explain how an Egyptian had come
%		to be the leader
%		of the Israelites. Freud’s interest (on this particular
%		point of his
%		larger study) was primarily historical, and his
%		hypothesis has never
%		been proved or disproved; but it is also important
%		because it indicates
%		what the Torah and its audience valued. In the Israelite
%		story, the
%		values are reversed. The royal house is step two, the
%		aberration, rather
%		than the prized position. Moses’ royal placement simply
%		is not what is
%		important. There is no information about his early life
%		in the Egyptian
%		court. We are informed that he is nursed by his own
%		mother, but we are
%		not certain what this report is supposed to establish.
%		We cannot even be
%		certain that it means that Moses thus knows that he is
%		Israelite. Later
%		the text says that he “went out to his brothers and saw
%		their burdens”
%		(2:11), but this wording, too, is not definitive as to
%		whether he knows
%		that the Israelites are his kin. There is even ambiguity
%		in his killing
%		of an Egyptian taskmaster whom he sees striking a slave:
%		is it because
%		of his bond with the Israelites or his sense of justice?
%		In a curious
%		parallel to the deity Himself, Moses’ background and
%		motives are
%		mysterious. Footnote 2:10. she called his name Moses.
%		Even learned
%		people often recall this story out of order, imagining
%		the Pharaoh’s
%		daughter naming Moses as she draws him from the water,
%		but she does not
%		in fact name him until after he has grown and his mother
%		brings him to
%		her. What was he called until that time? Classical and
%		recent
%		commentators have not addressed this. Since the text
%		does not tell us,
%		we must assume that the concern is to explain the origin
%		of the name
%		Moses and that there is no interest in pursuing whether
%		there was any
%		prior name given by his parents. Presumably the only
%		name known in
%		tradition and history was Moses, and so the author was
%		not free to make
%		up any other. And the story had to ascribe the naming to
%		the Pharaoh’s
%		daughter because she was the one in power, the one who
%		would present him
%		to the Egyptian society, and so on. Still, we can hardly
%		resist
%		wondering why the parents would not be pictured as
%		giving their son a
%		name. If he is with them until he is weaned, that may be
%		several years,
%		and we can hardly resist imagining what the parents
%		would call him. I
%		imagine—this is my midrash—that they do not give him a
%		name. They call
%		him “the child” (Hebrew hayyeled). When they talk to him
%		they call him
%		“my child” (yaldî). And this gives those years a
%		mysterious, portentous
%		quality. They know that his naming simply is not in
%		their power. And so
%		his fate is not in their hands either. Count how many
%		times you call
%		your child by his or her name in a day, and you will
%		know how many times
%		these parents are reminded of their unique situation:
%		thankful that
%		their son alone is spared from death but sad and
%		frightened that he will
%		be raised by others, from the very household that is
%		their enemy, and
%		worried that he will not know who his real people and
%		family are. From
%		the perspective of Jewish history, this is not a
%		singular experience. In
%		the twentieth century Jewish parents in Europe gave
%		their children to
%		non-Jewish families to save them during the holocaust.
%		Footnote 2:10.
%		Because I drew him. The naming of Moses argues both for
%		and against the
%		story’s historicity. On one hand, there is the
%		unlikelihood of the idea
%		that the princess would know Hebrew, let alone choose to
%		derive the
%		baby’s name from a Hebrew etymology. And in fact the
%		name Moses is not
%		Hebrew. It is Egyptian, meaning “is born,” as in the
%		name Ramesses,
%		meaning “Ra (the sun god) bore him.” On the other hand,
%		the fact that
%		the great leader of the Israelites has an Egyptian name
%		(as do other
%		early priests: Phinehas, Hophni) is evidence that
%		Israelites did indeed
%		live for some time in Egypt. Names are valuable evidence
%		in tracing a
%		community’s origins and history. One might suggest that
%		the Egyptian
%		name Moses was just made up to make the story sound
%		authentic. But we
%		can be fairly certain that the Israelites did not make
%		it up, precisely
%		because they told the story about the princess calling
%		him Moses
%		“because I drew him”—which shows that the Israelites
%		were not conscious
%		of the name’s Egyptian meaning!
%	}

So just a few quick notes...

• הִנֵּה (HNH). “Check this out.” An interjection used to call attention to an unexpected or noteworthy circumstance.

• הַסְּנֶה (HSNH). The bush.

• The Hebrew word in the narrative that is translated into English as bush is seneh (Hebrew: סְנֶה, romanized: SNH), which refers in particular to brambles.
• Seneh (SNH) is a dis legomenon, only appearing in two places, both of which describe the burning bush.
• The use of Ha Seneh (HSNH) may be a deliberate pun on Har Sinai (Heb: הר סיני), a feature common in Hebrew texts.

• בֹּעֵר BʿR.

• (intransitive) to burn.
• (archaic) to be stupid, dull-hearted, unreceptive.Don't worry, no one talks like this anymore.
• (dated) A fool, a stupid person.Ibd.

• בָּאֵשׁ BʾSH.

• A Hebrew root meaning “to stink” or “smell bad.”

• To be bad. Cognate with Aramaic 𐡁𐡀𐡔 (“to be bad, displeasing”).

• The preposition ב (b) meaning “in,” followed by אש (ash) meaning “fire.”

• (Biblical) To stink, have a foul smell. (Exodus 7:18, Exodus 16:20.)

• Derived terms: נִבְאַשׁ (“to become stinking; to become hateful”), הִבְאִישׁ (to make stinking; to ostracize”)

• A term translated by KJV as: stink (10x), abhor (3x), abomination (1x), loathsome (1x), stinking savour (1x), utterly (1x).

• Cognates:

• Akkadian ba'āshu (“to be bad”);
• Old Aramaic 𐡁𐡀𐡔;
• Biblical Aramaic 𐡁𐡀𐡔;
• Syriac ܒܐܫ;
• Arabic ba'isa (“to be unhappy”);
• Ethiopic ba'sa (“to be bitter”).

• בָּאֳשָׁה (f.n., MH): noxious plant. An ancient derivation from Semitic *b'sh (“to be bad”); compare Syriac ܒܝܫܐ and Ethiopic ba'sa (“to be bad”).

• From Northern Kurdish baş, from Classical Persian باش (bâš, “imperative of be”). This line is widely agreed to be a later scribal addition by a good for nothing trickster, likely to poke fun at entities or deities whose name is known to be “To Be” in some conjugation of the verb. Lit. eлtities or dㅌities in the original, perhaps a reference to El Shaddai. Or rather two of them, that is. Lit. tハt is.
• Outline of biblical usage across Hebrew verb forms:

• (Qal) to stink, smell bad;
• (Niphal) to become odious, to make oneself odious;
• (Hiphil) to stink, emit a stinking odour, to cause to stink, of wickedness (fig.);
• (Hithpael) to make oneself odious;
• (TWOT)Twʿt? to abhor.

• (Biblical) stench, stink, fetid smell. (Isaiah 34:3, Amos 4:10, Joel 2:20.) Esp. Joel. Lit. “ḇāš... ṣa-ḥă-nā (opens concordance; flip flip.) Word origin: from an unused word.” in the original, meaning of Heb. and Eng. straightforward. Game recognizes game.

• 2 Samuel 12:8. When YHWH's describing Saul's wives as having been given into David's [this word] now that they're his wives, and
• Exodus 4:6. Here.

Now for the word. Take it away, Lord.

verses.english: And Moses said to YHWH, “Please, my Lord, I’m not a man of words. Neither yesterday nor the day before—nor since you spoke to your servant! Because I’m heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.”
verses.commentary:
So then Drew says something that any of us would say after seeing three real actual miracles that definitely weren't just god tier wordplay.

He says “Please, my Lord, I'm not a man of words.”

He then goes on to deliver a very well-worded mini-speech.

Side Note: Heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue probably means “I don't speak Hebrew.” “Heavy of tongue” occurs elsewhere only in Ezekiel 3:5–7, where it describes foreigners whose language Ezekiel can't speak. In the current scene, where Moses is being asked to speak to Israel’s elders, Moses may be protesting that he doesn't speak Hebrew.

%		speak foreign

%		protest here in

%		has been raised

tex.commentary:
So then Drew says whatever this means.

%	\footnote{
%		send by the hand you’ll send. There are two opposite
%		meanings that this
%		strange clause may have. It may mean: send whoever—which
%		is to say,
%		anyone but me. Or it may mean that Moses now acquiesces
%		to the divine
%		will, in the sense of “Very well, then, send the one you
%		want.” The fact
%		that God is angry at Moses in the next verse fits more
%		naturally with
%		the former meaning. In either case, the one common
%		element of the two
%		meanings is: they both denote that Moses is out of
%		excuses. God has
%		nullified each of his four attempts to avoid this task.
%		He can only
%		acquiesce or beg off. He cannot raise problems or
%		objections. This is
%		also further evidence that fear of the task is what has
%		motivated Moses
%		all along. He is forced now to the essential point. It
%		is not “Who am I”
%		or “What shall I tell them?” or “They won’t believe me.”
%		It is Moses’
%		reluctance about the hand whom God has chosen to send.
%		Through all five
%		responses, Moses’ reluctance stands out and perhaps
%		comes as a surprise
%		to many who find it difficult to imagine someone’s
%		receiving a prophetic
%		commission directly from God and trying to avoid it. Yet
%		this image of
%		the reluctant prophet recurs in several other places in
%		the Bible
%		(Elijah, Jonah, Jeremiah). It does not appear to me to
%		be simply a
%		recurring literary motif in the way that some
%		understand, for example,
%		the “wise courtier” theme. It seems rather to reflect a
%		shared
%		conviction, by a number of the biblical authors, that it
%		is not
%		necessarily an honor or a joy to be a prophet. It is a
%		burden, almost
%		beyond human endurance. Here, in the book that
%		introduces the role of
%		the prophet as the individual who brings a revelation to
%		a community, we
%		learn from the beginning that this is not attractive. To
%		hear the voice
%		of God is frightening. To experience the divine power is
%		terrifying. To
%		deliver a divine message to the community is thankless,

%	\footnote{
%		your Levite brother. This means a fellow Levite. The
%		text does not yet
%		identify Aaron as Moses’ actual brother. That is not
%		stated explicitly
%		until Exod 6:20. After that, Aaron is referred to as
%		“your brother”

%		Footnote 4:14. I knew
%		that he will speak! This has usually been taken to mean
%		only that God is

%		and context

%		informing Moses

%		talking for

%		something in advance), not of God preordaining or
%		manipulating human
%		affairs. This in turn opens the question of why God
%		would be angry at
%		Moses’ protest. The ambiguity here is tied to the
%		complexity of Hebrew
%		verb tenses (which are not simply past, present, and

verses.english: And you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘YHWH said this: My child, my firstborn, is Israel.

tex.original: \hE{וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		My child, my firstborn, is Israel. God tells Moses to
%		say this to
%		Pharaoh, but Moses is never reported as saying it. He
%		also is never
%		reported as saying the rest of this message: “Should you
%		refuse to let
%		it go, here: I’m killing your child, your firstborn!”
%		Why does he not
%		say this to Pharaoh? It is apparently because his first
%		words to Pharaoh
%		do not work. Moses begins by speaking strongly to
%		Pharaoh: “YHWH said,
%		‘Let my people go.’” But Pharaoh, unmoved, replies, “I
%		don’t know YHWH,
%		and I won’t let Israel go.” Moses then changes his
%		approach
%		dramatically. He starts over and this time does not use
%		the commanding
%		wording (the imperative), but rather the polite particle
%		of request
%		(Hebrew n’) and the gentler form: “please that we might
%		go” (the
%		cohortative). Moses has backed off somewhat and taken a
%		more
%		conciliatory approach rather than taking the even
%		tougher approach of
%		threatening Pharaoh with the death of his own son. This
%		conciliatory
%		wording is given to Moses at the burning bush as well
%		(3:18), so it
%		appears that God is giving Moses both the tough and the
%		gentle options.
%		In any negotiation—in law, business, or any human
%		relationship,
%		including marriage—one must use wisdom to know when to
%		exercise each
%		approach.
%	}

verses.original: וָאֹמַר אֵלֶיךָ שַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנִי וְיַעַבְדֵנִי וַתְּמָאֵן לְשַׁלְּחוֹ הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הֹרֵג אֶת בִּנְךָ בְּכֹרֶךָ׃
verses.english: And I’ve said to you: Let my child go and serve me. And should you refuse to let it go, here: I’m killing your child, your firstborn!’”

tex.original: \hE{וָאֹמַר אֵלֶיךָ שַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנִי וְיַעַבְדֵנִי וַתְּמָאֵן לְשַׁלְּחוֹ הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הֹרֵג אֶת בִּנְךָ בְּכֹרֶךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיְהִי בַדֶּרֶךְ בַּמָּלוֹן וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁהוּ יְהֹוָה וַיְבַקֵּשׁ הֲמִיתוֹ׃
verses.english: And he was on the way, at a lodging place, and YHWH met him, and he asked to kill him.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיְהִי בַדֶּרֶךְ בַּמָּלוֹן וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁהוּ יְהֹוָה וַיְבַקֵּשׁ הֲמִיתוֹ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		he asked to kill him. No one knows what the episode at
%		the lodging place
%		means. The explanation that accounts for more of the
%		connections than
%		any other is that of my colleague William Propp: The
%		reason that God
%		seeks to put Moses to death is because Moses still bears
%		the bloodguilt
%		for having killed an Egyptian. The blood of the
%		circumcision serves to
%		expiate the guilt, making it possible for Moses to live
%		and return to
%		Egypt. The word for “blood” in this story is the plural
%		dmîm, which is
%		usually associated with bloodguilt. The word for
%		“bridegroom” also means
%		“circumcision” in Arabic (and in some cultures
%		circumcision is performed
%		just before marriage). Propp suggests that the original
%		bridegroom/circumcision connection had been lost by the
%		time this story
%		was composed, and so it was created to explain an old
%		expression: tan
%		dmîm, “bridegroom of blood.” Also, this use of blood to
%		avert death is a
%		foreshadowing of the tenth plague in Egypt. Still, like
%		all explanations
%		I have seen, this leaves the question of why God would
%		choose Moses,
%		make a miraculous appearance to him, insist on his going
%		to Egypt
%		despite his five attempts to avoid it, and then seek to
%		kill him. I
%		therefore understand the confused use of the pronoun
%		“he” in this story
%		in a different way. All commentators recognize that it
%		is unclear when
%		it refers to God, to Moses, or to Moses’ son. But they
%		all take the
%		first “he” to refer to God: He (God) sought to kill
%		Moses. I am raising
%		the possibility (reflected in my translation: “he asked
%		to kill him”)
%		that it means that Moses is asking God to take his life
%		(rather than
%		send him to Egypt). This is consistent with another time
%		in Moses’ life
%		when he will ask God to kill him (Num 11:15, where he
%		says emphatically:
%		“Kill me!”). And it fits with a model of prophets who
%		ask God to take
%		their lives—Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (4:4)—or say
%		that they
%		prefer death to being prophets—Jeremiah (20:14–18).
%		(Note that these are
%		the same three prophets who, like Moses, are famous for
%		being reluctant;
%		see the comment on 4:13.) If Moses is seeking his own
%		death here, then
%		Zipporah’s action might be understood as her passionate
%		response to her
%		husband’s wish to die: You have a wife! You have a son,
%		who should live
%		to marry and be a part of the covenant!
%	}

verses.original: וַתִּקַּח צִפֹּרָה צֹר וַתִּכְרֹת אֶת ערְלַת בְּנָהּ וַתַּגַּע לְרַגְלָיו וַתֹּאמֶר כִּי חֲתַן דָּמִים אַתָּה לִי׃

verses.original: וַיַּגֵּד מֹשֶׁה לְאַהֲרֹן אֵת כּל דִּבְרֵי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר שְׁלָחוֹ וְאֵת כּל הָאֹתֹת אֲשֶׁר צִוָּהוּ׃
verses.english: And Moses told Aaron all YHWH’s words that He had sent him and all the signs that He had commanded him.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּגֵּד מֹשֶׁה לְאַהֲרֹן אֵת כּל דִּבְרֵי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר שְׁלָחוֹ וְאֵת כּל הָאֹתֹת אֲשֶׁר צִוָּהוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּלֶךְ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן וַיַּאַסְפוּ אֶת כּל זִקְנֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃
verses.english: And Moses went, and Aaron, and they gathered all the elders of the children of Israel,

tex.original: \hE{וַיֵּלֶךְ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן וַיַּאַסְפוּ אֶת כּל זִקְנֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר אַהֲרֹן אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וַיַּעַשׂ הָאֹתֹת לְעֵינֵי הָעָם׃
verses.english: and Aaron spoke all the words that YHWH had spoken to Moses. And he did the signs before the people’s eyes.

tex.original: \hE{וַיְדַבֵּר אַהֲרֹן אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וַיַּעַשׂ הָאֹתֹת לְעֵינֵי הָעָם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּאֲמֵן הָעָם וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ כִּי פָקַד יְהֹוָה אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכִי רָאָה אֶת ענְיָם וַיִּקְּדוּ וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ׃
verses.english: And the people believed, and they heard that YHWH had taken account of the children of Israel and that He had seen their degradation. And they knelt and bowed.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּאֲמֵן הָעָם וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ כִּי פָקַד יְהֹוָה אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכִי רָאָה אֶת ענְיָם וַיִּקְּדוּ וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ׃}

verses.original: וְאַחַר בָּאוּ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיָחֹגּוּ לִי בַּמִּדְבָּר׃
verses.english: And after that Moses and Aaron came and said to Pharaoh, “YHWH, God of Israel, said this: ‘Let my people go, so they will celebrate a festival for me in the wilderness.’”

tex.original: \hJ{וְאַחַר בָּאוּ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיָחֹגּוּ לִי בַּמִּדְבָּר׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Moses and Aaron came and said to Pharaoh. It is against
%		the background
%		of the confrontation between Moses and God at the bush
%		that we must
%		picture the confrontation between Moses and the Pharaoh.
%		The narrative
%		that precedes the burning-bush scene gives us relatively
%		little
%		background of the sort that would add depth and
%		understanding of the
%		character of Moses at the point of his meeting God.
%		Moses’ meeting with
%		the Pharaoh, on the other hand, comes after we have seen
%		him in
%		conversation with the deity. That scene has revealed
%		facets of his
%		character, both strengths and weaknesses, that are now a
%		part of the
%		figure of Moses as he arrives on the scene of human
%		affairs. Moreover,
%		the encounter with God can hardly be disregarded itself
%		as having
%		impacted upon Moses’ personality. He has received more
%		than the three
%		miracles with which to impress the Israelites and the
%		Pharaoh. He has
%		spoken with God. Presumably, setting foot on the floor
%		of the palace is
%		different after one has set foot on holy ground, and
%		conversing with a
%		king is different after one has conversed with the
%		creator. Exodus leads
%		us through a series of dynamics as Moses confronts,
%		first, the deity,
%		then a king, and then a community, with each dynamic
%		growing more
%		complicated as it becomes richer in background.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה מִי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר אֶשְׁמַע בְּקֹלוֹ לְשַׁלַּח אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יָדַעְתִּי אֶת יְהֹוָה וְגַם אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא אֲשַׁלֵּחַ׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh said, “Who is YHWH that I should listen to His voice, to let Israel go?! I don’t know YHWH, and also I won’t let Israel go.”

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה מִי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר אֶשְׁמַע בְּקֹלוֹ לְשַׁלַּח אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יָדַעְתִּי אֶת יְהֹוָה וְגַם אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא אֲשַׁלֵּחַ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Who is YHWH. The issue of YHWH’s becoming known, which
%		is to become a
%		major component of subsequent books, begins in Exodus.
%		In Genesis, YHWH
%		is known personally only to a few individuals and to no
%		nations. God’s
%		actions in the world are not identifiably God’s. That
%		is, the narrator
%		informs the reader that it is YHWH who brings the flood,
%		but the masses
%		of humans in the narrative are not portrayed as being
%		aware of the
%		source of their catastrophe. There is likewise no
%		suggestion that the
%		generation of the tower of Babylon know whose force is
%		confounding and
%		scattering them. The same is true of the victims of the
%		destruction of
%		Sodom and Gomorrah, and the only eyewitness turns to
%		salt. Joseph
%		informs the Pharaoh that it is God who brings his dream,
%		who makes its
%		interpretation known, and who is the cause of the events
%		that it
%		reveals; but Joseph refers to the deity only
%		generically, as “God.” He
%		is never pictured as revealing to the Egyptians the name
%		of the deity
%		who is at work (Gen 41:16,25,28,32). In Exodus, however,
%		YHWH makes His
%		presence known to Israel, to Egypt, and to other
%		inhabitants of the
%		region (Exod 15:14–15). The Egyptian king’s first words
%		to Moses are,
%		“Who is YHWH . . . ? I don’t know YHWH” (5:2). By the
%		end of the story
%		he knows.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֱלֹהֵי הָעִבְרִים נִקְרָא עָלֵינוּ נֵלְכָה נָּא דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים בַּמִּדְבָּר וְנִזְבְּחָה לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ פֶּן יִפְגָּעֵנוּ בַּדֶּבֶר אוֹ בֶחָרֶב׃
verses.english: And they said, “The God of the Hebrews has communicated with us. Let us go on a trip of three days in the wilderness so we may sacrifice to YHWH, our God, or else He’ll strike us with an epidemic or with the sword.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֱלֹהֵי הָעִבְרִים נִקְרָא עָלֵינוּ נֵלְכָה נָּא דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים בַּמִּדְבָּר וְנִזְבְּחָה לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ פֶּן יִפְגָּעֵנוּ בַּדֶּבֶר אוֹ בֶחָרֶב׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Let us go on a trip of three days. Moses and Aaron do
%		not ask for the
%		Israelites’ liberation from Egypt. They ask only to make
%		a three-day
%		sacrificial pilgrimage. They just do not mention the
%		fact that they do
%		not plan to return! Footnote 5:3. strike. The word here
%		(Hebrew pg‘) is
%		the same as the word for the Israelites’ “meeting” Moses
%		later in v. 20.
%		The range of meanings of this root makes a wordplay that
%		is enhanced by
%		clustering with the blatant pun in the next verse.
%		Footnote 5:3. strike
%		us. Moses and Aaron say that God may strike “us,” the
%		Israelites, if
%		they don’t go to sacrifice to Him, but the Hebrew suffix
%		has a subtle
%		double meaning: it can also mean “strike him”—which
%		could apply to
%		Pharaoh himself or to a nonspecific person, that is, to
%		the Egyptians
%		who will in fact suffer the plagues. The double meaning
%		here is not
%		merely playful but meaningful to the context.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם לָמָּה מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן תַּפְרִיעוּ אֶת הָעָם מִמַּעֲשָׂיו לְכוּ לְסִבְלֹתֵיכֶם׃
verses.english: And the king of Egypt said to them, “Why, Moses and Aaron, do you turn the people loose from its work? Go to your burdens!”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם לָמָּה מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן תַּפְרִיעוּ אֶת הָעָם מִמַּעֲשָׂיו לְכוּ לְסִבְלֹתֵיכֶם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		turn loose. With the Hebrew root pr‘, this is a pun on
%		“Pharaoh.” An
%		even stronger play on this word will occur later, in the
%		middle of the
%		golden calf episode (Exod 32:25). Footnote 5:4. Go to
%		your burdens! He
%		talks down to Moses and Aaron, telling them to get back
%		to work, and
%		thus conveying to them that they are just slaves like
%		everyone else.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה הֵן רַבִּים עַתָּה עַם הָאָרֶץ וְהִשְׁבַּתֶּם אֹתָם מִסִּבְלֹתָם׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh said, “Here, the people of the land are now many, and you’ve made them cease from their burdens.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה הֵן רַבִּים עַתָּה עַם הָאָרֶץ וְהִשְׁבַּתֶּם אֹתָם מִסִּבְלֹתָם׃}

verses.original: וַיְצַו פַּרְעֹה בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת הַנֹּגְשִׂים בָּעָם וְאֶת שֹׁטְרָיו לֵאמֹר׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters among the people and its officers in that day, saying,

tex.original: \hE{וַיְצַו פַּרְעֹה בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת הַנֹּגְשִׂים בָּעָם וְאֶת שֹׁטְרָיו לֵאמֹר׃}

verses.original: לֹא תֹאסִפוּן לָתֵת תֶּבֶן לָעָם לִלְבֹּן הַלְּבֵנִים כִּתְמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם הֵם יֵלְכוּ וְקֹשְׁשׁוּ לָהֶם תֶּבֶן׃
verses.english: “You shall not continue to give straw to the people to make bricks as yesterday and the day before. They shall go and collect straw for themselves.

tex.original: \hE{לֹא תֹאסִפוּן לָתֵת תֶּבֶן לָעָם לִלְבֹּן הַלְּבֵנִים כִּתְמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם הֵם יֵלְכוּ וְקֹשְׁשׁוּ לָהֶם תֶּבֶן׃}

verses.original: וְאֶת מַתְכֹּנֶת הַלְּבֵנִים אֲשֶׁר הֵם עֹשִׂים תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם תָּשִׂימוּ עֲלֵיהֶם לֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִמֶּנּוּ כִּי נִרְפִּים הֵם עַל כֵּן הֵם צֹעֲקִים לֵאמֹר נֵלְכָה נִזְבְּחָה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ׃
verses.english: And you shall impose on them the quota of the bricks that they were making yesterday and the day before. You shall not subtract from it. Because they’re lazy. On account of this they’re crying, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’

tex.original: \hE{וְאֶת מַתְכֹּנֶת הַלְּבֵנִים אֲשֶׁר הֵם עֹשִׂים תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם תָּשִׂימוּ עֲלֵיהֶם לֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִמֶּנּוּ כִּי נִרְפִּים הֵם עַל כֵּן הֵם צֹעֲקִים לֵאמֹר נֵלְכָה נִזְבְּחָה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		And you shall impose on them the quota of the bricks that
		they were making yesterday and the day before. You shall
		not subtract from it. Because they’re lazy. On account of
		this they’re crying, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to
		our God.’
	}

verses.original: תִּכְבַּד הָעֲבֹדָה עַל הָאֲנָשִׁים וְיַעֲשׂוּ בָהּ וְאַל יִשְׁעוּ בְּדִבְרֵי שָׁקֶר׃
verses.english: Let the work be heavy on the people, and let them do it, and let them not pay attention to words that are a lie!”

tex.original: \hE{תִּכְבַּד הָעֲבֹדָה עַל הָאֲנָשִׁים וְיַעֲשׂוּ בָהּ וְאַל יִשְׁעוּ בְּדִבְרֵי שָׁקֶר׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Let the work be heavy. The idiom of Moses’ “heavy mouth
%		and heavy
%		tongue” initiates a chain of puns on the various shades
%		of meaning of
%		the word “heavy” (Hebrew kbd, meaning weighty,
%		difficult, or
%		substantial). Here Pharaoh orders that the work of the
%		Israelites be
%		made heavy. The hardening of the Pharaoh’s heart is
%		expressed several
%		times through this term (7:14; 8:11,28; 9:7,34; 10:1).
%		Four of the
%		plagues on Egypt are described as heavy: insects (8:20),
%		pestilence
%		(9:3), hail (9:18,24), and locusts (10:14). The
%		Israelites leave with a
%		heavy supply of livestock (12:38). As Moses holds up his
%		arms in support
%		of the Israelites while they battle the Amalekites, his
%		arms become
%		heavy (17:12). Moses’ father-in-law warns him that his
%		efforts to manage
%		the entire nation on his own are foolish, “because the
%		thing is too
%		heavy for you” (18:18). The chain of puns culminates at
%		Sinai, as a
%		heavy cloud is on the mountain while the people hear the
%		voice of God
%		(19:16). It is not that the narrator’s vocabulary is too
%		limited to
%		produce other adjectives. Rather, the construction of
%		such chains of
%		wordplay is a technique of biblical narrative, deployed
%		in other
%		biblical books as well. Here the chain contributes to
%		the narrative’s
%		unity, rather than the narrative’s appearing to be a
%		series of loosely
%		bound episodes.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֵּצְאוּ נֹגְשֵׂי הָעָם וְשֹׁטְרָיו וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל הָעָם לֵאמֹר כֹּה אָמַר פַּרְעֹה אֵינֶנִּי נֹתֵן לָכֶם תֶּבֶן׃
verses.english: And the people’s taskmasters and its officers went out and said to the people, saying, “Pharaoh said this: ‘I am not giving you straw.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֵּצְאוּ נֹגְשֵׂי הָעָם וְשֹׁטְרָיו וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל הָעָם לֵאמֹר כֹּה אָמַר פַּרְעֹה אֵינֶנִּי נֹתֵן לָכֶם תֶּבֶן׃}

verses.original: אַתֶּם לְכוּ קְחוּ לָכֶם תֶּבֶן מֵאֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָאוּ כִּי אֵין נִגְרָע מֵעֲבֹדַתְכֶם דָּבָר׃
verses.english: You, go, take straw for yourselves from wherever you’ll find it, because not a thing is subtracted from your work.’”

tex.original: \hE{אַתֶּם לְכוּ קְחוּ לָכֶם תֶּבֶן מֵאֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָאוּ כִּי אֵין נִגְרָע מֵעֲבֹדַתְכֶם דָּבָר׃}

verses.original: וַיָּפֶץ הָעָם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם לְקֹשֵׁשׁ קַשׁ לַתֶּבֶן׃
verses.english: And the people scattered through all the land of Egypt to collect stubble for straw.

tex.original: \hE{וַיָּפֶץ הָעָם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם לְקֹשֵׁשׁ קַשׁ לַתֶּבֶן׃}

verses.original: וְהַנֹּגְשִׂים אָצִים לֵאמֹר כַּלּוּ מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם דְּבַר יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר בִּהְיוֹת הַתֶּבֶן׃
verses.english: And the taskmasters were prodding, saying, “Finish your work, the day’s thing in that very day, as when there was the straw.”

tex.original: \hE{וְהַנֹּגְשִׂים אָצִים לֵאמֹר כַּלּוּ מַעֲשֵׂיכֶם דְּבַר יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר בִּהְיוֹת הַתֶּבֶן׃}

verses.original: וַיֻּכּוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר שָׂמוּ עֲלֵהֶם נֹגְשֵׂי פַרְעֹה לֵאמֹר מַדּוּעַ לֹא כִלִּיתֶם חקְכֶם לִלְבֹּן כִּתְמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם גַּם תְּמוֹל גַּם הַיּוֹם׃
verses.english: And the officers of the children of Israel whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them were beaten—saying, “Why haven’t you finished your requirement to make brick like the day before yesterday, also yesterday, also today?”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֻּכּוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר שָׂמוּ עֲלֵהֶם נֹגְשֵׂי פַרְעֹה לֵאמֹר מַדּוּעַ לֹא כִלִּיתֶם חקְכֶם לִלְבֹּן כִּתְמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם גַּם תְּמוֹל גַּם הַיּוֹם׃}

verses.original: וַיָּבֹאוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיִּצְעֲקוּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה לֵאמֹר לָמָּה תַעֲשֶׂה כֹה לַעֲבָדֶיךָ׃
verses.english: And the officers of the children of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, saying, “Why do you do a thing like this to your servants?

tex.original: \hE{וַיָּבֹאוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיִּצְעֲקוּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה לֵאמֹר לָמָּה תַעֲשֶׂה כֹה לַעֲבָדֶיךָ׃}

verses.original: תֶּבֶן אֵין נִתָּן לַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּלְבֵנִים אֹמְרִים לָנוּ עֲשׂוּ וְהִנֵּה עֲבָדֶיךָ מֻכִּים וְחָטָאת עַמֶּךָ׃
verses.english: Straw isn’t given to your servants, and they say to us: Make bricks. And here, your servants are beaten, and it’s your people’s sin.”

tex.original: \hE{תֶּבֶן אֵין נִתָּן לַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּלְבֵנִים אֹמְרִים לָנוּ עֲשׂוּ וְהִנֵּה עֲבָדֶיךָ מֻכִּים וְחָטָאת עַמֶּךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר נִרְפִּים אַתֶּם נִרְפִּים עַל כֵּן אַתֶּם אֹמְרִים נֵלְכָה נִזְבְּחָה לַיהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And he said, “You’re lazy, lazy! On account of this you’re saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to YHWH.’

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר נִרְפִּים אַתֶּם נִרְפִּים עַל כֵּן אַתֶּם אֹמְרִים נֵלְכָה נִזְבְּחָה לַיהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וְעַתָּה לְכוּ עִבְדוּ וְתֶבֶן לֹא יִנָּתֵן לָכֶם וְתֹכֶן לְבֵנִים תִּתֵּנוּ׃
verses.english: And now go, work! And straw will not be given to you, and you shall give the quota of bricks!”

tex.original: \hE{וְעַתָּה לְכוּ עִבְדוּ וְתֶבֶן לֹא יִנָּתֵן לָכֶם וְתֹכֶן לְבֵנִים תִּתֵּנוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיִּרְאוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֹתָם בְּרָע לֵאמֹר לֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִלִּבְנֵיכֶם דְּבַר יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ׃
verses.english: And the officers of the children of Israel saw themselves in a bad state—saying, “You shall not subtract from your bricks, the day’s thing in that very day.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּרְאוּ שֹׁטְרֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֹתָם בְּרָע לֵאמֹר לֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִלִּבְנֵיכֶם דְּבַר יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ׃}

verses.original: וַיִּפְגְּעוּ אֶת מֹשֶׁה וְאֶת אַהֲרֹן נִצָּבִים לִקְרָאתָם בְּצֵאתָם מֵאֵת פַּרְעֹה׃
verses.english: And they met Moses and Aaron, standing opposite them when they came out from Pharaoh,

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּפְגְּעוּ אֶת מֹשֶׁה וְאֶת אַהֲרֹן נִצָּבִים לִקְרָאתָם בְּצֵאתָם מֵאֵת פַּרְעֹה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֲלֵהֶם יֵרֶא יְהֹוָה עֲלֵיכֶם וְיִשְׁפֹּט אֲשֶׁר הִבְאַשְׁתֶּם אֶת רֵיחֵנוּ בְּעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה וּבְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו לָתֶת חֶרֶב בְּיָדָם לְהרְגֵנוּ׃
verses.english: and they said to them, “May YHWH look on you and judge, that you’ve made our smell odious in Pharaoh’s eyes and in his servants’ eyes, to give a sword in their hand to kill us!”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֲלֵהֶם יֵרֶא יְהֹוָה עֲלֵיכֶם וְיִשְׁפֹּט אֲשֶׁר הִבְאַשְׁתֶּם אֶת רֵיחֵנוּ בְּעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה וּבְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו לָתֶת חֶרֶב בְּיָדָם לְהרְגֵנוּ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		our smell odious in Pharaoh’s eyes. People smell with
%		their noses, not
%		their eyes! This may be just an expression or even the
%		author’s
%		oversight, but I rather think that the contradiction is
%		purposeful: the
%		people’s officers misspeak because they are upset. We
%		frequently do
%		that.
%	}

verses.original: וַיָּשׁב מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה וַיֹּאמַר אֲדֹנָי לָמָה הֲרֵעֹתָה לָעָם הַזֶּה לָמָּה זֶּה שְׁלַחְתָּנִי׃
verses.english: And Moses went back to YHWH and said, “My Lord, why have you done bad to this people? Why did you send me here?

tex.original: \hE{וַיָּשׁב מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה וַיֹּאמַר אֲדֹנָי לָמָה הֲרֵעֹתָה לָעָם הַזֶּה לָמָּה זֶּה שְׁלַחְתָּנִי׃}

verses.original: וּמֵאָז בָּאתִי אֶל פַּרְעֹה לְדַבֵּר בִּשְׁמֶךָ הֵרַע לָעָם הַזֶּה וְהַצֵּל לֹא הִצַּלְתָּ אֶת עַמֶּךָ׃
verses.english: And since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name he has done bad to this people, and you haven’t rescued your people!”

tex.original: \hE{וּמֵאָז בָּאתִי אֶל פַּרְעֹה לְדַבֵּר בִּשְׁמֶךָ הֵרַע לָעָם הַזֶּה וְהַצֵּל לֹא הִצַּלְתָּ אֶת עַמֶּךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה עַתָּה תִרְאֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶעֱשֶׂה לְפַרְעֹה כִּי בְיָד חֲזָקָה יְשַׁלְּחֵם וּבְיָד חֲזָקָה יְגָרְשֵׁם מֵאַרְצוֹ׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Now you’ll see what I shall do to Pharaoh, because with a strong hand he’ll let them go, and with a strong hand he’ll drive them from his land.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה עַתָּה תִרְאֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶעֱשֶׂה לְפַרְעֹה כִּי בְיָד חֲזָקָה יְשַׁלְּחֵם וּבְיָד חֲזָקָה יְגָרְשֵׁם מֵאַרְצוֹ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		with a strong hand he’ll let them go. But with whose
%		strong hand? God’s
%		or Moses’ own? The probable meaning is: God’s. But the
%		ambiguity is rich
%		because either meaning is instructive.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֶל מֹשֶׁה וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו אֲנִי יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am YHWH.

tex.original: \hP{וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֶל מֹשֶׁה וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו אֲנִי יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וָאֵרָא אֶל אַבְרָהָם אֶל יִצְחָק וְאֶל יַעֲקֹב בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי וּשְׁמִי יְהֹוָה לֹא נוֹדַעְתִּי לָהֶם׃
verses.english: And I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as El Shadday, and I was not known to them by my name, YHWH.

tex.original: \hP{וָאֵרָא אֶל אַבְרָהָם אֶל יִצְחָק וְאֶל יַעֲקֹב בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי וּשְׁמִי יְהֹוָה לֹא נוֹדַעְתִּי לָהֶם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		I was not known to them by my name, YHWH. But God was
%		known to them by
%		this name (Gen 13:4; 15:2; 22:14,16; 26:22,25; 28:13). I
%		have discussed
%		the significance of the understanding of this problem in
%		critical
%		scholarship elsewhere (Who Wrote the Bible?). It has to
%		do with the case
%		for multiple sources from which the Torah was composed.
%		But in terms of
%		the final composition, the full Torah as we know it, how
%		shall we
%		understand this verse? Perhaps covenantally: In the
%		Noahic covenant (Gen
%		9:8–9), God is called ’lhîm. In the Abrahamic covenant,
%		God is known as
%		El Shadday (Gen 17:1–2). But the covenant that will be
%		made with this
%		generation at Sinai will be with the use of the name
%		YHWH (Exod 20:2).
%		In support of this understanding: the very next words
%		here are “And I
%		also established my covenant with them.”
%	}

verses.original: וְגַם הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתָּם לָתֵת לָהֶם אֶת אֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן אֵת אֶרֶץ מְגֻרֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר גָּרוּ בָהּ׃
verses.english: And I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their residences, in which they resided.

tex.original: \hP{וְגַם הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתָּם לָתֵת לָהֶם אֶת אֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן אֵת אֶרֶץ מְגֻרֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר גָּרוּ בָהּ׃}

verses.original: וְגַם אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת נַאֲקַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר מִצְרַיִם מַעֲבִדִים אֹתָם וָאֶזְכֹּר אֶת בְּרִיתִי׃
verses.english: And also: I’ve heard the cry of the children of Israel as Egypt is enslaving them, and I’ve remembered my covenant.

tex.original: \hP{וְגַם אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת נַאֲקַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר מִצְרַיִם מַעֲבִדִים אֹתָם וָאֶזְכֹּר אֶת בְּרִיתִי׃}

verses.original: לָכֵן אֱמֹר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲנִי יְהֹוָה וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם מִתַּחַת סִבְלֹת מִצְרַיִם וְהִצַּלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם מֵעֲבֹדָתָם וְגָאַלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בִּזְרוֹעַ נְטוּיָה וּבִשְׁפָטִים גְּדֹלִים׃
verses.english: Therefore, say to the children of Israel: ‘I am YHWH, and I shall bring you out from under Egypt’s burdens, and I shall rescue you from their toil, and I shall redeem you with an outstretched arm and with tremendous judgments,

tex.original: \hP{לָכֵן אֱמֹר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲנִי יְהֹוָה וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם מִתַּחַת סִבְלֹת מִצְרַיִם וְהִצַּלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם מֵעֲבֹדָתָם וְגָאַלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בִּזְרוֹעַ נְטוּיָה וּבִשְׁפָטִים גְּדֹלִים׃}

verses.original: וְלָקַחְתִּי אֶתְכֶם לִי לְעָם וְהָיִיתִי לָכֶם לֵאלֹהִים וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הַמּוֹצִיא אֶתְכֶם מִתַּחַת סִבְלוֹת מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: and I shall take you to me as a people, and I shall become your God, and you’ll know that I am YHWH, your God, who is bringing you out from under Egypt’s burdens.

tex.original: \hP{וְלָקַחְתִּי אֶתְכֶם לִי לְעָם וְהָיִיתִי לָכֶם לֵאלֹהִים וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הַמּוֹצִיא אֶתְכֶם מִתַּחַת סִבְלוֹת מִצְרָיִם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		you’ll know that I am YHWH, your God, who is bringing
%		you out. The
%		dominant theme of Exodus, YHWH’s becoming known, is
%		connected explicitly
%		here to the rescue from slavery and to the “judgments”
%		that will occur
%		in Egypt. It will continue to be stated, several times,
%		as a reason for
%		the miraculous plagues.
%	}

verses.original: וְהֵבֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר נָשָׂאתִי אֶת יָדִי לָתֵת אֹתָהּ לְאַבְרָהָם לְיִצְחָק וּלְיַעֲקֹב וְנָתַתִּי אֹתָהּ לָכֶם מוֹרָשָׁה אֲנִי יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And I shall bring you to the land that I raised my hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, and I shall give it to you as a possession. I am YHWH.’”

tex.original: \hP{וְהֵבֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר נָשָׂאתִי אֶת יָדִי לָתֵת אֹתָהּ לְאַבְרָהָם לְיִצְחָק וּלְיַעֲקֹב וְנָתַתִּי אֹתָהּ לָכֶם מוֹרָשָׁה אֲנִי יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר מֹשֶׁה כֵּן אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא שָׁמְעוּ אֶל מֹשֶׁה מִקֹּצֶר רוּחַ וּמֵעֲבֹדָה קָשָׁה׃
verses.english: And Moses spoke this to the children of Israel, and they did not listen to Moses because of shortage of spirit and because of hard work.

tex.original: \hP{וַיְדַבֵּר מֹשֶׁה כֵּן אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא שָׁמְעוּ אֶל מֹשֶׁה מִקֹּצֶר רוּחַ וּמֵעֲבֹדָה קָשָׁה׃}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר׃
verses.english: And YHWH spoke to Moses, saying,

tex.original: \hP{וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר׃}
tex.english: \eP{And YHWH spoke to Moses, saying,}

verses.original: בֹּא דַבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם וִישַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאַרְצוֹ׃
verses.english: “Come, speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, that he should let the children of Israel go from his land.”

tex.original: \hP{בֹּא דַבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם וִישַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאַרְצוֹ׃}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה לֵאמֹר הֵן בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא שָׁמְעוּ אֵלַי וְאֵיךְ יִשְׁמָעֵנִי פַרְעֹה וַאֲנִי עֲרַל שְׂפָתָיִם׃
verses.english: And Moses spoke in front of YHWH, saying, “Here, the children of Israel didn’t listen to me, and how will Pharaoh listen to me?! And I’m uncircumcised of lips!”

tex.original: \hP{וַיְדַבֵּר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה לֵאמֹר הֵן בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא שָׁמְעוּ אֵלַי וְאֵיךְ יִשְׁמָעֵנִי פַרְעֹה וַאֲנִי עֲרַל שְׂפָתָיִם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		uncircumcised of lips. Does this shed light on the
%		meaning of “heavy of
%		tongue and heavy of mouth”? It seems rather to be even
%		harder to
%		interpret. Uncircumcision is used elsewhere in the Torah
%		as a metaphor
%		as well. Lev 26:41 and Deut 10:16 refer to the people’s
%		uncircumcised
%		heart. (The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel use this image
%		also.) There it
%		is a strong image, criticizing the people who understand
%		that their
%		covenant requires circumcision of the skin that covers
%		the penis, but
%		who do not appreciate that they must likewise remove the
%		impediment to
%		their hearts. But the meaning of the image here is less
%		clear. We still
%		do not know what the impediment is. All we can say is
%		that Moses is
%		again pictured as unconfident, feeling inadequate to the
%		task. The
%		repeated emphasis on this point will make the eventual
%		success of the
%		exodus that much more dramatic.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן וַיְצַוֵּם אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And YHWH spoke to Moses and to Aaron and commanded them regarding the children of Israel and regarding Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt.

tex.original: \hR{וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן וַיְצַוֵּם אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: אֵלֶּה רָאשֵׁי בֵית אֲבֹתָם בְּנֵי רְאוּבֵן בְּכֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל חֲנוֹךְ וּפַלּוּא חֶצְרֹן וְכַרְמִי אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת רְאוּבֵן׃
verses.english: These are the heads of their fathers’ houses: The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the families of Reuben.

tex.original: \hP{אֵלֶּה רָאשֵׁי בֵית אֲבֹתָם בְּנֵי רְאוּבֵן בְּכֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל חֲנוֹךְ וּפַלּוּא חֶצְרֹן וְכַרְמִי אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת רְאוּבֵן׃}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי שִׁמְעוֹן יְמוּאֵל וְיָמִין וְאֹהַד וְיָכִין וְצֹחַר וְשָׁאוּל בֶּן הַכְּנַעֲנִית אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת שִׁמְעוֹן׃
verses.english: And the sons of Simeon: Jemuel and Jamin and Ohad and Jachin and Zohar and Saul, son of a Canaanite woman. These are the families of Simeon.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי שִׁמְעוֹן יְמוּאֵל וְיָמִין וְאֹהַד וְיָכִין וְצֹחַר וְשָׁאוּל בֶּן הַכְּנַעֲנִית אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת שִׁמְעוֹן׃}

verses.original: וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי לֵוִי לְתֹלְדֹתָם גֵּרְשׁוֹן וּקְהָת וּמְרָרִי וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי לֵוִי שֶׁבַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃
verses.english: And these are the names of the sons of Levi by their records: Gershon and Kohath and Merari. And the years of Levi’s life were a hundred thirty-seven years.

tex.original: \hP{וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי לֵוִי לְתֹלְדֹתָם גֵּרְשׁוֹן וּקְהָת וּמְרָרִי וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי לֵוִי שֶׁבַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃}

verses.original: בְּנֵי גֵרְשׁוֹן לִבְנִי וְשִׁמְעִי לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם׃
verses.english: The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their families.

tex.original: \hP{בְּנֵי גֵרְשׁוֹן לִבְנִי וְשִׁמְעִי לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם׃}
tex.english: \eP{The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their families.}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי קְהָת עַמְרָם וְיִצְהָר וְחֶבְרוֹן וְעֻזִּיאֵל וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי קְהָת שָׁלֹשׁ וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃
verses.english: And the sons of Kohath: Amram and Izhar and Hebron and Uzziel. And the years of Kohath’s life were a hundred thirty-three years.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי קְהָת עַמְרָם וְיִצְהָר וְחֶבְרוֹן וְעֻזִּיאֵל וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי קְהָת שָׁלֹשׁ וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי מְרָרִי מַחְלִי וּמוּשִׁי אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַלֵּוִי לְתֹלְדֹתָם׃
verses.english: And the sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the families of Levi by their records.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי מְרָרִי מַחְלִי וּמוּשִׁי אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַלֵּוִי לְתֹלְדֹתָם׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקַּח עַמְרָם אֶת יוֹכֶבֶד דֹּדָתוֹ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת אַהֲרֹן וְאֶת מֹשֶׁה וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי עַמְרָם שֶׁבַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃
verses.english: And Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as a wife; and she gave birth to Aaron and Moses for him. And the years of Amram’s life were a hundred thirty-seven years.

tex.original: \hP{וַיִּקַּח עַמְרָם אֶת יוֹכֶבֶד דֹּדָתוֹ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת אַהֲרֹן וְאֶת מֹשֶׁה וּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי עַמְרָם שֶׁבַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		she gave birth to Aaron and Moses. Until now, it has not
%		been clear that
%		Moses and Aaron are brothers. There is no reference to a
%		brother in the
%		story of Moses’ birth, and at the bush Aaron is referred
%		to as “your
%		Levite brother,” which sounds like a fellow Levite, not
%		an actual
%		brother. The list in which this appears (6:13–25) seems
%		strange: it
%		comes in the middle of a conversation between God and
%		Moses, and it
%		covers only Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, and then leaves
%		out the rest of
%		the tribes. But it appears that the point of the list
%		was to get to
%		Aaron: to identify him as Moses’ brother, to state that
%		he is married to
%		the sister of the chieftain of the tribe of Judah, and
%		to name his son
%		and grandson who will be his successors. The order also
%		indicates that
%		Aaron is the firstborn; this is confirmed in Exod 7:7.
%		Footnote 6:20.
%		Aaron and Moses. And what about Miriam? One Hebrew
%		manuscript and the
%		Septuagint and Samaritan texts have the words “and their
%		sister Miriam.”
%		The scribe appears to have accidentally omitted these
%		words here.
%	}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי יִצְהָר קֹרַח וָנֶפֶג וְזִכְרִי׃
verses.english: And the sons of Izhar: Korah and Nepheg and Zichri.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי יִצְהָר קֹרַח וָנֶפֶג וְזִכְרִי׃}
tex.english: \eP{And the sons of Izhar: Korah and Nepheg and Zichri.}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי עֻזִּיאֵל מִישָׁאֵל וְאֶלְצָפָן וְסִתְרִי׃
verses.english: And the sons of Uzziel: Mishael and Elzaphan and Sithri.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי עֻזִּיאֵל מִישָׁאֵל וְאֶלְצָפָן וְסִתְרִי׃}
tex.english: \eP{And the sons of Uzziel: Mishael and Elzaphan and Sithri.}

verses.original: וַיִּקַּח אַהֲרֹן אֶת אֱלִישֶׁבַע בַּת עַמִּינָדָב אֲחוֹת נַחְשׁוֹן לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת נָדָב וְאֶת אֲבִיהוּא אֶת אֶלְעָזָר וְאֶת אִיתָמָר׃
verses.english: And Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon as a wife; and she gave birth to Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar for him.

tex.original: \hP{וַיִּקַּח אַהֲרֹן אֶת אֱלִישֶׁבַע בַּת עַמִּינָדָב אֲחוֹת נַחְשׁוֹן לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת נָדָב וְאֶת אֲבִיהוּא אֶת אֶלְעָזָר וְאֶת אִיתָמָר׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon. Aaron marries
%		the sister of
%		the chieftain of the tribe of Judah. It is noteworthy
%		that the priestly
%		and political elite marry (and this suggests that such
%		marriages occurred
%		later between the royal and high priestly families of
%		Israel).
%	}

verses.original: וּבְנֵי קֹרַח אַסִּיר וְאֶלְקָנָה וַאֲבִיאָסָף אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַקּרְחִי׃
verses.english: And the sons of Korah: Assir and Elkanah and Abiasaph. These are the families of the Korahites.

tex.original: \hP{וּבְנֵי קֹרַח אַסִּיר וְאֶלְקָנָה וַאֲבִיאָסָף אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַקּרְחִי׃}

verses.original: וְאֶלְעָזָר בֶּן אַהֲרֹן לָקַח לוֹ מִבְּנוֹת פּוּטִיאֵל לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת פִּינְחָס אֵלֶּה רָאשֵׁי אֲבוֹת הַלְוִיִּם לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם׃
verses.english: And Eleazar son of Aaron had taken one of the daughters of Putiel as a wife, and she gave birth for him to Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers of the Levites according to their families.

tex.original: \hP{וְאֶלְעָזָר בֶּן אַהֲרֹן לָקַח לוֹ מִבְּנוֹת פּוּטִיאֵל לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ אֶת פִּינְחָס אֵלֶּה רָאשֵׁי אֲבוֹת הַלְוִיִּם לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם׃}

verses.original: הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה אֲשֶׁר אָמַר יְהֹוָה לָהֶם הוֹצִיאוּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם עַל צִבְאֹתָם׃
verses.english: That is Aaron and Moses, to whom YHWH said, “Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt by their masses.”

tex.original: \hR{הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה אֲשֶׁר אָמַר יְהֹוָה לָהֶם הוֹצִיאוּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם עַל צִבְאֹתָם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Aaron and Moses … Moses and Aaron. Both word orders are
%		given: Aaron
%		first, then Moses first, suggesting that each is
%		important in a
%		different way. The recognition of Aaron here is
%		especially significant
%		because it is natural to think of Moses first, but this
%		notice follows a
%		genealogy that has listed Aaron as the firstborn and
%		identified his wife
%		and children. (The Septuagint and Qumran texts have the
%		order in v. 27
%		reversed, which unfortunately loses this point.)
%	}

verses.original: הֵם הַמְדַבְּרִים אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם הוּא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן׃
verses.english: They were the ones speaking to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring out the children of Israel from Egypt. That is Moses and Aaron.

tex.original: \hR{הֵם הַמְדַבְּרִים אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם הוּא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן׃}

verses.original: וַיְהִי בְּיוֹם דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And it was in the day that YHWH spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,

tex.original: \hR{וַיְהִי בְּיוֹם דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר אֲנִי יְהֹוָה דַּבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי דֹּבֵר אֵלֶיךָ׃
verses.english: and YHWH spoke to Moses, saying, “I am YHWH. Speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything that I speak to you.”

tex.original: \hR{וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר אֲנִי יְהֹוָה דַּבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי דֹּבֵר אֵלֶיךָ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה הֵן אֲנִי עֲרַל שְׂפָתַיִם וְאֵיךְ יִשְׁמַע אֵלַי פַּרְעֹה׃
verses.english: And Moses said in front of YHWH, “Here, I’m uncircumcised of lips, and how will Pharaoh listen to me?!”

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה הֵן אֲנִי עֲרַל שְׂפָתַיִם וְאֵיךְ יִשְׁמַע אֵלַי פַּרְעֹה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה רְאֵה נְתַתִּיךָ אֱלֹהִים לְפַרְעֹה וְאַהֲרֹן אָחִיךָ יִהְיֶה נְבִיאֶךָ׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “See, I’ve made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron, your brother, will be your prophet.

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה רְאֵה נְתַתִּיךָ אֱלֹהִים לְפַרְעֹה וְאַהֲרֹן אָחִיךָ יִהְיֶה נְבִיאֶךָ׃}

verses.original: אַתָּה תְדַבֵּר אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר אֲצַוֶּךָּ וְאַהֲרֹן אָחִיךָ יְדַבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה וְשִׁלַּח אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאַרְצוֹ׃
verses.english: You shall speak everything that I’ll command you; and Aaron, your brother, shall speak to Pharaoh, that he let the children of Israel go from his land.

tex.original: \hP{אַתָּה תְדַבֵּר אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר אֲצַוֶּךָּ וְאַהֲרֹן אָחִיךָ יְדַבֵּר אֶל פַּרְעֹה וְשִׁלַּח אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאַרְצוֹ׃}

verses.original: וַאֲנִי אַקְשֶׁה אֶת לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְהִרְבֵּיתִי אֶת אֹתֹתַי וְאֶת מוֹפְתַי בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And I, I’ll harden Pharaoh’s heart, and I’ll multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.

tex.original: \hP{וַאֲנִי אַקְשֶׁה אֶת לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְהִרְבֵּיתִי אֶת אֹתֹתַי וְאֶת מוֹפְתַי בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וְלֹא יִשְׁמַע אֲלֵכֶם פַּרְעֹה וְנָתַתִּי אֶת יָדִי בְּמִצְרָיִם וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת צִבְאֹתַי אֶת עַמִּי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בִּשְׁפָטִים גְּדֹלִים׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh won’t listen to you, and I’ll set my hand in Egypt and bring out my masses, my people, the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt with great judgments.

tex.original: \hP{וְלֹא יִשְׁמַע אֲלֵכֶם פַּרְעֹה וְנָתַתִּי אֶת יָדִי בְּמִצְרָיִם וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת צִבְאֹתַי אֶת עַמִּי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בִּשְׁפָטִים גְּדֹלִים׃}

verses.original: וְיָדְעוּ מִצְרַיִם כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה בִּנְטֹתִי אֶת יָדִי עַל מִצְרָיִם וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתּוֹכָם׃
verses.english: And Egypt will know that I am YHWH when I reach out my hand on Egypt, and I’ll bring out the children of Israel from among them.”

tex.original: \hP{וְיָדְעוּ מִצְרַיִם כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה בִּנְטֹתִי אֶת יָדִי עַל מִצְרָיִם וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתּוֹכָם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה אֹתָם כֵּן עָשׂוּ׃
verses.english: And Moses and Aaron did as YHWH had commanded them. They did so.

tex.original: \hP{וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה אֹתָם כֵּן עָשׂוּ׃}

verses.original: וּמֹשֶׁה בֶּן שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה וְאַהֲרֹן בֶּן שָׁלֹשׁ וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה בְּדַבְּרָם אֶל פַּרְעֹה׃
verses.english: And Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron was eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.

tex.original: \hP{וּמֹשֶׁה בֶּן שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה וְאַהֲרֹן בֶּן שָׁלֹשׁ וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה בְּדַבְּרָם אֶל פַּרְעֹה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן לֵאמֹר׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן לֵאמֹר׃}
tex.english: \eP{And YHWH said to Moses and to Aaron, saying,}

verses.original: כִּי יְדַבֵּר אֲלֵכֶם פַּרְעֹה לֵאמֹר תְּנוּ לָכֶם מוֹפֵת וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל אַהֲרֹן קַח אֶת מַטְּךָ וְהַשְׁלֵךְ לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה יְהִי לְתַנִּין׃
verses.english: “When Pharaoh will speak to you, saying, ‘Produce a wonder!’ then say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it in front of Pharaoh. Let it become a serpent.’”

tex.original: \hP{כִּי יְדַבֵּר אֲלֵכֶם פַּרְעֹה לֵאמֹר תְּנוּ לָכֶם מוֹפֵת וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל אַהֲרֹן קַח אֶת מַטְּךָ וְהַשְׁלֵךְ לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה יְהִי לְתַנִּין׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		a serpent. Not a snake. This is different from the snake
%		(Hebrew nh)
%		that Moses’ staff became in Exod 4:3. Moses performed
%		that miracle for
%		the Israelite elders (4:30). Now, in front of Pharaoh,
%		Aaron’s staff
%		becomes a tannîn. This is the term that is used for the
%		big sea serpents
%		that God makes on the fifth day of creation (Gen 1:21).
%		They are not
%		merely snakes, as people have often pictured them. They
%		are
%		extraordinary creatures from a seemingly unearthly
%		realm.
%	}

verses.original: וַיָּבֹא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן אֶל פַּרְעֹה וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ אַהֲרֹן אֶת מַטֵּהוּ לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה וְלִפְנֵי עֲבָדָיו וַיְהִי לְתַנִּין׃
verses.english: And Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and did so, as YHWH had commanded, and Aaron threw his staff in front of Pharaoh and in front of his servants, and it became a serpent.

tex.original: \hP{וַיָּבֹא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן אֶל פַּרְעֹה וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ אַהֲרֹן אֶת מַטֵּהוּ לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה וְלִפְנֵי עֲבָדָיו וַיְהִי לְתַנִּין׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא גַּם פַּרְעֹה לַחֲכָמִים וְלַמְכַשְּׁפִים וַיַּעֲשׂוּ גַם הֵם חַרְטֻמֵּי מִצְרַיִם בְּלַהֲטֵיהֶם כֵּן׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh, too, called the wise men and the sorcerers; and they, too, Egypt’s magicians, did so with their charms:

tex.original: \hP{וַיִּקְרָא גַּם פַּרְעֹה לַחֲכָמִים וְלַמְכַשְּׁפִים וַיַּעֲשׂוּ גַם הֵם חַרְטֻמֵּי מִצְרַיִם בְּלַהֲטֵיהֶם כֵּן׃}

verses.original: וַיַּשְׁלִיכוּ אִישׁ מַטֵּהוּ וַיִּהְיוּ לְתַנִּינִם וַיִּבְלַע מַטֵּה אַהֲרֹן אֶת מַטֹּתָם׃
verses.english: and they each threw his staff, and they became serpents. And Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs!

tex.original: \hP{וַיַּשְׁלִיכוּ אִישׁ מַטֵּהוּ וַיִּהְיוּ לְתַנִּינִם וַיִּבְלַע מַטֵּה אַהֲרֹן אֶת מַטֹּתָם׃}

verses.original: וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh’s heart was strong, and he did not listen to them—as YHWH had spoken.

tex.original: \hP{וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה כָּבֵד לֵב פַּרְעֹה מֵאֵן לְשַׁלַּח הָעָם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is heavy. He has refused to let the people go.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה כָּבֵד לֵב פַּרְעֹה מֵאֵן לְשַׁלַּח הָעָם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Pharaoh’s heart is heavy. The stream of descriptions of
%		elements as
%		“heavy” that began in Exod 4:10 with Moses’ heavy mouth
%		and heavy tongue
%		continues to flow here and in what follows.
%	}

verses.original: לֵךְ אֶל פַּרְעֹה בַּבֹּקֶר הִנֵּה יֹצֵא הַמַּיְמָה וְנִצַּבְתָּ לִקְרָאתוֹ עַל שְׂפַת הַיְאֹר וְהַמַּטֶּה אֲשֶׁר נֶהְפַּךְ לְנָחָשׁ תִּקַּח בְּיָדֶךָ׃
verses.english: Go to Pharaoh in the morning—here, he’ll be going out to the water—and you’ll stand opposite him on the bank of the Nile, and you shall take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake.

tex.original: \hE{לֵךְ אֶל פַּרְעֹה בַּבֹּקֶר הִנֵּה יֹצֵא הַמַּיְמָה וְנִצַּבְתָּ לִקְרָאתוֹ עַל שְׂפַת הַיְאֹר וְהַמַּטֶּה אֲשֶׁר נֶהְפַּךְ לְנָחָשׁ תִּקַּח בְּיָדֶךָ׃}

verses.original: וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הָעִבְרִים שְׁלָחַנִי אֵלֶיךָ לֵאמֹר שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי בַּמִּדְבָּר וְהִנֵּה לֹא שָׁמַעְתָּ עַד כֹּה׃
verses.english: And you’ll say to him, ‘YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying: “Let my people go so they may serve me in the wilderness.” And here, you haven’t listened so far.

tex.original: \hE{וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הָעִבְרִים שְׁלָחַנִי אֵלֶיךָ לֵאמֹר שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי בַּמִּדְבָּר וְהִנֵּה לֹא שָׁמַעְתָּ עַד כֹּה׃}

verses.original: כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה בְּזֹאת תֵּדַע כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מַכֶּה בַּמַּטֶּה אֲשֶׁר בְּיָדִי עַל הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר וְנֶהֶפְכוּ לְדָם׃
verses.english: YHWH said this: “By this you’ll know that I am YHWH.” Here, I’m striking with the staff that’s in my hand on the waters that are in the Nile, and they’ll be changed into blood.

tex.original: \hE{כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה בְּזֹאת תֵּדַע כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מַכֶּה בַּמַּטֶּה אֲשֶׁר בְּיָדִי עַל הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר וְנֶהֶפְכוּ לְדָם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		By this you’ll know that I am YHWH. This is the story of
%		the
%		introduction of the deity by name to the world, so this
%		statement can be
%		understood not only as establishing the existence of the
%		named deity to
%		Pharaoh, but also as establishing what the name conveys.
%		Thus: By this
%		(a miracle involving a change in nature) you’ll know
%		that I am the one
%		who causes being.
%	}

verses.original: וְהַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר תָּמוּת וּבָאַשׁ הַיְאֹר וְנִלְאוּ מִצְרַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם מִן הַיְאֹר׃
verses.english: And the fish that are in the Nile will die, and the Nile will stink, and Egypt will weary themselves to drink water from the Nile.’”

tex.original: \hE{וְהַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר תָּמוּת וּבָאַשׁ הַיְאֹר וְנִלְאוּ מִצְרַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם מִן הַיְאֹר׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		will stink. Hebrew (b’). This is the same word that the
%		people used
%		metaphorically in their complaint to Moses earlier:
%		“You’ve made our
%		smell odious in Pharaoh’s eyes” (5:21). They now see the
%		divine power
%		giving the Egyptians something literally odious to
%		smell. This in turn
%		demonstrates how mistaken they were when they judged the
%		situation so
%		early in the process.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן קַח מַטְּךָ וּנְטֵה יָדְךָ עַל מֵימֵי מִצְרַיִם עַל נַהֲרֹתָם עַל יְאֹרֵיהֶם וְעַל אַגְמֵיהֶם וְעַל כּל מִקְוֵה מֵימֵיהֶם וְיִהְיוּ דָם וְהָיָה דָם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וּבָעֵצִים וּבָאֲבָנִים׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and reach your hand over Egypt’s waters, over their rivers, over their canals, and over their pools, and over every concentration of their waters.’ And they will be blood! And blood will be in all the land of Egypt—and in the trees and in the stones!”

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן קַח מַטְּךָ וּנְטֵה יָדְךָ עַל מֵימֵי מִצְרַיִם עַל נַהֲרֹתָם עַל יְאֹרֵיהֶם וְעַל אַגְמֵיהֶם וְעַל כּל מִקְוֵה מֵימֵיהֶם וְיִהְיוּ דָם וְהָיָה דָם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וּבָעֵצִים וּבָאֲבָנִים׃}
tex.english:
\eP{
		And YHWH said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff
		and reach your hand over Egypt’s waters, over their
		rivers, over their canals, and over their pools, and over
		every concentration of their waters.’ And they will be
		blood! And blood will be in all the land of Egypt—and in
		the trees and in the stones!”
	}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה וַיָּרֶם בַּמַּטֶּה וַיַּךְ אֶת הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר לְעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה וּלְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו וַיֵּהָפְכוּ כּל הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר לְדָם׃
verses.english: And Moses and Aaron did so, as YHWH had commanded. And he raised the staff and struck the waters that were in the Nile before Pharaoh’s eyes and before his servants’ eyes, and all the waters that were in the Nile were changed into blood.

tex.original:
\hP{וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה}
	\hE{וַיָּרֶם בַּמַּטֶּה וַיַּךְ אֶת הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר לְעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה וּלְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו וַיֵּהָפְכוּ כּל הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר לְדָם׃}

verses.original: וְהַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר מֵתָה וַיִּבְאַשׁ הַיְאֹר וְלֹא יָכְלוּ מִצְרַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם מִן הַיְאֹר וַיְהִי הַדָּם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile had an odor, and Egypt was not able to drink water from the Nile. And the blood was in all the land of Egypt.

tex.original:
\hE{וְהַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר מֵתָה וַיִּבְאַשׁ הַיְאֹר וְלֹא יָכְלוּ מִצְרַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם מִן הַיְאֹר}
	\hP{וַיְהִי הַדָּם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן חַרְטֻמֵּי מִצְרַיִם בְּלָטֵיהֶם וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Egypt’s magicians did so with their charms. And Pharaoh’s heart was strong, and he did not listen to them—as YHWH had spoken.

tex.original: \hP{וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן חַרְטֻמֵּי מִצְרַיִם בְּלָטֵיהֶם וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיִּפֶן פַּרְעֹה וַיָּבֹא אֶל בֵּיתוֹ וְלֹא שָׁת לִבּוֹ גַּם לָזֹאת׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh turned and came into his house and did not pay heed to this as well.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּפֶן פַּרְעֹה וַיָּבֹא אֶל בֵּיתוֹ וְלֹא שָׁת לִבּוֹ גַּם לָזֹאת׃}

verses.original: וַיַּחְפְּרוּ כל מִצְרַיִם סְבִיבֹת הַיְאֹר מַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת כִּי לֹא יָכְלוּ לִשְׁתֹּת מִמֵּימֵי הַיְאֹר׃
verses.english: And all Egypt dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they were not able to drink from the Nile’s waters.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּחְפְּרוּ כל מִצְרַיִם סְבִיבֹת הַיְאֹר מַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת כִּי לֹא יָכְלוּ לִשְׁתֹּת מִמֵּימֵי הַיְאֹר׃}

verses.original: וַיִּמָּלֵא שִׁבְעַת יָמִים אַחֲרֵי הַכּוֹת יְהֹוָה אֶת הַיְאֹר׃
verses.english: And seven days were filled after YHWH’s striking the Nile.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּמָּלֵא שִׁבְעַת יָמִים אַחֲרֵי הַכּוֹת יְהֹוָה אֶת הַיְאֹר׃}
tex.english: \eE{And seven days were filled after YHWH’s striking the Nile.}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה בֹּא אֶל פַּרְעֹה וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Come to Pharaoh, and you’ll say to him, ‘YHWH said this: Let my people go, so they may serve me.

tex.original: \hOther{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה בֹּא אֶל פַּרְעֹה וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה שַׁלַּח אֶת עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי׃}

verses.original: וְאִם מָאֵן אַתָּה לְשַׁלֵּחַ הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי נֹגֵף אֶת כּל גְּבוּלְךָ בַּצְפַרְדְּעִים׃
verses.english: And if you refuse to let go, here, I’m plaguing all your border with frogs,

tex.original: \hOther{וְאִם מָאֵן אַתָּה לְשַׁלֵּחַ הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי נֹגֵף אֶת כּל גְּבוּלְךָ בַּצְפַרְדְּעִים׃}

verses.original: וְשָׁרַץ הַיְאֹר צְפַרְדְּעִים וְעָלוּ וּבָאוּ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבַחֲדַר מִשְׁכָּבְךָ וְעַל מִטָּתֶךָ וּבְבֵית עֲבָדֶיךָ וּבְעַמֶּךָ וּבְתַנּוּרֶיךָ וּבְמִשְׁאֲרוֹתֶיךָ׃
verses.english: and the Nile will teem with frogs, and they’ll go up and come in your house and in your bedroom and on your bed and in your servants’ house and among your people and in your ovens and in your bowls,

tex.original: \hOther{וְשָׁרַץ הַיְאֹר צְפַרְדְּעִים וְעָלוּ וּבָאוּ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבַחֲדַר מִשְׁכָּבְךָ וְעַל מִטָּתֶךָ וּבְבֵית עֲבָדֶיךָ וּבְעַמֶּךָ וּבְתַנּוּרֶיךָ וּבְמִשְׁאֲרוֹתֶיךָ׃}

verses.original: וּבְכָה וּבְעַמְּךָ וּבְכל עֲבָדֶיךָ יַעֲלוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים׃
verses.english: and the frogs will go up on you and on your people and on all your servants.’”

tex.original: \hOther{וּבְכָה וּבְעַמְּךָ וּבְכל עֲבָדֶיךָ יַעֲלוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן נְטֵה אֶת יָדְךָ בְּמַטֶּךָ עַל הַנְּהָרֹת עַל הַיְאֹרִים וְעַל הָאֲגַמִּים וְהַעַל אֶת הַצְפַרְדְּעִים עַל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Reach out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals, and over the pools, and bring up the frogs on the land of Egypt.’”

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן נְטֵה אֶת יָדְךָ בְּמַטֶּךָ עַל הַנְּהָרֹת עַל הַיְאֹרִים וְעַל הָאֲגַמִּים וְהַעַל אֶת הַצְפַרְדְּעִים עַל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּט אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדוֹ עַל מֵימֵי מִצְרָיִם וַתַּעַל הַצְּפַרְדֵּעַ וַתְּכַס אֶת אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And Aaron reached out his hand over Egypt’s waters, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.

tex.original: \hP{וַיֵּט אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדוֹ עַל מֵימֵי מִצְרָיִם וַתַּעַל הַצְּפַרְדֵּעַ וַתְּכַס אֶת אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים בְּלָטֵיהֶם וַיַּעֲלוּ אֶת הַצְפַרְדְּעִים עַל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And the magicians did so with their charms. And they brought up the frogs on the land of Egypt.

tex.original:
\hP{וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים בְּלָטֵיהֶם}
	\hE{וַיַּעֲלוּ אֶת הַצְפַרְדְּעִים עַל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה לְמֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמֶר הַעְתִּירוּ אֶל יְהֹוָה וְיָסֵר הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמֶּנִּי וּמֵעַמִּי וַאֲשַׁלְּחָה אֶת הָעָם וְיִזְבְּחוּ לַיהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to YHWH that He will take away the frogs from me and from my people so I may let the people go, and they’ll sacrifice to YHWH.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה לְמֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמֶר הַעְתִּירוּ אֶל יְהֹוָה וְיָסֵר הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמֶּנִּי וּמֵעַמִּי וַאֲשַׁלְּחָה אֶת הָעָם וְיִזְבְּחוּ לַיהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לְפַרְעֹה הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי לְמָתַי אַעְתִּיר לְךָ וְלַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּלְעַמְּךָ לְהַכְרִית הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמְּךָ וּמִבָּתֶּיךָ רַק בַּיְאֹר תִּשָּׁאַרְנָה׃
verses.english: And Moses said to Pharaoh, “Be honored over me as to when I’ll pray for you and for your servants and for your people to cut off the frogs from you and from your houses—they’ll be left only in the river.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לְפַרְעֹה הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי לְמָתַי אַעְתִּיר לְךָ וְלַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּלְעַמְּךָ לְהַכְרִית הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמְּךָ וּמִבָּתֶּיךָ רַק בַּיְאֹר תִּשָּׁאַרְנָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר לְמָחָר וַיֹּאמֶר כִּדְבָרְךָ לְמַעַן תֵּדַע כִּי אֵין כַּיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ׃
verses.english: And he said, “As of tomorrow.” And he said, “According to your word: so that you’ll know that there’s none like YHWH, our God.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר לְמָחָר וַיֹּאמֶר כִּדְבָרְךָ לְמַעַן תֵּדַע כִּי אֵין כַּיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ׃}

verses.original: וְסָרוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמְּךָ וּמִבָּתֶּיךָ וּמֵעֲבָדֶיךָ וּמֵעַמֶּךָ רַק בַּיְאֹר תִּשָּׁאַרְנָה׃
verses.english: And the frogs will turn away from you and from your houses and from your servants and from your people—they’ll be left only in the river.”

tex.original: \hE{וְסָרוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִמְּךָ וּמִבָּתֶּיךָ וּמֵעֲבָדֶיךָ וּמֵעַמֶּךָ רַק בַּיְאֹר תִּשָּׁאַרְנָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּצֵא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן מֵעִם פַּרְעֹה וַיִּצְעַק מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה עַל דְּבַר הַצְפַרְדְּעִים אֲשֶׁר שָׂם לְפַרְעֹה׃
verses.english: And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh. And Moses cried to YHWH over the matter of the frogs that he had set upon Pharaoh.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֵּצֵא מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן מֵעִם פַּרְעֹה וַיִּצְעַק מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה עַל דְּבַר הַצְפַרְדְּעִים אֲשֶׁר שָׂם לְפַרְעֹה׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעַשׂ יְהֹוָה כִּדְבַר מֹשֶׁה וַיָּמֻתוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִן הַבָּתִּים מִן הַחֲצֵרֹת וּמִן הַשָּׂדֹת׃
verses.english: And YHWH did according to Moses’ word, and the frogs died from the houses, from the yards, and from the fields.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּעַשׂ יְהֹוָה כִּדְבַר מֹשֶׁה וַיָּמֻתוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים מִן הַבָּתִּים מִן הַחֲצֵרֹת וּמִן הַשָּׂדֹת׃}

verses.original: וַיִּצְבְּרוּ אֹתָם חֳמָרִם חֳמָרִם וַתִּבְאַשׁ הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And they piled them up, heaps and heaps, and the land smelled.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּצְבְּרוּ אֹתָם חֳמָרִם חֳמָרִם וַתִּבְאַשׁ הָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		they piled them up. This term was used twice for
%		Joseph’s piling up the
%		grain (Gen 41:35,49), and these are its only occurrences
%		in biblical
%		prose. The wordplay appears to make the point that the
%		good that Joseph
%		did for Egypt was repaid with bad by the subsequent
%		Pharaohs, and this
%		makes the current plague more clearly a punishment to
%		suit the crime.
%		Also, the term for “were left” in 8:5,7 plays on the
%		“bowls” (both have
%		root ’r) in 7:28. And this whole paragraph is filled
%		with words using
%		the Hebrew letter adeh, perhaps playing on pard‛a
%		(frogs).
%	}

verses.original: וַיַּרְא פַּרְעֹה כִּי הָיְתָה הָרְוָחָה וְהַכְבֵּד אֶת לִבּוֹ וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh saw that there was a break, and he made his heart heavy, and he did not listen to them—as YHWH had spoken.

tex.original:
\hE{וַיַּרְא פַּרְעֹה כִּי הָיְתָה הָרְוָחָה וְהַכְבֵּד אֶת לִבּוֹ}
	\hR{וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן נְטֵה אֶת מַטְּךָ וְהַךְ אֶת עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ וְהָיָה לְכִנִּם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Say to Aaron, ‘Reach out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and it will become lice in all the land of Egypt.’”

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה אֱמֹר אֶל אַהֲרֹן נְטֵה אֶת מַטְּךָ וְהַךְ אֶת עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ וְהָיָה לְכִנִּם בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן וַיֵּט אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדוֹ בְמַטֵּהוּ וַיַּךְ אֶת עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ וַתְּהִי הַכִּנָּם בָּאָדָם וּבַבְּהֵמָה כּל עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ הָיָה כִנִּים בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And they did so, and Aaron reached out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the lice were in the humans and in the animals. All the dust of the earth was lice in all the land of Egypt.

tex.original: \hP{וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן וַיֵּט אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדוֹ בְמַטֵּהוּ וַיַּךְ אֶת עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ וַתְּהִי הַכִּנָּם בָּאָדָם וּבַבְּהֵמָה כּל עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ הָיָה כִנִּים בְּכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים בְּלָטֵיהֶם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת הַכִּנִּים וְלֹא יָכֹלוּ וַתְּהִי הַכִּנָּם בָּאָדָם וּבַבְּהֵמָה׃
verses.english: And the magicians did so with their charms, to bring out the lice, and they were not able. And the lice were in the humans and in the animals.

tex.original: \hP{וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים בְּלָטֵיהֶם לְהוֹצִיא אֶת הַכִּנִּים וְלֹא יָכֹלוּ וַתְּהִי הַכִּנָּם בָּאָדָם וּבַבְּהֵמָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמְרוּ הַחַרְטֻמִּם אֶל פַּרְעֹה אֶצְבַּע אֱלֹהִים הִוא וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And the magicians said to Pharaoh, “It’s the finger of God!” And Pharaoh’s heart was strong, and he did not listen to them—as YHWH had spoken.

tex.original: \hP{וַיֹּאמְרוּ הַחַרְטֻמִּם אֶל פַּרְעֹה אֶצְבַּע אֱלֹהִים הִוא וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב פַּרְעֹה וְלֹא שָׁמַע אֲלֵהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הַשְׁכֵּם בַּבֹּקֶר וְהִתְיַצֵּב לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה הִנֵּה יוֹצֵא הַמָּיְמָה וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה שַׁלַּח עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning and stand up in front of Pharaoh. Here, he’s going out to the water. And you’ll say to him, ‘YHWH said this: Let my people go so they may serve me.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הַשְׁכֵּם בַּבֹּקֶר וְהִתְיַצֵּב לִפְנֵי פַרְעֹה הִנֵּה יוֹצֵא הַמָּיְמָה וְאָמַרְתָּ אֵלָיו כֹּה אָמַר יְהֹוָה שַׁלַּח עַמִּי וְיַעַבְדֻנִי׃}

verses.original: כִּי אִם אֵינְךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ אֶת עַמִּי הִנְנִי מַשְׁלִיחַ בְּךָ וּבַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּבְעַמְּךָ וּבְבָתֶּיךָ אֶת הֶעָרֹב וּמָלְאוּ בָּתֵּי מִצְרַיִם אֶת הֶעָרֹב וְגַם הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר הֵם עָלֶיהָ׃
verses.english: Because if you’re not letting my people go, here, I’m causing an insect swarm to be let go on you and on your servants and on your people and on your houses. And the houses of Egypt will be filled with the insect swarm, and also the ground that they’re on.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי אִם אֵינְךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ אֶת עַמִּי הִנְנִי מַשְׁלִיחַ בְּךָ וּבַעֲבָדֶיךָ וּבְעַמְּךָ וּבְבָתֶּיךָ אֶת הֶעָרֹב וּמָלְאוּ בָּתֵּי מִצְרַיִם אֶת הֶעָרֹב וְגַם הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר הֵם עָלֶיהָ׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		Because if you’re not letting my people go, here, I’m
		causing an insect swarm to be let go on you and on your
		servants and on your people and on your houses. And the
		houses of Egypt will be filled with the insect swarm, and
		also the ground that they’re on.
	}

verses.original: וְהִפְלֵיתִי בַיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת אֶרֶץ גֹּשֶׁן אֲשֶׁר עַמִּי עֹמֵד עָלֶיהָ לְבִלְתִּי הֱיוֹת שָׁם עָרֹב לְמַעַן תֵּדַע כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And I shall distinguish in that day the land of Goshen, on which my people is standing, for no insect swarm to be there, so that you will know that I, YHWH, am within the land.

tex.original: \hE{וְהִפְלֵיתִי בַיּוֹם הַהוּא אֶת אֶרֶץ גֹּשֶׁן אֲשֶׁר עַמִּי עֹמֵד עָלֶיהָ לְבִלְתִּי הֱיוֹת שָׁם עָרֹב לְמַעַן תֵּדַע כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		I, YHWH, am within the land. As earlier (7:17), this can
%		also be
%		understood in terms of the meaning of the divine name,
%		thus meaning “So
%		that you will know that I am the one who causes being in
%		the land.”
%	}

verses.original: וְשַׂמְתִּי פְדֻת בֵּין עַמִּי וּבֵין עַמֶּךָ לְמָחָר יִהְיֶה הָאֹת הַזֶּה׃
verses.english: And I shall set a distinction between my people and your people. This sign will be tomorrow.’”

tex.original: \hE{וְשַׂמְתִּי פְדֻת בֵּין עַמִּי וּבֵין עַמֶּךָ לְמָחָר יִהְיֶה הָאֹת הַזֶּה׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		distinction. The Hebrew reads pdt, “ransom?” The Greek
%		and the Vulgate
%		read “distinction,” which makes more apparent sense and
%		relates to the
%		distinguishing that is predicted in the preceding verse.
%	}

verses.original: וַיַּעַשׂ יְהֹוָה כֵּן וַיָּבֹא עָרֹב כָּבֵד בֵּיתָה פַרְעֹה וּבֵית עֲבָדָיו וּבְכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם תִּשָּׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ מִפְּנֵי הֶעָרֹב׃
verses.english: And YHWH did so. And a heavy insect swarm came to Pharaoh’s house and his servants’ house, and in all the land of Egypt the land was corrupted because of the insect swarm.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּעַשׂ יְהֹוָה כֵּן וַיָּבֹא עָרֹב כָּבֵד בֵּיתָה פַרְעֹה וּבֵית עֲבָדָיו וּבְכל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם תִּשָּׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ מִפְּנֵי הֶעָרֹב׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמֶר לְכוּ זִבְחוּ לֵאלֹהֵיכֶם בָּאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron. And he said, “Go. Sacrifice to your God in the land.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן וַיֹּאמֶר לְכוּ זִבְחוּ לֵאלֹהֵיכֶם בָּאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Sacrifice to your God in the land. Pharaoh is not fooled
%		by the request
%		for a “trip of three days.” He takes a step back from
%		his tough stance,
%		and he turns to negotiation: You can sacrifice to your
%		God, but do it
%		here in Egypt, not out in the wilderness. A process of
%		bargaining will
%		follow, but note that, really, all the bargaining is on
%		Pharaoh’s part.
%		Moses’ position never changes, and in the end Pharaoh
%		must capitulate
%		completely.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לֹא נָכוֹן לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן כִּי תּוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם נִזְבַּח לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ הֵן נִזְבַּח אֶת תּוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם לְעֵינֵיהֶם וְלֹא יִסְקְלֻנוּ׃
verses.english: And Moses said, “It’s not right to do so, because we’ll be sacrificing to YHWH, our God, an offensive thing to Egypt. Here, we’ll be sacrificing an offensive thing to Egypt before their eyes; and will they not stone us?!

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לֹא נָכוֹן לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן כִּי תּוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם נִזְבַּח לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ הֵן נִזְבַּח אֶת תּוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם לְעֵינֵיהֶם וְלֹא יִסְקְלֻנוּ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		It’s not right. “Right” (nkôn) is the word Joseph used
%		to tell Pharaoh
%		that the repetition of his dream meant that the seven
%		good and seven bad
%		years were certainly coming (Gen 41:32). In that same
%		speech, Joseph
%		used the word “heavy” for the famine (41:31). As with
%		the “piling up” in
%		Exod 8:10, the cluster of language from the Joseph story
%		suggests that
%		the good that Joseph did for Egypt was repaid with bad
%		by the subsequent
%		Pharaohs, and this, again, suggests that the current
%		plague suits the
%		crime. Footnote 8:22. an offensive thing to Egypt. As we
%		have seen in
%		the Joseph story, there are matters relating to the
%		Israelites’ food
%		that are pictured as being “an offensive thing to
%		Egypt.” There the
%		Egyptians will not eat with Israelites (Gen 43:32), and
%		they disdain the
%		Israelite consumption of sheep. Now Moses uses this
%		fact—which worked
%		against the Israelites in Joseph’s day—in the
%		Israelites’ favor.
%	}

verses.original: דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים נֵלֵךְ בַּמִּדְבָּר וְזָבַחְנוּ לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר אֵלֵינוּ׃
verses.english: We’ll go on a trip of three days in the wilderness, and we’ll sacrifice to YHWH, our God, whatever He’ll say to us.”

tex.original: \hE{דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים נֵלֵךְ בַּמִּדְבָּר וְזָבַחְנוּ לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר אֵלֵינוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה אָנֹכִי אֲשַׁלַּח אֶתְכֶם וּזְבַחְתֶּם לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם בַּמִּדְבָּר רַק הַרְחֵק לֹא תַרְחִיקוּ לָלֶכֶת הַעְתִּירוּ בַּעֲדִי׃
verses.english: And Pharaoh said, “I’ll let you go, and you’ll sacrifice to YHWH, your God, in the wilderness. Only you shall not go far. Pray for me.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה אָנֹכִי אֲשַׁלַּח אֶתְכֶם וּזְבַחְתֶּם לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם בַּמִּדְבָּר רַק הַרְחֵק לֹא תַרְחִיקוּ לָלֶכֶת הַעְתִּירוּ בַּעֲדִי׃}
