%		Moses’ wife and
%		sons, but only Moses’ meeting with Jethro is described.
%		There is nothing
%		about his reunion with his family. The Bible’s silences
%		are frustrating
%		(where did Cain find his wife? how did Sarah feel about
%		her son’s being
%		sacrificed?), but I think that we should learn to live
%		with them. Often
%		they are very loud silences—which is to say: very
%		powerful. Why does the
%		Torah announce the arrival of Moses’ wife and children
%		but not describe
%		a personal meeting scene between them and Moses?
%		Presumably, this is
%		because it was important to let us know that his wife
%		and children were
%		present with the Israelites during the wilderness
%		period, but it was not
%		deemed important to describe their family relations.
%		Family relations
%		are described in the age of the patriarchs and in the
%		age of the kings
%		because, there, they play a role in the destiny of the
%		people. They are
%		described in the cases of Jephthah and Samson because
%		they propel the
%		life events of those persons. But in Moses’ case the
%		family episodes are
%		few: his mother and sister protect him as a baby, his
%		wife has a
%		confrontation with him at the inn on the way to Egypt,
%		Aaron and Miriam
%		criticize his Cushite wife and are rebuked by God. The
%		rest of Moses’
%		family life is personal. His wife speaks three sentences
%		in the Torah.
%		His sons speak none. That tells us, at the very least,
%		that his
%		particular life mission is primarily about him and God,
%		on the one hand,
%		and him and the people, on the other. And the nature of
%		that mission is
%		such that his family situation is not permitted to
%		impinge upon it. The
%		missions of Abraham, David, and the rest of us are not
%		like that. It is
%		our frustration with the silences and our hunger for
%		more Torah that
%		give birth to midrash. So I was once asked to make a
%		midrash on what
%		might have happened between Moses and his wife and sons.
%		I suggested: He
%		told them everything—the confrontations with Pharaoh,
%		the snakes, the
%		plagues, the splitting of the sea. And his sons asked
%		him why he had
%		sent them away and thus kept them from seeing all that.
%		And he told them
%		that it was dangerous, and he was protecting them. Did
%		that show
%		insufficient faith on his part that things would go well
%		in Egypt? Of
%		course, he says. But he was just starting out and did
%		not yet know the
%		divine power—or the divine character. And so a father’s
%		love was his
%		first motive. But now, he assured them, they would stay
%		with him and get
%		to see an even greater event: Sinai.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְסַפֵּר מֹשֶׁה לְחֹתְנוֹ אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה לְפַרְעֹה וּלְמִצְרַיִם עַל אוֹדֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵת כּל הַתְּלָאָה אֲשֶׁר מְצָאָתַם בַּדֶּרֶךְ וַיַּצִּלֵם יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Moses told his father-in-law everything that YHWH had done to Pharaoh and to Egypt with regard to Israel, all the hardship that had found them on the way, and YHWH rescued them.

tex.original: \hE{וַיְסַפֵּר מֹשֶׁה לְחֹתְנוֹ אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה לְפַרְעֹה וּלְמִצְרַיִם עַל אוֹדֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵת כּל הַתְּלָאָה אֲשֶׁר מְצָאָתַם בַּדֶּרֶךְ וַיַּצִּלֵם יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיִּחַדְּ יִתְרוֹ עַל כּל הַטּוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר הִצִּילוֹ מִיַּד מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And Jethro rejoiced over all the good that YHWH had done for Israel, that He had rescued it from Egypt’s hand.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּחַדְּ יִתְרוֹ עַל כּל הַטּוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר הִצִּילוֹ מִיַּד מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יִתְרוֹ בָּרוּךְ יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֶתְכֶם מִיַּד מִצְרַיִם וּמִיַּד פַּרְעֹה אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֶת הָעָם מִתַּחַת יַד מִצְרָיִם׃
verses.english: And Jethro said, “Blessed is YHWH, who rescued you from Egypt’s hand and from Pharaoh’s hand, who rescued the people from under Egypt’s hand:

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יִתְרוֹ בָּרוּךְ יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֶתְכֶם מִיַּד מִצְרַיִם וּמִיַּד פַּרְעֹה אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֶת הָעָם מִתַּחַת יַד מִצְרָיִם׃}

verses.original: עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי גָדוֹל יְהֹוָה מִכּל הָאֱלֹהִים כִּי בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם׃
verses.english: now I know that YHWH is bigger than all the gods, because of the thing that they plotted against them.”

tex.original: \hE{עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי גָדוֹל יְהֹוָה מִכּל הָאֱלֹהִים כִּי בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם׃}

verses.original: וַיִּקַּח יִתְרוֹ חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה עֹלָה וּזְבָחִים לֵאלֹהִים וַיָּבֹא אַהֲרֹן וְכֹל זִקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֶאֱכל לֶחֶם עִם חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים׃
verses.english: And Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. And Aaron and all of Israel’s elders came to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּקַּח יִתְרוֹ חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה עֹלָה וּזְבָחִים לֵאלֹהִים וַיָּבֹא אַהֲרֹן וְכֹל זִקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֶאֱכל לֶחֶם עִם חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים׃}

verses.original: וַיְהִי מִמּחֳרָת וַיֵּשֶׁב מֹשֶׁה לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת הָעָם וַיַּעֲמֹד הָעָם עַל מֹשֶׁה מִן הַבֹּקֶר עַד הָעָרֶב׃
verses.english: And it was the next day, and Moses sat to judge the people. And the people stood by Moses from the morning to the evening.

tex.original: \hE{וַיְהִי מִמּחֳרָת וַיֵּשֶׁב מֹשֶׁה לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת הָעָם וַיַּעֲמֹד הָעָם עַל מֹשֶׁה מִן הַבֹּקֶר עַד הָעָרֶב׃}

verses.original: וַיַּרְא חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר הוּא עֹשֶׂה לָעָם וַיֹּאמֶר מָה הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה עֹשֶׂה לָעָם מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה יוֹשֵׁב לְבַדֶּךָ וְכל הָעָם נִצָּב עָלֶיךָ מִן בֹּקֶר עַד עָרֶב׃
verses.english: And Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, and he said, “What’s this thing that you’re doing for the people? Why are you sitting by yourself, and the entire people is standing up by you from morning until evening?”

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּרְא חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה אֵת כּל אֲשֶׁר הוּא עֹשֶׂה לָעָם וַיֹּאמֶר מָה הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה עֹשֶׂה לָעָם מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה יוֹשֵׁב לְבַדֶּךָ וְכל הָעָם נִצָּב עָלֶיךָ מִן בֹּקֶר עַד עָרֶב׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		And Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the
		people, and he said, “What’s this thing that you’re doing
		for the people? Why are you sitting by yourself, and the
		entire people is standing up by you from morning until
		evening?”
	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לְחֹתְנוֹ כִּי יָבֹא אֵלַי הָעָם לִדְרֹשׁ אֱלֹהִים׃
verses.english: And Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לְחֹתְנוֹ כִּי יָבֹא אֵלַי הָעָם לִדְרֹשׁ אֱלֹהִים׃}

verses.original: כִּי יִהְיֶה לָהֶם דָּבָר בָּא אֵלַי וְשָׁפַטְתִּי בֵּין אִישׁ וּבֵין רֵעֵהוּ וְהוֹדַעְתִּי אֶת חֻקֵּי הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֶת תּוֹרֹתָיו׃
verses.english: When they have a matter, it comes to me, and I judge between each one and his companion, and I make known God’s laws and His instructions.”

tex.original: \hE{כִּי יִהְיֶה לָהֶם דָּבָר בָּא אֵלַי וְשָׁפַטְתִּי בֵּין אִישׁ וּבֵין רֵעֵהוּ וְהוֹדַעְתִּי אֶת חֻקֵּי הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֶת תּוֹרֹתָיו׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה אֵלָיו לֹא טוֹב הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה עֹשֶׂה׃
verses.english: And Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you’re doing isn’t good.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה אֵלָיו לֹא טוֹב הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה עֹשֶׂה׃}

verses.original: נָבֹל תִּבֹּל גַּם אַתָּה גַּם הָעָם הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר עִמָּךְ כִּי כָבֵד מִמְּךָ הַדָּבָר לֹא תוּכַל עֲשֹׂהוּ לְבַדֶּךָ׃
verses.english: You’ll be worn out, both you and this people who are with you, because the thing is too heavy for you. You won’t be able to do it by yourself.

tex.original: \hE{נָבֹל תִּבֹּל גַּם אַתָּה גַּם הָעָם הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר עִמָּךְ כִּי כָבֵד מִמְּךָ הַדָּבָר לֹא תוּכַל עֲשֹׂהוּ לְבַדֶּךָ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		too heavy for you. “Heavy” again. See the comment on
%		Exod 5:9. And see
%		Num 11:14. Footnote 18:18. able to do it by yourself.
%		The convergence of
%		the terms for “to be by oneself” and “to be able”
%		(twice: vv. 18 and 23)
%		in this passage is striking because they both appear in
%		the story of
%		Jacob wrestling with God (Gen 32:24–33), which begins
%		with the notice
%		that “he was left by himself” and later notes (twice)
%		that Jacob “was
%		able” in the struggle. It is remarkable that Jacob was
%		pictured as able
%		to struggle with God by himself but Moses is pictured as
%		not being able
%		to manage the people by himself. Does a person stand a
%		better chance of
%		being successful in a personal struggle with God than in
%		taking on a
%		community of humans?
%	}

verses.original: עַתָּה שְׁמַע בְּקֹלִי אִיעָצְךָ וִיהִי אֱלֹהִים עִמָּךְ הֱיֵה אַתָּה לָעָם מוּל הָאֱלֹהִים וְהֵבֵאתָ אַתָּה אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים׃
verses.english: Now listen to my voice, and I’ll advise you, and may God be with you. You be for the people toward God, and you will bring the matters to God.

tex.original: \hE{עַתָּה שְׁמַע בְּקֹלִי אִיעָצְךָ וִיהִי אֱלֹהִים עִמָּךְ הֱיֵה אַתָּה לָעָם מוּל הָאֱלֹהִים וְהֵבֵאתָ אַתָּה אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים׃}

verses.original: וְהִזְהַרְתָּה אֶתְהֶם אֶת הַחֻקִּים וְאֶת הַתּוֹרֹת וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ יֵלְכוּ בָהּ וְאֶת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשׂוּן׃
verses.english: And you’ll enlighten them with the laws and the instructions, and you’ll make known to them the way in which they’ll go and the thing that they’ll do.

tex.original: \hE{וְהִזְהַרְתָּה אֶתְהֶם אֶת הַחֻקִּים וְאֶת הַתּוֹרֹת וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ יֵלְכוּ בָהּ וְאֶת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשׂוּן׃}

verses.original: וְאַתָּה תֶחֱזֶה מִכּל הָעָם אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל יִרְאֵי אֱלֹהִים אַנְשֵׁי אֱמֶת שֹׂנְאֵי בָצַע וְשַׂמְתָּ עֲלֵהֶם שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת שָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים וְשָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרֹת׃
verses.english: And you will envision, out of all the people, worthy men, who fear God, men of truth, who hate bribery, and you’ll set chiefs of thousands, chiefs of hundreds, chiefs of fifties, and chiefs of tens over them.

tex.original: \hE{וְאַתָּה תֶחֱזֶה מִכּל הָעָם אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל יִרְאֵי אֱלֹהִים אַנְשֵׁי אֱמֶת שֹׂנְאֵי בָצַע וְשַׂמְתָּ עֲלֵהֶם שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת שָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים וְשָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרֹת׃}

verses.original: וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכל עֵת וְהָיָה כּל הַדָּבָר הַגָּדֹל יָבִיאוּ אֵלֶיךָ וְכל הַדָּבָר הַקָּטֹן יִשְׁפְּטוּ הֵם וְהָקֵל מֵעָלֶיךָ וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתָּךְ׃
verses.english: And they’ll judge the people at all times. And it will be: they’ll bring every matter that is big to you, and they will judge every matter that is small. And make it lighter on you, and they’ll bear it with you.

tex.original: \hE{וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכל עֵת וְהָיָה כּל הַדָּבָר הַגָּדֹל יָבִיאוּ אֵלֶיךָ וְכל הַדָּבָר הַקָּטֹן יִשְׁפְּטוּ הֵם וְהָקֵל מֵעָלֶיךָ וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתָּךְ׃}

verses.original: אִם אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה תַּעֲשֶׂה וְצִוְּךָ אֱלֹהִים וְיָכלְתָּ עֲמֹד וְגַם כּל הָעָם הַזֶּה עַל מְקֹמוֹ יָבֹא בְשָׁלוֹם׃
verses.english: If you’ll do this thing, and YHWH will command you, then you’ll be able to stand, and also this entire people will come to its place in peace.”

tex.original: \hE{אִם אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה תַּעֲשֶׂה וְצִוְּךָ אֱלֹהִים וְיָכלְתָּ עֲמֹד וְגַם כּל הָעָם הַזֶּה עַל מְקֹמוֹ יָבֹא בְשָׁלוֹם׃}

verses.original: וַיִּשְׁמַע מֹשֶׁה לְקוֹל חֹתְנוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָמָר׃
verses.english: And Moses listened to his father-in-law’s voice and did everything that he had said.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּשְׁמַע מֹשֶׁה לְקוֹל חֹתְנוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָמָר׃}

verses.original: וַיִּבְחַר מֹשֶׁה אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל מִכּל יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָם רָאשִׁים עַל הָעָם שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת שָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים וְשָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרֹת׃
verses.english: And Moses chose worthy men out of all of Israel and made them heads over the people: chiefs of thousands, chiefs of hundreds, chiefs of fifties, and chiefs of tens.

tex.original: \hE{וַיִּבְחַר מֹשֶׁה אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל מִכּל יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָם רָאשִׁים עַל הָעָם שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת שָׂרֵי חֲמִשִּׁים וְשָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרֹת׃}

verses.original: וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכל עֵת אֶת הַדָּבָר הַקָּשֶׁה יְבִיאוּן אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְכל הַדָּבָר הַקָּטֹן יִשְׁפּוּטוּ הֵם׃
verses.english: And they judged the people at all times. They would bring the matter that was hard to Moses, and they would judge every matter that was small.

tex.original: \hE{וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכל עֵת אֶת הַדָּבָר הַקָּשֶׁה יְבִיאוּן אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְכל הַדָּבָר הַקָּטֹן יִשְׁפּוּטוּ הֵם׃}

verses.original: וַיְשַׁלַּח מֹשֶׁה אֶת חֹתְנוֹ וַיֵּלֶךְ לוֹ אֶל אַרְצוֹ׃
verses.english: And Moses let his father-in-law go, and he went to his land.

tex.original: \hE{וַיְשַׁלַּח מֹשֶׁה אֶת חֹתְנוֹ וַיֵּלֶךְ לוֹ אֶל אַרְצוֹ׃}

verses.original: בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁי לְצֵאת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה בָּאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינָי׃
verses.english: In the third month after the exodus of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, on this day, they came to the wilderness of Sinai.

tex.original: \hP{בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁי לְצֵאת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה בָּאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינָי׃}

verses.original: וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי וַיַּחֲנוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר וַיִּחַן שָׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶגֶד הָהָר׃
verses.english: And they traveled from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai and camped in the wilderness. And Israel camped there opposite the mountain.

tex.original:
\hR{וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי וַיַּחֲנוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר}
	\hE{וַיִּחַן שָׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶגֶד הָהָר׃}

verses.original: וּמֹשֶׁה עָלָה אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּקְרָא אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה מִן הָהָר לֵאמֹר כֹּה תֹאמַר לְבֵית יַעֲקֹב וְתַגֵּיד לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃
verses.english: And Moses had gone up to God. And YHWH called to him from the mountain, saying, “This is what you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell to the children of Israel:

tex.original: \hE{וּמֹשֶׁה עָלָה אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּקְרָא אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה מִן הָהָר לֵאמֹר כֹּה תֹאמַר לְבֵית יַעֲקֹב וְתַגֵּיד לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Moses had gone up to God. While “going up to God” is an
%		intriguing
%		image, the Septuagint text is more probably correct. It
%		reads “up to the
%		mountain of God,” which fits better with the words that
%		follow: “And
%		YHWH called to him from the mountain.”
%	}

verses.original: אַתֶּם רְאִיתֶם אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי לְמִצְרָיִם וָאֶשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם עַל כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים וָאָבִא אֶתְכֶם אֵלָי׃
verses.english: ‘You’ve seen what I did to Egypt, and I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to me.

tex.original: \hE{אַתֶּם רְאִיתֶם אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי לְמִצְרָיִם וָאֶשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם עַל כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים וָאָבִא אֶתְכֶם אֵלָי׃}

verses.original: וְעַתָּה אִם שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ בְּקֹלִי וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת בְּרִיתִי וִהְיִיתֶם לִי סְגֻלָּה מִכּל הָעַמִּים כִּי לִי כּל הָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: And now, if you’ll listen to my voice and observe my covenant, then you’ll be a treasure to me out of all the peoples, because all the earth is mine.

tex.original: \hE{וְעַתָּה אִם שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ בְּקֹלִי וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת בְּרִיתִי וִהְיִיתֶם לִי סְגֻלָּה מִכּל הָעַמִּים כִּי לִי כּל הָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		if. This first occurrence of the word segullah
%		(treasure) is not
%		ambiguous in context: The people of Israel will be a
%		treasured
%		possession of God only if they listen and fulfill their
%		covenant. Their
%		status is not based on some intrinsic quality but on
%		their behavior. God
%		is about to make a covenant with them. If they keep
%		their part of it,
%		then they will be segullah. (For more on the matter of
%		being chosen and
%		a treasured people, see the comment on Deut 7:6.)
%		Footnote 19:5. a
%		treasure to me out of all the peoples. Since the verse
%		says explicitly
%		that this treasured status is based on their behavior,
%		and not on their
%		being superior to anyone else, what then is the purpose
%		of their being
%		chosen to observe this covenant? The reason was stated,
%		no less
%		explicitly, to their ancestor Abraham: to be a blessing
%		to all the
%		families of the earth.
%	}

verses.original: וְאַתֶּם תִּהְיוּ לִי מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים וְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר תְּדַבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃
verses.english: And you’ll be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation to me.’ These are the words that you shall speak to the children of Israel.”

tex.original: \hE{וְאַתֶּם תִּהְיוּ לִי מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים וְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר תְּדַבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		holy. For a long time we have taught that this word,
%		Hebrew qdš, does
%		not refer to some sacred, elevated condition but rather
%		that it denotes
%		being separate, set aside for some particular purpose.
%		But, really, it
%		does in fact refer to a special consecrated state. When
%		God tells Moses
%		at the bush, “Take off your shoes from your feet,
%		because the place on
%		which you’re standing: it’s holy ground,” this means
%		more than that the
%		ground is “set aside.” It means “holy” in just the way
%		that people
%		naturally understand it on first reading. The ground has
%		a special
%		quality deriving from the realm of the divine which
%		makes shoes
%		inappropriate there. And in the present context, “holy
%		nation” does not
%		mean that Israel will be separate from other nations. It
%		means that
%		Israel will be consecrated if the people will live the
%		life that their
%		divine covenant requires of them. (See also the comment
%		on Exod 29:37.)
%	}

verses.original: וַיָּבֹא מֹשֶׁה וַיִּקְרָא לְזִקְנֵי הָעָם וַיָּשֶׂם לִפְנֵיהֶם אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּהוּ יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And Moses came and called the people’s elders and set before them all these words that YHWH had commanded him.

tex.original: \hE{וַיָּבֹא מֹשֶׁה וַיִּקְרָא לְזִקְנֵי הָעָם וַיָּשֶׂם לִפְנֵיהֶם אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּהוּ יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲנוּ כל הָעָם יַחְדָּו וַיֹּאמְרוּ כֹּל אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה נַעֲשֶׂה וַיָּשֶׁב מֹשֶׁה אֶת דִּבְרֵי הָעָם אֶל יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And all the people responded together, and they said, “We’ll do everything that YHWH has spoken.” And Moses brought back the people’s words to YHWH.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּעֲנוּ כל הָעָם יַחְדָּו וַיֹּאמְרוּ כֹּל אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהֹוָה נַעֲשֶׂה וַיָּשֶׁב מֹשֶׁה אֶת דִּבְרֵי הָעָם אֶל יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי בָּא אֵלֶיךָ בְּעַב הֶעָנָן בַּעֲבוּר יִשְׁמַע הָעָם בְּדַבְּרִי עִמָּךְ וְגַם בְּךָ יַאֲמִינוּ לְעוֹלָם וַיַּגֵּד מֹשֶׁה אֶת דִּבְרֵי הָעָם אֶל יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Here, I am coming to you in a mass of cloud for the purpose that the people will hear when I am speaking with you, and they will believe in you as well forever.” And Moses told the people’s words to YHWH.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי בָּא אֵלֶיךָ בְּעַב הֶעָנָן בַּעֲבוּר יִשְׁמַע הָעָם בְּדַבְּרִי עִמָּךְ וְגַם בְּךָ יַאֲמִינוּ לְעוֹלָם וַיַּגֵּד מֹשֶׁה אֶת דִּבְרֵי הָעָם אֶל יְהֹוָה׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		And YHWH said to Moses, “Here, I am coming to you in a
		mass of cloud for the purpose that the people will hear
		when I am speaking with you, and they will believe in you
		as well forever.” And Moses told the people’s words to
		YHWH.
	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵךְ אֶל הָעָם וְקִדַּשְׁתָּם הַיּוֹם וּמָחָר וְכִבְּסוּ שִׂמְלֹתָם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow; and they shall wash their clothes

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵךְ אֶל הָעָם וְקִדַּשְׁתָּם הַיּוֹם וּמָחָר וְכִבְּסוּ שִׂמְלֹתָם׃}

verses.original: וְהָיוּ נְכֹנִים לַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי כִּי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִשִׁי יֵרֵד יְהֹוָה לְעֵינֵי כל הָעָם עַל הַר סִינָי׃
verses.english: and be ready for the third day, because on the third day YHWH will come down on Mount Sinai before the eyes of all the people.

tex.original: \hJ{וְהָיוּ נְכֹנִים לַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי כִּי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִשִׁי יֵרֵד יְהֹוָה לְעֵינֵי כל הָעָם עַל הַר סִינָי׃}

verses.original: וְהִגְבַּלְתָּ אֶת הָעָם סָבִיב לֵאמֹר הִשָּׁמְרוּ לָכֶם עֲלוֹת בָּהָר וּנְגֹעַ בְּקָצֵהוּ כּל הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהָר מוֹת יוּמָת׃
verses.english: And you shall limit the people all around, saying, ‘Watch yourselves about going up in the mountain and touching its edge. Anyone who touches the mountain shall be put to death.

tex.original: \hJ{וְהִגְבַּלְתָּ אֶת הָעָם סָבִיב לֵאמֹר הִשָּׁמְרוּ לָכֶם עֲלוֹת בָּהָר וּנְגֹעַ בְּקָצֵהוּ כּל הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהָר מוֹת יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: לֹא תִגַּע בּוֹ יָד כִּי סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל אוֹ יָרֹה יִיָּרֶה אִם בְּהֵמָה אִם אִישׁ לֹא יִחְיֶה בִּמְשֹׁךְ הַיֹּבֵל הֵמָּה יַעֲלוּ בָהָר׃
verses.english: A hand shall not touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot. Whether animal or man, he will not live.’ At the blowing of the horn they shall go up the mountain.”

tex.original: \hJ{לֹא תִגַּע בּוֹ יָד כִּי סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל אוֹ יָרֹה יִיָּרֶה אִם בְּהֵמָה אִם אִישׁ לֹא יִחְיֶה בִּמְשֹׁךְ הַיֹּבֵל הֵמָּה יַעֲלוּ בָהָר׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּרֶד מֹשֶׁה מִן הָהָר אֶל הָעָם וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֶת הָעָם וַיְכַבְּסוּ שִׂמְלֹתָם׃
verses.english: And Moses went down from the mountain to the people. And he consecrated the people, and they washed their clothes.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֵּרֶד מֹשֶׁה מִן הָהָר אֶל הָעָם וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֶת הָעָם וַיְכַבְּסוּ שִׂמְלֹתָם׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל הָעָם הֱיוּ נְכֹנִים לִשְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים אַל תִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל אִשָּׁה׃
verses.english: And he said to the people, “Be ready for three days. Don’t come close to a woman.”

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל הָעָם הֱיוּ נְכֹנִים לִשְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים אַל תִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל אִשָּׁה׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		he said to the people, “Don’t come close to a woman.” If
%		he is speaking
%		to “the people,” which includes both men and women, why
%		does he say,
%		“Don’t come close to a woman”? Like many passages, this
%		may have two
%		opposite interpretations. It may be a case of male
%		chauvinism in
%		language, in which an address to “the people” means the
%		men. Or it may
%		reflect a perception that a command to abstain from sex
%		for three days
%		needs to be particularly directed to men because men are
%		more likely
%		than women to violate the instruction.
%	}

verses.original: וַיְהִי בַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי בִּהְיֹת הַבֹּקֶר וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים וְעָנָן כָּבֵד עַל הָהָר וְקֹל שֹׁפָר חָזָק מְאֹד וַיֶּחֱרַד כּל הָעָם אֲשֶׁר בַּמַּחֲנֶה׃
verses.english: And it was on the third day, when it was morning, and it was: thunders and lightning and a heavy cloud on the mountain, and a sound of a horn, very strong. And the entire people that was in the camp trembled.

tex.original:
\hJ{וַיְהִי בַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי בִּהְיֹת הַבֹּקֶר}
	\hE{וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים וְעָנָן כָּבֵד עַל הָהָר וְקֹל שֹׁפָר חָזָק מְאֹד וַיֶּחֱרַד כּל הָעָם אֲשֶׁר בַּמַּחֲנֶה׃}

verses.original: וַיּוֹצֵא מֹשֶׁה אֶת הָעָם לִקְרַאת הָאֱלֹהִים מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה וַיִּתְיַצְּבוּ בְּתַחְתִּית הָהָר׃
verses.english: And Moses brought out the people toward God from the camp, and they stood up at the bottom of the mountain.

tex.original: \hE{וַיּוֹצֵא מֹשֶׁה אֶת הָעָם לִקְרַאת הָאֱלֹהִים מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה וַיִּתְיַצְּבוּ בְּתַחְתִּית הָהָר׃}

verses.original: וְהַר סִינַי עָשַׁן כֻּלּוֹ מִפְּנֵי אֲשֶׁר יָרַד עָלָיו יְהֹוָה בָּאֵשׁ וַיַּעַל עֲשָׁנוֹ כְּעֶשֶׁן הַכִּבְשָׁן וַיֶּחֱרַד כּל הָהָר מְאֹד׃
verses.english: And Mount Sinai was all smoke because YHWH came down on it in fire, and its smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled greatly.

tex.original: \hJ{וְהַר סִינַי עָשַׁן כֻּלּוֹ מִפְּנֵי אֲשֶׁר יָרַד עָלָיו יְהֹוָה בָּאֵשׁ וַיַּעַל עֲשָׁנוֹ כְּעֶשֶׁן הַכִּבְשָׁן וַיֶּחֱרַד כּל הָהָר מְאֹד׃}

verses.original: וַיְהִי קוֹל הַשֹּׁפָר הוֹלֵךְ וְחָזֵק מְאֹד מֹשֶׁה יְדַבֵּר וְהָאֱלֹהִים יַעֲנֶנּוּ בְקוֹל׃
verses.english: And the sound of the horn was getting much stronger. Moses would speak, and God would answer him in a voice.

tex.original: \hE{וַיְהִי קוֹל הַשֹּׁפָר הוֹלֵךְ וְחָזֵק מְאֹד מֹשֶׁה יְדַבֵּר וְהָאֱלֹהִים יַעֲנֶנּוּ בְקוֹל׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		in a voice. Here, Hebrew bqôl can mean “in a voice” or
%		“with sound”
%		(i.e., aloud) or “with thunder.” In v. 16 the word
%		refers first to
%		thunder sounds and then to the sound of a horn. But the
%		divine statement
%		in v. 9 that “the people will hear when I am speaking
%		with you” suggests
%		that the people will hear spoken words between God and
%		Moses, and that
%		is what now happens in v. 19.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֵּרֶד יְהֹוָה עַל הַר סִינַי אֶל רֹאשׁ הָהָר וַיִּקְרָא יְהֹוָה לְמֹשֶׁה אֶל רֹאשׁ הָהָר וַיַּעַל מֹשֶׁה׃
verses.english: And YHWH came down on Mount Sinai, at the top of the mountain, and YHWH called to Moses at the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֵּרֶד יְהֹוָה עַל הַר סִינַי אֶל רֹאשׁ הָהָר וַיִּקְרָא יְהֹוָה לְמֹשֶׁה אֶל רֹאשׁ הָהָר וַיַּעַל מֹשֶׁה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה רֵד הָעֵד בָּעָם פֶּן יֶהֶרְסוּ אֶל יְהֹוָה לִרְאוֹת וְנָפַל מִמֶּנּוּ רָב׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “Go down. Warn the people in case they break through to YHWH, to see, and many of them fall.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה רֵד הָעֵד בָּעָם פֶּן יֶהֶרְסוּ אֶל יְהֹוָה לִרְאוֹת וְנָפַל מִמֶּנּוּ רָב׃}

verses.original: וְגַם הַכֹּהֲנִים הַנִּגָּשִׁים אֶל יְהֹוָה יִתְקַדָּשׁוּ פֶּן יִפְרֹץ בָּהֶם יְהֹוָה׃
verses.english: And also let the priests who approach YHWH consecrate themselves, or else YHWH will break out against them.”

tex.original: \hJ{וְגַם הַכֹּהֲנִים הַנִּגָּשִׁים אֶל יְהֹוָה יִתְקַדָּשׁוּ פֶּן יִפְרֹץ בָּהֶם יְהֹוָה׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה לֹא יוּכַל הָעָם לַעֲלֹת אֶל הַר סִינָי כִּי אַתָּה הַעֵדֹתָה בָּנוּ לֵאמֹר הַגְבֵּל אֶת הָהָר וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ׃
verses.english: And Moses said to YHWH, “The people is not able to go up to Mount Sinai, because you warned us, saying, ‘Limit the mountain and consecrate it.’”

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל יְהֹוָה לֹא יוּכַל הָעָם לַעֲלֹת אֶל הַר סִינָי כִּי אַתָּה הַעֵדֹתָה בָּנוּ לֵאמֹר הַגְבֵּל אֶת הָהָר וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה לֶךְ רֵד וְעָלִיתָ אַתָּה וְאַהֲרֹן עִמָּךְ וְהַכֹּהֲנִים וְהָעָם אַל יֶהֶרְסוּ לַעֲלֹת אֶל יְהֹוָה פֶּן יִפְרץ בָּם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to him, “Go. Go down. Then you’ll come up, you and Aaron with you. And let the priests and the people not break through to come up to YHWH, or else He’ll break out against them.”

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו יְהֹוָה לֶךְ רֵד וְעָלִיתָ אַתָּה וְאַהֲרֹן עִמָּךְ וְהַכֹּהֲנִים וְהָעָם אַל יֶהֶרְסוּ לַעֲלֹת אֶל יְהֹוָה פֶּן יִפְרץ בָּם׃}

verses.original: וַיֵּרֶד מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעָם וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם׃
verses.english: And Moses went down to the people, and he said it to them.

tex.original: \hJ{וַיֵּרֶד מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעָם וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם׃}
tex.english: \eJ{And Moses went down to the people, and he said it to them.}

verses.original: וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה לֵאמֹר׃
verses.english: And God spoke all these words, saying:

tex.original: \hR{וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֵת כּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה לֵאמֹר׃}
tex.english: \eR{And God spoke all these words, saying:}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		God spoke all these words. God speaks the words of the
%		Ten Commandments
%		aloud directly to the people. The Ten Commandments are
%		the text of the
%		covenant between God and Israel. One of the most
%		fruitful discoveries of
%		biblical research was the independent recognition by
%		three scholars (E.
%		Bickermann, G. Mendenhall, and K. Baltzer) in the 1950s
%		that there is a
%		formal similarity between the Israelite covenant and
%		international legal
%		documents of the ancient Near Eastern countries. The
%		treaty documents,
%		dictated by regional kings (suzerains) to the local city
%		kings (vassals)
%		who were subject to them, formalized the relationship
%		between the two.
%		They regularly included a specific group of formal
%		elements: 1. The
%		suzerain’s introduction of himself by name. 2. An
%		historical prologue,
%		giving the history of the relations between the parties,
%		generally
%		showing what the suzerain had done for his vassal, and
%		thus establishing
%		that the vassal was in the suzerain’s debt. 3. The prime
%		stipulation of
%		the treaty, namely that the vassal was to have
%		allegiance to this
%		suzerain and to no other. 4. The rest of the
%		stipulations, e.g., the
%		vassal’s obligation to pay tribute, to come when
%		summoned to the
%		suzerain’s court, and to provide troops for the
%		suzerain’s military
%		defense. The Sinai covenant here exhibits striking
%		parallels to this
%		legal structure, containing the key elements:
%		+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
%		| 1. Introduction: | I am YHWH your God |
%		+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
%		| 2. Historical Prologue: | who brought you out from the
%		land | | | of
%		Egypt, from a house of slaves |
%		+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
%		| 3. Prime Stipulation: | You shall not have other gods
%		|
%		+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
%		| 4. Other Stipulations: | You shall not make a statue |
%		| | | | | You
%		shall not bring up the name | | | of YHWH, your God, for
%		a | | |
%		falsehood | | | | | | Remember the Sabbath … | | | | | |
%		Honor your
%		father and your mother | | | … |
%		+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
%		The Near Eastern suzerainty treaties also include other
%		features that
%		appear here in the covenant. They included an oath sworn
%		by the vassal
%		pledging fidelity to the suzerain and to the
%		requirements of the treaty,
%		and they included provision for the treaty document,
%		requiring that it
%		be deposited in a sacred place. In Exodus the people
%		pledge their
%		obedience (24:3,7), and the covenant text is deposited
%		in the ark in the
%		Tabernacle (25:16,21; 40:20). Thus Israel’s relations
%		with its God are
%		conceived in the legal terms of that world. The words of
%		the Ten
%		Commandments and of the Covenant Code are not only
%		orders that must be
%		obeyed. They are legal corpora, concluded contractually
%		between the
%		creator and a human community.
%	}

verses.original: אָנֹכִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבֵּית עֲבָדִ͏ים׃
verses.english: I am YHWH, your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt, from a house of slaves.

tex.original: \hOther{אָנֹכִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבֵּית עֲבָדִ͏ים׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		I am YHWH, your God. People question whether this first
%		verse of the
%		covenant is a commandment or a statement, and they argue
%		over what,
%		exactly, it commands. The evidence from the ancient Near
%		Eastern
%		documents makes clear that this is not to be counted as
%		one of the
%		commandments. Introductory statements such as this one
%		are common and
%		fundamental to these documents: stating the name of the
%		one who is
%		dictating the terms and stating the history of what this
%		one has done
%		for the recipient of these terms. They leave no doubt
%		that the first
%		commandment is not “I am YHWH . . .” but rather “You
%		shall have no other
%		gods….” This is confirmed by the fact that when one
%		counts “I am YHWH .
%		. .” as a commandment, one comes out with eleven
%		commandments. Those who
%		have thought this to be a commandment have had to
%		combine two of the
%		later commandments into one. In any case, the question
%		of what the
%		opening words command arises in part because in English
%		we call this
%		text by the name “the Ten Commandments.” That misleads
%		us, though,
%		because in the Torah itself (Exod 34:28; Deut 10:4),
%		this text is called
%		simply the Ten Things (or Ten Words, or Ten Statements;
%		Hebrew ‘eret
%		haddbrîm). Footnote 20:2. who brought you out from the
%		land of Egypt. In
%		the relationship between the covenant and the ancient
%		Near Eastern legal
%		texts, the historical prologue has special importance:
%		In the Torah, law
%		is set in history. Law is never given in the Tanak in
%		the abstract,
%		apart from a historical context. There is always an
%		understanding that
%		the commandments are to be followed because God did
%		something for the
%		humans who are being commanded. There are more than
%		sixty chapters of
%		Torah before the first law to Israel occurs (Exodus 12).
%		Indeed, as I
%		said in my first comment (Gen 1:1), Rashi began his
%		commentary with the
%		question of why the Torah starts with creation and
%		subsequent history
%		rather than being strictly a law code and starting with
%		the first law in
%		Exodus 12. I would now add another answer: that biblical
%		Israel
%		understood this law to require historical context. The
%		law was conceived
%		to have been born at a turning point in history.
%	}

verses.original: לֹא יִהְיֶ͏ה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָ͏ַי׃
verses.english: You shall not have other gods before my face.

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא יִהְיֶ͏ה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָ͏ַי׃}
tex.english: \eOther{You shall not have other gods before my face.}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		You shall not have other gods. Various groups have
%		counted the Ten
%		Commandments differently because of the matter of the
%		historical
%		prologue. Some identify the first commandment as “I am
%		YHWH, your God,
%		who brought you out from the land of Egypt, from a house
%		of slaves.”
%		Others list “You shall have no other gods before me” as
%		the first
%		commandment. The evidence from the Near Eastern treaties
%		indicates that
%		the latter way is correct. The first line is not a
%		commandment. It is
%		the historical prologue. (See the comment on 20:2.)
%		Footnote 20:3.
%		before my face. Hebrew ‘al pny has no good English
%		equivalent. The point
%		is that everywhere is ‘al pny, i.e., before God’s face,
%		so the
%		commandment means that one simply cannot have any other
%		gods. Monotheism
%		has become so successful in Western civilization and
%		much of Eastern
%		civilization that it is difficult now for us to
%		recapture the original
%		force of this commandment. The profound has become the
%		norm, so people
%		forget that it is profound. Some argue that the wording
%		of the first
%		commandment is not properly monotheistic. They say the
%		commandment “You
%		shall not have other gods before my face (or: in my
%		presence, or: before
%		me)” suggests a recognition that other gods exist. They
%		therefore argue
%		that the commandment only prohibits the worship of other
%		deities but
%		does not deny their reality. This appears to be a
%		too-careful reading of
%		these words. The fact is that it is difficult to word a
%		command of
%		monotheism without referring to other deities. This is
%		simply a fact of
%		language. (I frequently suggest to my students that they
%		try to compose
%		a number of formulations of a command of monotheism, and
%		we regularly
%		find that a substantial number of the possible
%		formulations will contain
%		reference to other gods.) Those who hold the view that
%		monotheism came
%		late in Israel cannot build a case on the wording of the
%		first
%		commandment. The issue here is linguistic, not
%		theological.
%	}

verses.original: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל וְכל תְּמוּנָה אֲשֶׁר בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וַאֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ מִתָּ͏ַחַת וַאֲשֶׁר בַּמַּיִם מִתַּחַת לָאָרֶץ׃
verses.english: You shall not make a statue or any form that is in the skies above or that is in the earth below or that is in the water below the earth.

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל וְכל תְּמוּנָה אֲשֶׁר בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וַאֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ מִתָּ͏ַחַת וַאֲשֶׁר בַּמַּיִם מִתַּחַת לָאָרֶץ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		statue. Pagan religion in the ancient Near East, as in
%		Greece, was not
%		idol worship. The statues of the gods and goddesses were
%		icons, symbols
%		that represented the deities’ presence. They provided a
%		direction for
%		prayer, a feeling of awe, a sense of one’s god’s
%		closeness. But pagans
%		did not believe that the statue was the god. The god was
%		a force, known
%		through its particular power in the universe: sky,
%		earth, sun, wind,
%		grain, fertility. So, if the statues were not themselves
%		worshiped, why
%		are Israelites forbidden to have them? One reason may be
%		that they were
%		inconsistent with monotheism: If Israel was not
%		permitted to have other
%		gods, of course they could not have statues of them. And
%		the issue then
%		was not making statues of the pagan gods but making
%		statues of YHWH. In
%		the first place, YHWH was not to be identified with any
%		single force in
%		nature. Likewise, a statue would limit what YHWH was,
%		identifying God
%		with something visible in this world. Moreover, multiple
%		statues of YHWH
%		in multiple places would not be felt to be consistent
%		with God’s
%		oneness. In the Torah, only one Temple is permitted,
%		only one
%		sacrificial altar. Sacrifice to YHWH is not permitted
%		anywhere else on
%		earth (Leviticus 17; Deuteronomy 12). Confirmation of
%		the fact that the
%		issue is making statues of YHWH comes from
%		archaeological evidence:
%		small figures of females are extremely common finds, but
%		in all the
%		excavations in Israel so far only two male figures have
%		ever been found.
%		(And one of them, which my friend Yigal Shiloh uncovered
%		in the City of
%		David excavations of biblical Jerusalem, was clearly not
%		Israelite.)
%		That is, female figures often escaped the ban on
%		statues, but male
%		figures did not—not because they were Baal or Dagon
%		figures, but because
%		they could be YHWH.
%	}

verses.original: לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לָהֶם וְלֹא תעבְדֵם כִּי אָנֹכִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵל קַנָּא פֹּקֵד עֲוֺן אָבֹת עַל בָּנִים עַל שִׁלֵּשִׁים וְעַל רִבֵּעִים לְשֹׂנְאָי׃
verses.english: You shall not bow to them, and you shall not serve them. Because I, YHWH, your God, am a jealous God, counting parents’ crime on children, on the third generation, and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לָהֶם וְלֹא תעבְדֵם כִּי אָנֹכִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵל קַנָּא פֹּקֵד עֲוֺן אָבֹת עַל בָּנִים עַל שִׁלֵּשִׁים וְעַל רִבֵּעִים לְשֹׂנְאָי׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		a jealous God. What could it mean for a god to be
%		jealous? A pagan deity
%		might be thought to be jealous of another deity’s powers
%		or possessions
%		but would not be jealous of another god’s existence.
%		Jealousy is a
%		profoundly monotheistic quality in a god. The God of
%		Israel does not
%		tolerate making a statue of another god, bowing to
%		another god, or
%		serving another god, of any form.
%	}

verses.original: וְעֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד לַאֲלָפִים לְאֹהֲבַי וּלְשֹׁמְרֵי מִצְוֺתָי׃
verses.english: but practicing kindness to thousands for those who love me and for those who observe my commandments.

tex.original: \hOther{וְעֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד לַאֲלָפִים לְאֹהֲבַי וּלְשֹׁמְרֵי מִצְוֺתָי׃}

verses.original: לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת שֵׁם יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה יְהֹוָה אֵת אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׂא אֶת שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא׃
verses.english: You shall not bring up the name of YHWH, your God, for a falsehood, because YHWH will not make one innocent who will bring up His name for a falsehood.

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת שֵׁם יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה יְהֹוָה אֵת אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׂא אֶת שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		bring up His name for a falsehood. (Traditionally
%		translated “take His
%		name in vain.”) This does not mean that one cannot say
%		the divine name
%		in an exclamation—much less does it mean saying the
%		words “God” or
%		“Lord” in an exclamation. It refers to falsehood. The
%		term refers to a
%		false report (Exod 23:1) and a false witness (Deut 5:17;
%		which
%		corresponds to the term “lying witness” here in Exod
%		20:13). This
%		commandment means that one cannot make an oath in God’s
%		name and not
%		fulfill it. To appreciate the seriousness of this
%		commandment, note the
%		case of Joshua, who is deceived by the Gibeonites into
%		making an oath of
%		nonaggression. When Joshua learns that the Gibeonites
%		are among the
%		Canaanite residents whom he was commanded by God to
%		destroy, he lets
%		them live, disobeying a direct command from God rather
%		than violate one
%		of the Ten Commandments (Joshua 9). And note the case of
%		Jephthah, who
%		makes an oath to sacrifice the first thing to come out
%		of his gate,
%		which turns out to be his daughter. He sacrifices her
%		rather than
%		violate this commandment (Judges 11). (It is not
%		reckoned legally as
%		murder. Human sacrifice is forbidden, but it is legally
%		distinguished
%		from murder, which involves malice.) As horrible as this
%		is (especially
%		in light of the Aqedah), it conveys the seriousness of
%		this commandment
%		and of the principle that the Ten Commandments outweigh
%		other laws.
%	}

verses.original: זָכוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ׃
verses.english: Remember the Sabbath day, to make it holy.

tex.original: \hOther{זָכוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ׃}
tex.english: \eOther{Remember the Sabbath day, to make it holy.}

verses.original: שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים תַּעֲבֹד וְעָשִׂיתָ כּל מְלַאכְתֶּךָ׃
verses.english: Six days you shall labor and do all your work,

tex.original: \hOther{שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים תַּעֲבֹד וְעָשִׂיתָ כּל מְלַאכְתֶּךָ׃}
tex.english: \eOther{Six days you shall labor and do all your work,}

verses.original: וְיוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי שַׁבָּת לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כל מְלָאכָה אַתָּה וּבִנְךָ͏ וּבִתֶּךָ עַבְדְּךָ וַאֲמָתְךָ וּבְהֶמְתֶּךָ וְגֵרְךָ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ׃
verses.english: and the seventh day is a Sabbath to YHWH, your God. You shall not do any work: you and your son and your daughter, your servant and your maid and your animal and your alien who is in your gates.

tex.original: \hOther{וְיוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי שַׁבָּת לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כל מְלָאכָה אַתָּה וּבִנְךָ͏ וּבִתֶּךָ עַבְדְּךָ וַאֲמָתְךָ וּבְהֶמְתֶּךָ וְגֵרְךָ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ׃}

verses.original: כִּי שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת הָאָרֶץ אֶת הַיָּם וְאֶת כּל אֲשֶׁר בָּם וַיָּנַח בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי עַל כֵּן בֵּרַךְ יְהֹוָה אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת וַיְקַדְּשֵׁהוּ׃
verses.english: Because for six days YHWH made the skies and the earth, the sea, and everything that is in them, and He rested on the seventh day. On account of this, YHWH blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

tex.original: \hR{כִּי שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים עָשָׂה יְהֹוָה אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת הָאָרֶץ אֶת הַיָּם וְאֶת כּל אֲשֶׁר בָּם וַיָּנַח בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי עַל כֵּן בֵּרַךְ יְהֹוָה אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת וַיְקַדְּשֵׁהוּ׃}

verses.original: כַּבֵּד אֶת אָבִיךָ וְאֶת אִמֶּךָ לְמַעַן יַאֲרִכוּן יָמֶיךָ עַל הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ נֹתֵן לָךְ׃
verses.english: Honor your father and your mother, so that your days will be extended on the land that YHWH, your God, is giving you.

tex.original: \hOther{כַּבֵּד אֶת אָבִיךָ וְאֶת אִמֶּךָ לְמַעַן יַאֲרִכוּן יָמֶיךָ עַל הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ נֹתֵן לָךְ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		your days will be extended on the land. My father taught
%		me that the
%		commandment to honor one’s parents is the only
%		commandment that offers a
%		reward. People have sometimes understood these words to
%		mean that the
%		reward is that if one honors one’s parents one will have
%		a long life.
%		That is not a correct understanding. The commandment
%		speaks of duration
%		of days on the land. It means that if the people of
%		Israel is composed
%		of individuals who honor their parents then they will
%		endure in their
%		land. This suggests the enormous importance of the fifth
%		commandment
%		relative to the other nine. Those who honor their
%		parents are likely to
%		be people who will not murder, steal, or violate the
%		other commandments.
%		In thus preserving the terms of the covenant, they would
%		be deserving of
%		the covenant promise of the homeland. At the same time,
%		this is a
%		commandment on the father and mother as well: to be
%		worthy of honor, and
%		to convey the value of the commandments themselves in
%		such a way that
%		their children, in honoring the parents, will be moved
%		to keep the
%		commandments. This pivotal importance of the commandment
%		to honor one’s
%		parents may account for its position in the order of the
%		commandments:
%		The first four commandments concern the relationship
%		between humans and
%		God. The last five concern the relationship between
%		humans and other
%		humans. And the commandment that comes between—and
%		connects?—these two
%		groups is: Honor your father and your mother!
%	}

verses.original: לֹא תִּרְצָ͏ח׃ ס לֹא תִּנְאָ͏ף׃ ס לֹא תִּגְנֹב׃ ס לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר׃
verses.english: You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not testify against your neighbor as a lying witness.

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא תִּרְצָ͏ח׃ {ס} לֹא תִּנְאָ͏ף׃ {ס} לֹא תִּגְנֹב׃ {ס} לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		murder. Hebrew, like English, distinguishes between
%		“murder” and
%		“killing.” “Murder” refers only to the taking of human
%		life, and it is
%		subject to the death penalty only when committed with
%		malicious intent.
%		The cases of manslaughter, killing through negligence,
%		killing in war,
%		execution for crimes, killing animals, animals killing
%		humans, and human
%		sacrifice are all treated separately from this in the
%		Torah, and terms
%		other than “murder” are used. (On the special
%		circumstance of the one
%		who murders without malice, see Deut 4:41–42.) At the
%		time that I am
%		writing this, technology has raised new cases, including
%		abortion and
%		assisted suicide. Whatever one’s view of these matters,
%		one cannot
%		simply claim that they are prohibited by the commandment
%		against murder.
%		One must argue whether they are consistent with the
%		other cases that
%		constitute murder or if they belong among the cases that
%		involve taking
%		life but still are not murder. Footnote 20:13. adultery.
%		It is commonly
%		said that adultery in the Torah is defined as sex
%		between a man and a
%		married woman—but not between a single woman and a
%		married man. The
%		reason for this definition is that ancient Israel was
%		polygamous, and it
%		was acceptable for a man to have several wives or
%		concubines (as long as
%		none of them was married to another man). But now, for
%		those who live in
%		monogamous societies, the issue for either spouse is the
%		same: violation
%		of their marriage commitment to each other. Sex with
%		someone other than
%		one’s spouse is equally prohibited for husbands and
%		wives by this
%		commandment. Footnote 20:13. neighbor. See the
%		explanation of this term
%		on Lev 19:18. Footnote 20:13. lying witness. Is false
%		testimony not
%		already forbidden by the command against taking God’s
%		name in vain by
%		lying in an oath sworn to God? This question assumes
%		that testimony in
%		court was in fact taken under oath in biblical times.
%		But: (1) The Torah
%		does not say that oaths are required—except for the case
%		of the
%		suspected adulteress in Numbers 5. (2) The case of the
%		suspected
%		adulteress may well be the exception that proves that
%		the rule was not
%		to take oaths. (3) The inclusion in the Decalogue of
%		this commandment
%		against being a false witness appears to me to be itself
%		the evidence
%		that testimony was not taken under oath, because, if it
%		were, this
%		commandment would indeed be unnecessary.
%	}

verses.original: לֹא תַחְמֹד בֵּית רֵעֶךָ ס לֹא תַחְמֹד אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ וְעַבְדּוֹ וַאֲמָתוֹ וְשׁוֹרוֹ וַחֲמֹרוֹ וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר לְרֵעֶךָ׃
verses.english: You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife or his servant or his maid or his ox or his ass or anything that your neighbor has.

tex.original: \hOther{לֹא תַחְמֹד בֵּית רֵעֶךָ {ס} לֹא תַחְמֹד אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ וְעַבְדּוֹ וַאֲמָתוֹ וְשׁוֹרוֹ וַחֲמֹרוֹ וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר לְרֵעֶךָ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		covet. This comes at the end of the Ten Commandments,
%		and it is
%		different: it commands regarding an emotional state.
%		This seems like an
%		extra burden, but it comes as a help. It is saying: Do
%		you want some
%		help to avoid breaking the other commandments? Very
%		well, don’t covet!
%	}

verses.original: וְכל הָעָם רֹאִים אֶת הַקּוֹלֹת וְאֶת הַלַּפִּידִם וְאֵת קוֹל הַשֹּׁפָר וְאֶת הָהָר עָשֵׁן וַיַּרְא הָעָם וַיָּנֻעוּ וַיַּעַמְדוּ מֵרָחֹק׃
verses.english: And all the people were seeing the thunders and the flashes and the sound of the horn and the mountain smoking. And the people saw, and they moved and stood at a distance,

tex.original: \hE{וְכל הָעָם רֹאִים אֶת הַקּוֹלֹת וְאֶת הַלַּפִּידִם וְאֵת קוֹל הַשֹּׁפָר וְאֶת הָהָר עָשֵׁן וַיַּרְא הָעָם וַיָּנֻעוּ וַיַּעַמְדוּ מֵרָחֹק׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		the people saw. The Masoretic Text reads “saw,” but the
%		Greek,
%		Samaritan, and other versions of the text read “were
%		afraid.” The
%		consonants of the Hebrew words for “saw” and for “were
%		afraid” are the
%		same (). “Were afraid” is probably correct, because
%		Moses tells the
%		people, “Don’t be afraid,” two verses later. This
%		technical point of
%		Hebrew consonants is important because it establishes
%		the people’s state
%		of mind: hearing the voice of God terrifies them, and
%		that is why they
%		tell Moses, “Let God not speak with us or else we’ll
%		die.”
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל מֹשֶׁה דַּבֵּר אַתָּה עִמָּנוּ וְנִשְׁמָעָה וְאַל יְדַבֵּר עִמָּנוּ אֱלֹהִים פֶּן נָמוּת׃
verses.english: and they said to Moses, “You speak with us so we may listen, but let God not speak with us or else we’ll die.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֶל מֹשֶׁה דַּבֵּר אַתָּה עִמָּנוּ וְנִשְׁמָעָה וְאַל יְדַבֵּר עִמָּנוּ אֱלֹהִים פֶּן נָמוּת׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		You speak with us. The absence of prophecy in Genesis—in
%		the way that it
%		is usually meant in the rest of the Hebrew Bible—is not
%		extraordinary,
%		for prophecy by its very essence relates to a community;
%		and Genesis, as
%		we have already observed, is primarily about
%		individuals, not
%		communities. The birth of prophecy in Exodus is related
%		to the birth of
%		the Israelite community in this book. In Exodus, YHWH
%		initially sends
%		Moses with His words to the Israelites and to the
%		Egyptians. That is
%		already a straightforward depiction of prophecy, but,
%		more crucially,
%		the book proceeds to formalize the prophetic role. When
%		the Israelites
%		come to Sinai, YHWH personally speaks directly to the
%		entire nation,
%		pronouncing the Ten Commandments aloud from the sky. The
%		Israelites’
%		response here is to tell Moses: “You speak with us so we
%		may listen, but
%		let God not speak with us or else we’ll die.” From this
%		moment on, all
%		revelation to Israel is mediated by a prophet. God never
%		speaks directly
%		to the people again in any book of the Tanak.
%	}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעָם אַל תִּירָאוּ כִּי לְבַעֲבוּר נַסּוֹת אֶתְכֶם בָּא הָאֱלֹהִים וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ׃
verses.english: And Moses said to the people, “Don’t be afraid, because God is coming for the purpose of testing you and for the purpose that his fear will be on your faces so that you won’t sin.”

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעָם אַל תִּירָאוּ כִּי לְבַעֲבוּר נַסּוֹת אֶתְכֶם בָּא הָאֱלֹהִים וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ׃}

verses.original: וַיַּעֲמֹד הָעָם מֵרָחֹק וּמֹשֶׁה נִגַּשׁ אֶל הָעֲרָפֶל אֲשֶׁר שָׁם הָאֱלֹהִים׃
verses.english: And the people stood at a distance, and Moses went over to the nimbus where God was.

tex.original: \hE{וַיַּעֲמֹד הָעָם מֵרָחֹק וּמֹשֶׁה נִגַּשׁ אֶל הָעֲרָפֶל אֲשֶׁר שָׁם הָאֱלֹהִים׃}

verses.original: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה כֹּה תֹאמַר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אַתֶּם רְאִיתֶם כִּי מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם דִּבַּרְתִּי עִמָּכֶם׃
verses.english: And YHWH said to Moses, “You shall say this to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken with you from the skies.

tex.original: \hE{וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה כֹּה תֹאמַר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אַתֶּם רְאִיתֶם כִּי מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם דִּבַּרְתִּי עִמָּכֶם׃}

verses.original: לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן אִתִּי אֱלֹהֵי כֶסֶף וֵאלֹהֵי זָהָב לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ לָכֶם׃
verses.english: You shall not make gods of silver with me, and you shall not make gods of gold for yourselves.

tex.original: \hE{לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן אִתִּי אֱלֹהֵי כֶסֶף וֵאלֹהֵי זָהָב לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ לָכֶם׃}

verses.original: מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה תַּעֲשֶׂה לִּי וְזָבַחְתָּ עָלָיו אֶת עֹלֹתֶיךָ וְאֶת שְׁלָמֶיךָ אֶת צֹאנְךָ וְאֶת בְּקָרֶךָ בְּכל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבוֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ׃
verses.english: You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I’ll have my name commemorated I’ll come to you, and I’ll bless you.

tex.original: \hE{מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה תַּעֲשֶׂה לִּי וְזָבַחְתָּ עָלָיו אֶת עֹלֹתֶיךָ וְאֶת שְׁלָמֶיךָ אֶת צֹאנְךָ וְאֶת בְּקָרֶךָ בְּכל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבוֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall
		sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace
		offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where
		I’ll have my name commemorated I’ll come to you, and I’ll
		bless you.
	}

verses.original: וְאִם מִזְבַּח אֲבָנִים תַּעֲשֶׂה לִּי לֹא תִבְנֶה אֶתְהֶן גָּזִית כִּי חַרְבְּךָ הֵנַפְתָּ עָלֶיהָ וַתְּחַלְלֶהָ׃
verses.english: And if you’ll make an altar of stones for me, you shall not make them cut. When you have elevated your sword over it, then you have desecrated it.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם מִזְבַּח אֲבָנִים תַּעֲשֶׂה לִּי לֹא תִבְנֶה אֶתְהֶן גָּזִית כִּי חַרְבְּךָ הֵנַפְתָּ עָלֶיהָ וַתְּחַלְלֶהָ׃}

verses.original: וְלֹא תַעֲלֶה בְמַעֲלֹת עַל מִזְבְּחִי אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִגָּלֶה עֶרְוָתְךָ עָלָיו׃
verses.english: And you shall not go up by stairs on my altar, so that your nudity will not be exposed over it.”

tex.original: \hE{וְלֹא תַעֲלֶה בְמַעֲלֹת עַל מִזְבְּחִי אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִגָּלֶה עֶרְוָתְךָ עָלָיו׃}

verses.original: וְאֵלֶּה הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תָּשִׂים לִפְנֵיהֶם׃
verses.english: “And these are the judgments that you shall set before them:

tex.original: \hE{וְאֵלֶּה הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תָּשִׂים לִפְנֵיהֶם׃}

verses.original: כִּי תִקְנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד וּבַשְּׁבִעִת יֵצֵא לַחפְשִׁי חִנָּם׃
verses.english: “When you will buy a Hebrew slave, he shall work six years, and in the seventh he shall go out liberated for free.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי תִקְנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד וּבַשְּׁבִעִת יֵצֵא לַחפְשִׁי חִנָּם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		Hebrew slave. In biblical narrative the term “Hebrew” is
%		used to
%		identify Israelites only when speaking among foreigners.
%		It is not the
%		standard term for the people, which is rather
%		“Israelite” at first, and
%		“Jew” later. Its use here in biblical law, where we
%		would have expected
%		“Israelite slave,” probably occurs because this had
%		become a fixed
%		phrase through assonance: the two words, “slave” (,
%		‘ebed) and “Hebrew”
%		(, ‘ibrî), begin with the same two letters.
%	}

verses.original: אִם בְּגַפּוֹ יָבֹא בְּגַפּוֹ יֵצֵא אִם בַּעַל אִשָּׁה הוּא וְיָצְאָה אִשְׁתּוֹ עִמּוֹ׃
verses.english: If he will come by himself, he shall go out by himself. If he is a woman’s husband, then his wife shall go out with him.

tex.original: \hE{אִם בְּגַפּוֹ יָבֹא בְּגַפּוֹ יֵצֵא אִם בַּעַל אִשָּׁה הוּא וְיָצְאָה אִשְׁתּוֹ עִמּוֹ׃}

verses.original: אִם אֲדֹנָיו יִתֶּן לוֹ אִשָּׁה וְיָלְדָה לוֹ בָנִים אוֹ בָנוֹת הָאִשָּׁה וִילָדֶיהָ תִּהְיֶה לַאדֹנֶיהָ וְהוּא יֵצֵא בְגַפּוֹ׃
verses.english: If his master will give him a wife, and she will give birth to sons or daughters for him, the wife and her children will be her master’s, and he shall go out by himself.

tex.original: \hE{אִם אֲדֹנָיו יִתֶּן לוֹ אִשָּׁה וְיָלְדָה לוֹ בָנִים אוֹ בָנוֹת הָאִשָּׁה וִילָדֶיהָ תִּהְיֶה לַאדֹנֶיהָ וְהוּא יֵצֵא בְגַפּוֹ׃}

verses.original: וְאִם אָמֹר יֹאמַר הָעֶבֶד אָהַבְתִּי אֶת אֲדֹנִי אֶת אִשְׁתִּי וְאֶת בָּנָי לֹא אֵצֵא חפְשִׁי׃
verses.english: And if the slave will say: ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I won’t go out liberated!’

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם אָמֹר יֹאמַר הָעֶבֶד אָהַבְתִּי אֶת אֲדֹנִי אֶת אִשְׁתִּי וְאֶת בָּנָי לֹא אֵצֵא חפְשִׁי׃}

verses.original: וְהִגִּישׁוֹ אֲדֹנָיו אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וְהִגִּישׁוֹ אֶל הַדֶּלֶת אוֹ אֶל הַמְּזוּזָה וְרָצַע אֲדֹנָיו אֶת אזְנוֹ בַּמַּרְצֵעַ וַעֲבָדוֹ לְעֹלָם׃
verses.english: then his master shall bring him over to God and bring him over to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.

tex.original: \hE{וְהִגִּישׁוֹ אֲדֹנָיו אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וְהִגִּישׁוֹ אֶל הַדֶּלֶת אוֹ אֶל הַמְּזוּזָה וְרָצַע אֲדֹנָיו אֶת אזְנוֹ בַּמַּרְצֵעַ וַעֲבָדוֹ לְעֹלָם׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יִמְכֹּר אִישׁ אֶת בִּתּוֹ לְאָמָה לֹא תֵצֵא כְּצֵאת הָעֲבָדִים׃
verses.english: “And if a man will sell his daughter as a maid, she shall not go out as the slaves go out.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יִמְכֹּר אִישׁ אֶת בִּתּוֹ לְאָמָה לֹא תֵצֵא כְּצֵאת הָעֲבָדִים׃}

verses.original: אִם רָעָה בְּעֵינֵי אֲדֹנֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר [לוֹ] (לא) יְעָדָהּ וְהֶפְדָּהּ לְעַם נכְרִי לֹא יִמְשֹׁל לְמכְרָהּ בְּבִגְדוֹ בָהּ׃
verses.english: If she is bad in the eyes of her master who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall not dominate so as to sell her to a foreign people in his betrayal of her.
verses.commentary: Qere Ketiv.

tex.original: \hE{אִם רָעָה בְּעֵינֵי אֲדֹנֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר [לוֹ] (לא) יְעָדָהּ וְהֶפְדָּהּ לְעַם נכְרִי לֹא יִמְשֹׁל לְמכְרָהּ בְּבִגְדוֹ בָהּ׃}
tex.commentary:
Qere Ketiv.

%	\footnote{
%		He shall not dominate. Recall that part of the curse on
%		woman in Eden
%		was that “he’ll dominate you” (Gen 3:16). But here we
%		are told of a case
%		in which a man is explicitly not free to dominate a
%		woman. Even in that
%		worldview that recognized male control of women, there
%		was an
%		understanding that this control is not unlimited. This
%		point of respect
%		for women and recognition of a legal right that they
%		possessed was a
%		first small step in the breakdown of that worldview. And
%		this passage
%		teaches that a commandment can change or become limited
%		even within the
%		Torah itself.
%	}

verses.original: וְאִם לִבְנוֹ יִיעָדֶנָּה כְּמִשְׁפַּט הַבָּנוֹת יַעֲשֶׂה לָּהּ׃
verses.english: And if he will designate her for his son, he shall treat her according to the manner of daughters.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם לִבְנוֹ יִיעָדֶנָּה כְּמִשְׁפַּט הַבָּנוֹת יַעֲשֶׂה לָּהּ׃}

verses.original: אִם אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע׃
verses.english: If he will take another for himself, he shall not subtract from her food, her apparel, and her hygiene.

tex.original: \hE{אִם אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		hygiene. Shalom Paul has shown parallels from ancient
%		Near Eastern texts
%		that indicate that, beside providing food and clothing,
%		the husband must
%		provide the necessary cosmetics for his wife’s
%		cleanliness and
%		appearance. A second possibility is that the word here,
%		‘nth, is cognate
%		to Hebrew m‘ôn, meaning a dwelling, in which case the
%		text means that
%		the husband provides food, clothing, and shelter. A
%		third possibility is
%		the traditional view that this refers to sex, but there
%		is no evidence
%		in support of this.
%	}

verses.original: וְאִם שְׁלשׁ אֵלֶּה לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה לָהּ וְיָצְאָה חִנָּם אֵין כָּסֶף׃
verses.english: And if he will not do these three for her, then she shall go out free. There is no money.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם שְׁלשׁ אֵלֶּה לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה לָהּ וְיָצְאָה חִנָּם אֵין כָּסֶף׃}

verses.original: מַכֵּה אִישׁ וָמֵת מוֹת יוּמָת׃
verses.english: “One who strikes a man, and he dies, he shall be put to death.

tex.original: \hE{מַכֵּה אִישׁ וָמֵת מוֹת יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: וַאֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה וְהָאֱלֹהִים אִנָּה לְיָדוֹ וְשַׂמְתִּי לְךָ מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יָנוּס שָׁמָּה׃
verses.english: And one who did not scheme, but God conveyed it to his hand, I shall set a place for you, that he shall flee there.

tex.original: \hE{וַאֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה וְהָאֱלֹהִים אִנָּה לְיָדוֹ וְשַׂמְתִּי לְךָ מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יָנוּס שָׁמָּה׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יָזִד אִישׁ עַל רֵעֵהוּ לְהרְגוֹ בְערְמָה מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת׃
verses.english: But if a man will plot against his neighbor, to kill him with treachery, you shall take him from my altar to die.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יָזִד אִישׁ עַל רֵעֵהוּ לְהרְגוֹ בְערְמָה מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		plot. The verb zyd elsewhere refers to cooking (e.g.,
%		Jacob’s cooking
%		the stew in Gen 25:29). Here it refers to someone’s
%		committing murder
%		with intent, rather than manslaughter. (It also refers
%		to the Egyptians’
%		scheme to enslave the Israelites in Exod 18:11.) Like
%		the English
%		expression “to cook up,” the Hebrew word has the range
%		of both cooking
%		and plotting.
%	}

verses.original: וּמַכֵּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃
verses.english: “And one who strikes his father and his mother shall be put to death.

tex.original: \hE{וּמַכֵּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: וְגֹנֵב אִישׁ וּמְכָרוֹ וְנִמְצָא בְיָדוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃
verses.english: “And one who steals a man and has sold him, or he was found in his hand, will be put to death.

tex.original: \hE{וְגֹנֵב אִישׁ וּמְכָרוֹ וְנִמְצָא בְיָדוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃
verses.english: “And one who curses his father and his mother shall be put to death.

tex.original: \hE{וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יְרִיבֻן אֲנָשִׁים וְהִכָּה אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ בְּאֶבֶן אוֹ בְאֶגְרֹף וְלֹא יָמוּת וְנָפַל לְמִשְׁכָּב׃
verses.english: “And if people will quarrel, and a man strikes his neighbor with a stone or with a fist, and he does not die, and he falls to bed,

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יְרִיבֻן אֲנָשִׁים וְהִכָּה אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ בְּאֶבֶן אוֹ בְאֶגְרֹף וְלֹא יָמוּת וְנָפַל לְמִשְׁכָּב׃}

verses.original: אִם יָקוּם וְהִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּחוּץ עַל מִשְׁעַנְתּוֹ וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא׃
verses.english: if he will get up and walk himself outside on his staff, then the one who struck will be innocent. Only he shall compensate for his staying home and shall have him healed.

tex.original: \hE{אִם יָקוּם וְהִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּחוּץ עַל מִשְׁעַנְתּוֹ וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ אֶת עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ אֶת אֲמָתוֹ בַּשֵּׁבֶט וּמֵת תַּחַת יָדוֹ נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם׃
verses.english: “And if a man will strike his slave or his maid with a rod, and he dies by his hand, he shall be avenged.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ אֶת עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ אֶת אֲמָתוֹ בַּשֵּׁבֶט וּמֵת תַּחַת יָדוֹ נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם׃}

verses.original: אַךְ אִם יוֹם אוֹ יוֹמַיִם יַעֲמֹד לֹא יֻקַּם כִּי כַסְפּוֹ הוּא׃
verses.english: Just: if he will stand for a day or two days, he shall not be avenged, because he is his money.

tex.original: \hE{אַךְ אִם יוֹם אוֹ יוֹמַיִם יַעֲמֹד לֹא יֻקַּם כִּי כַסְפּוֹ הוּא׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		stand. If he will not die immediately but will live for
%		a day or two
%		after being struck. Footnote 21:21. he is his money. The
%		slave is the
%		master’s property. This indicates that the master is
%		empowered to strike
%		his slave, but he is not free to be the immediate cause
%		of the slave’s
%		death.
%	}

verses.original: וְכִי יִנָּצוּ אֲנָשִׁים וְנָגְפוּ אִשָּׁה הָרָה וְיָצְאוּ יְלָדֶיהָ וְלֹא יִהְיֶה אָסוֹן עָנוֹשׁ יֵעָנֵשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשִׁית עָלָיו בַּעַל הָאִשָּׁה וְנָתַן בִּפְלִלִים׃
verses.english: “And if people will fight, and they strike a pregnant woman, and her children go out, and there will not be an injury, he shall be penalized according to what the woman’s husband will impose on him, and he will give it by the judges.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יִנָּצוּ אֲנָשִׁים וְנָגְפוּ אִשָּׁה הָרָה וְיָצְאוּ יְלָדֶיהָ וְלֹא יִהְיֶה אָסוֹן עָנוֹשׁ יֵעָנֵשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשִׁית עָלָיו בַּעַל הָאִשָּׁה וְנָתַן בִּפְלִלִים׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		“And if people will fight, and they strike a pregnant
		woman, and her children go out, and there will not be an
		injury, he shall be penalized according to what the
		woman’s husband will impose on him, and he will give it by
		the judges.
	}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		her children go out, and there will not be an injury.
%		This can mean: if
%		the woman has a miscarriage, but there is no other
%		physical damage to
%		the woman herself. Or it can mean: if the woman goes
%		into labor, and the
%		child is born without any physical damage. Scholars
%		generally understand
%		it to be the former. This passage has been cited in
%		debates over
%		abortion. However, the issues in this case are
%		different, and the
%		wording is so complex, and its meaning is so uncertain,
%		that one should
%		be extremely hesitant to use this case for either side
%		of that debate.
%		Footnote 21:22. he will give it by the judges. The
%		meaning is uncertain,
%		but the penalty is determined and enforced in some way
%		involving both
%		the husband and the judges.
%	}

verses.original: וְאִם אָסוֹן יִהְיֶה וְנָתַתָּה נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ׃
verses.english: And if there will be an injury, then you shall give a life for a life,

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם אָסוֹן יִהְיֶה וְנָתַתָּה נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		a life for a life, an eye for an eye …The inclusion of
%		“a burn for a
%		burn” here—in a case in which “burn” has no apparent
%		relevance—indicates
%		that this list comes to apply a fundamental principle to
%		this case.
%		Concerning the eye-for-an-eye principle, see the comment
%		on Lev 24:20.
%	}

verses.original: עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן שֵׁן תַּחַת שֵׁן יָד תַּחַת יָד רֶגֶל תַּחַת רָגֶל׃
verses.english: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot,

tex.original: \hE{עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן שֵׁן תַּחַת שֵׁן יָד תַּחַת יָד רֶגֶל תַּחַת רָגֶל׃}

verses.original: כְּוִיָּה תַּחַת כְּוִיָּה פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע חַבּוּרָה תַּחַת חַבּוּרָה׃
verses.english: a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, a hurt for a hurt.

tex.original: \hE{כְּוִיָּה תַּחַת כְּוִיָּה פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע חַבּוּרָה תַּחַת חַבּוּרָה׃}
tex.english: \eE{a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, a hurt for a hurt.}

verses.original: וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ אֶת עֵין עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ אֶת עֵין אֲמָתוֹ וְשִׁחֲתָהּ לַחפְשִׁי יְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ תַּחַת עֵינוֹ׃
verses.english: “And if a man will strike his slave’s eye or his maid’s eye and destroy it, he shall let him go, liberated, for his eye.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ אֶת עֵין עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ אֶת עֵין אֲמָתוֹ וְשִׁחֲתָהּ לַחפְשִׁי יְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ תַּחַת עֵינוֹ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		liberated, for his eye. Even in a system that allows
%		slavery, a master
%		does not own the slave’s body. The master can require
%		work from a slave,
%		but damaging the slave’s eye or tooth steps over the
%		line, and the
%		master no longer owns the slave. This reminds us also of
%		the Egyptian
%		enslavement of Israel. The Egyptians are not criticized
%		for having
%		slaves, but rather for the way they treat the slaves:
%		“They degraded
%		them…. They made them serve with harshness … they made
%		their lives
%		bitter with hard work …” They killed the male infants.
%		The Torah did not
%		bring about the end of slavery by abolishing it. It
%		established
%		principles regarding slaves’ dignity, rights, and
%		treatment. And these
%		gradually contributed to humans’ own rejection of
%		slavery in much
%		(though not yet all) of the world. This is a crucial
%		point itself: that
%		some of the laws of the Torah command things outright,
%		while others lead
%		humans to grow and change themselves.
%	}

verses.original: וְאִם שֵׁן עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ שֵׁן אֲמָתוֹ יַפִּיל לַחפְשִׁי יְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ תַּחַת שִׁנּוֹ׃
verses.english: And if he will knock out his slave’s tooth or his maid’s tooth, he shall let him go liberated for his tooth.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם שֵׁן עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ שֵׁן אֲמָתוֹ יַפִּיל לַחפְשִׁי יְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ תַּחַת שִׁנּוֹ׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יִגַּח שׁוֹר אֶת אִישׁ אוֹ אֶת אִשָּׁה וָמֵת סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל הַשּׁוֹר וְלֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי׃
verses.english: “And if an ox will gore a man or a woman and they die, the ox shall be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten—and the ox’s owner is innocent.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יִגַּח שׁוֹר אֶת אִישׁ אוֹ אֶת אִשָּׁה וָמֵת סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל הַשּׁוֹר וְלֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי׃}

verses.original: וְאִם שׁוֹר נַגָּח הוּא מִתְּמֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם וְהוּעַד בִּבְעָלָיו וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ וְהֵמִית אִישׁ אוֹ אִשָּׁה הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת׃
verses.english: And if it was a goring ox from the day before yesterday, and it had been so testified to its owner, and he did not watch it, and it killed a man or a woman, the ox will be stoned, and its owner will be put to death as well.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם שׁוֹר נַגָּח הוּא מִתְּמֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם וְהוּעַד בִּבְעָלָיו וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ וְהֵמִית אִישׁ אוֹ אִשָּׁה הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת׃}

verses.original: אִם כֹּפֶר יוּשַׁת עָלָיו וְנָתַן פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר יוּשַׁת עָלָיו׃
verses.english: If a ransom will be set on him, then he shall give everything that will be set on him for the redemption of his life.

tex.original: \hE{אִם כֹּפֶר יוּשַׁת עָלָיו וְנָתַן פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר יוּשַׁת עָלָיו׃}

verses.original: אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הַזֶּה יֵעָשֶׂה לּוֹ׃
verses.english: Whether it will gore a son or it will gore a daughter, according to this judgment shall be done to it.

tex.original: \hE{אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הַזֶּה יֵעָשֶׂה לּוֹ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		a son or … a daughter … a slave or a maid. No
%		distinction is made on the
%		basis of sex; a distinction is made on the basis of
%		class: free versus
%		slave.
%	}

verses.original: אִם עֶבֶד יִגַּח הַשּׁוֹר אוֹ אָמָה כֶּסֶף שְׁלֹשִׁים שְׁקָלִים יִתֵּן לַאדֹנָיו וְהַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל׃
verses.english: If the ox will gore a slave or a maid, he shall pay thirty silver shekels to his owner, and the ox shall be stoned.

tex.original: \hE{אִם עֶבֶד יִגַּח הַשּׁוֹר אוֹ אָמָה כֶּסֶף שְׁלֹשִׁים שְׁקָלִים יִתֵּן לַאדֹנָיו וְהַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יִפְתַּח אִישׁ בּוֹר אוֹ כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בֹּר וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ וְנָפַל שָׁמָּה שּׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר׃
verses.english: “And if a man will open a pit, or if a man will dig a pit, and he will not cover it, and an ox or an ass will fall there,

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יִפְתַּח אִישׁ בּוֹר אוֹ כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בֹּר וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ וְנָפַל שָׁמָּה שּׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר׃}

verses.original: בַּעַל הַבּוֹר יְשַׁלֵּם כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ׃
verses.english: the owner of the pit shall pay; he shall pay back money to its owner, and the dead one will be his.

tex.original: \hE{בַּעַל הַבּוֹר יְשַׁלֵּם כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ׃}

verses.original: וְכִי יִגֹּף שׁוֹר אִישׁ אֶת שׁוֹר רֵעֵהוּ וָמֵת וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן׃
verses.english: And if a man’s ox will strike his neighbor’s ox, and it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and split the money for it, and they shall split the dead one as well.

tex.original: \hE{וְכִי יִגֹּף שׁוֹר אִישׁ אֶת שׁוֹר רֵעֵהוּ וָמֵת וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן׃}

verses.original: אוֹ נוֹדַע כִּי שׁוֹר נַגָּח הוּא מִתְּמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ בְּעָלָיו שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם שׁוֹר תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ׃
verses.english: Or: if it was known that it was a goring ox from the day before yesterday, and its owner did not watch it, he shall pay an ox for the ox, and the dead one shall be his.

tex.original: \hE{אוֹ נוֹדַע כִּי שׁוֹר נַגָּח הוּא מִתְּמוֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ בְּעָלָיו שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם שׁוֹר תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לּוֹ׃}

verses.original: כִּי יִגְנֹב אִישׁ שׁוֹר אוֹ שֶׂה וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה בָקָר יְשַׁלֵּם תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר וְאַרְבַּע צֹאן תַּחַת הַשֶּׂה׃
verses.english: “If a man will steal an ox or a sheep and slaughter it or sell it, he shall pay five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי יִגְנֹב אִישׁ שׁוֹר אוֹ שֶׂה וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה בָקָר יְשַׁלֵּם תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר וְאַרְבַּע צֹאן תַּחַת הַשֶּׂה׃}

verses.original: אִם בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב וְהֻכָּה וָמֵת אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים׃
verses.english: “If the thief will be found while breaking in and will be struck, and he dies, there is no blood for him.

tex.original: \hE{אִם בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב וְהֻכָּה וָמֵת אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		no blood for him. Meaning: there is no bloodguilt for
%		killing him. The
%		person who killed the thief who was in the act of
%		breaking in (at night)
%		cannot be held legally responsible for the death.
%	}

verses.original: אִם זָרְחָה הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ עָלָיו דָּמִים לוֹ שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם אִם אֵין לוֹ וְנִמְכַּר בִּגְנֵבָתוֹ׃
verses.english: If the sun has risen on him there is blood for him. He shall pay. If he does not have it, then he shall be sold for his theft.

tex.original: \hE{אִם זָרְחָה הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ עָלָיו דָּמִים לוֹ שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם אִם אֵין לוֹ וְנִמְכַּר בִּגְנֵבָתוֹ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		22.2. If the sun has risen on him there is blood for
%		him. If the
%		theft was in the daytime—which is less frightening and
%		when escape,
%		help, and witnesses are more possible—then one is
%		legally
%		responsible if one kills the thief.
%
%		Footnote 22:2. He shall pay. If the thief is caught, not
%		killed, he
%		must pay for his theft.
%
%		Footnote 22:2. If he does not have it, then he shall be
%		sold for his
%		theft. If the thief does not have the money to pay for
%		his theft,
%		then he is sold into servitude.
%	}

verses.original: אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא בְיָדוֹ הַגְּנֵבָה מִשּׁוֹר עַד חֲמוֹר עַד שֶׂה חַיִּים שְׁנַיִם יְשַׁלֵּם׃
verses.english: If the theft will be found in his hand—from ox to ass to sheep—alive, he shall pay two.

tex.original: \hE{אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא בְיָדוֹ הַגְּנֵבָה מִשּׁוֹר עַד חֲמוֹר עַד שֶׂה חַיִּים שְׁנַיִם יְשַׁלֵּם׃}

verses.original: כִּי יַבְעֶר אִישׁ שָׂדֶה אוֹ כֶרֶם וְשִׁלַּח אֶת בְּעִירֹה וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם׃
verses.english: “If a man will have a field or a vineyard grazed, and he will let his beast go and graze in another person’s field, he shall pay the best of his field and the best of his vineyard.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי יַבְעֶר אִישׁ שָׂדֶה אוֹ כֶרֶם וְשִׁלַּח אֶת בְּעִירֹה וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם׃}

verses.original: כִּי תֵצֵא אֵשׁ וּמָצְאָה קֹצִים וְנֶאֱכַל גָּדִישׁ אוֹ הַקָּמָה אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם הַמַּבְעִר אֶת הַבְּעֵרָה׃
verses.english: “If fire will break out and find thorns and stacked grain or standing grain or a field is consumed, the one who set the blaze shall pay.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי תֵצֵא אֵשׁ וּמָצְאָה קֹצִים וְנֶאֱכַל גָּדִישׁ אוֹ הַקָּמָה אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם הַמַּבְעִר אֶת הַבְּעֵרָה׃}

verses.original: כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ כֶּסֶף אוֹ כֵלִים לִשְׁמֹר וְגֻנַּב מִבֵּית הָאִישׁ אִם יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב יְשַׁלֵּם שְׁנָיִם׃
verses.english: “If a man will give his neighbor money or items to watch, and it will be stolen from the man’s house, if the thief will be found he shall pay two.

tex.original: \hE{כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ כֶּסֶף אוֹ כֵלִים לִשְׁמֹר וְגֻנַּב מִבֵּית הָאִישׁ אִם יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב יְשַׁלֵּם שְׁנָיִם׃}

verses.original: אִם לֹא יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב וְנִקְרַב בַּעַל הַבַּיִת אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים אִם לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ בִּמְלֶאכֶת רֵעֵהוּ׃
verses.english: If the thief will not be found, then the owner of the house shall be brought near to God: that he has not put out his hand into his neighbor’s property.

tex.original: \hE{אִם לֹא יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב וְנִקְרַב בַּעַל הַבַּיִת אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים אִם לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ בִּמְלֶאכֶת רֵעֵהוּ׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		brought near to God: that he has not put out his hand.
%		The wording
%		(starting with ’im) plus the notice of being brought
%		“near to God”
%		indicate that he is to take an oath that he has not
%		taken the missing
%		property for which he was responsible. The wording
%		occurs again in 22:10
%		with an explicit reference to an oath.
%	}

verses.original: עַל כּל דְּבַר פֶּשַׁע עַל שׁוֹר עַל חֲמוֹר עַל שֶׂה עַל שַׂלְמָה עַל כּל אֲבֵדָה אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר כִּי הוּא זֶה עַד הָאֱלֹהִים יָבֹא דְּבַר שְׁנֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר יַרְשִׁיעֻן אֱלֹהִים יְשַׁלֵּם שְׁנַיִם לְרֵעֵהוּ׃
verses.english: “Over every case of an offense, over an ox, over an ass, over a sheep, over clothing, over every loss about which one will say that ‘This is it,’ the word of the two of them shall come to God. The one whom God will implicate shall pay two to his neighbor.

tex.original: \hE{עַל כּל דְּבַר פֶּשַׁע עַל שׁוֹר עַל חֲמוֹר עַל שֶׂה עַל שַׂלְמָה עַל כּל אֲבֵדָה אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר כִּי הוּא זֶה עַד הָאֱלֹהִים יָבֹא דְּבַר שְׁנֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר יַרְשִׁיעֻן אֱלֹהִים יְשַׁלֵּם שְׁנַיִם לְרֵעֵהוּ׃}
tex.english:
\eE{
		“Over every case of an offense, over an ox, over an ass,
		over a sheep, over clothing, over every loss about which
		one will say that ‘This is it,’ the word of the two of
		them shall come to God. The one whom God will implicate
		shall pay two to his neighbor.
	}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
%		implicate. The verb here is plural. Some therefore take
%		its subject,
%		’lhîm, not to refer to God here and in the preceding
%		verse. (See Rashi
%		and Ibn Ezra.) Rather, it is understood to refer to the
%		judges before
%		whom the case is brought.
%	}

verses.original: כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ חֲמוֹר אוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ שֶׂה וְכל בְּהֵמָה לִשְׁמֹר וּמֵת אוֹ נִשְׁבַּר אוֹ נִשְׁבָּה אֵין רֹאֶה׃
verses.english: “If a man will give an ass or an ox or a sheep or any animal to his neighbor to watch, and it dies or is injured or is seized—no one seeing—

tex.original: \hE{כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ חֲמוֹר אוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ שֶׂה וְכל בְּהֵמָה לִשְׁמֹר וּמֵת אוֹ נִשְׁבַּר אוֹ נִשְׁבָּה אֵין רֹאֶה׃}

verses.original: שְׁבֻעַת יְהֹוָה תִּהְיֶה בֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם אִם לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ בִּמְלֶאכֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְלָקַח בְּעָלָיו וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם׃
verses.english: an oath of YHWH shall be between the two of them: that he has not put out his hand into his neighbor’s property; and its owner shall take it, and he shall not pay.

tex.original: \hE{שְׁבֻעַת יְהֹוָה תִּהְיֶה בֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם אִם לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ בִּמְלֶאכֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְלָקַח בְּעָלָיו וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם׃}

verses.original: וְאִם גָּנֹב יִגָּנֵב מֵעִמּוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם לִבְעָלָיו׃
verses.english: And if it will be stolen from him, he shall pay its owner.

tex.original: \hE{וְאִם גָּנֹב יִגָּנֵב מֵעִמּוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם לִבְעָלָיו׃}
tex.english: \eE{And if it will be stolen from him, he shall pay its owner.}

verses.original: אִם טָרֹף יִטָּרֵף יְבִאֵהוּ עֵד הַטְּרֵפָה לֹא יְשַׁלֵּם׃
verses.english: If it will be torn, he shall bring it in witness; he shall not pay for the torn one.

tex.original: \hE{אִם טָרֹף יִטָּרֵף יְבִאֵהוּ עֵד הַטְּרֵפָה לֹא יְשַׁלֵּם׃}
tex.commentary:
%	\footnote{
